findings.claim: Reducing agent 2 (diPPBS) selectively reduces engineered cysteines without reducing interchain disulfide bonds, as evidenced by the absence of free light- or heavy chains after 8 days incubation.

2-diphenylphosphino benzenesulfonic acid (diPPBS) had no reductive capacity towards interchain disulfide bonds but was able to reduce the (capped) engineered cysteines in the Fab cavity overnight in a robust manner.
The use of diPPBS led to the absence of the scrambled disulfide species in the end product and an overall simplification of the manufacturing process.
Conjugating a linker-drug to sites inside the cavity of the Fab part allows the antibody to shield the hydrophobic character of the linker-drug.
Site-specific ADCs generated by this platform maintain cytotoxic potency in vitro.
Site-specific ADCs show improved efficacy and exposure compared to randomly conjugated ADCs in an in vivo xenograft model.
The selective reducing agent reduces engineered cysteines while leaving interchain disulfides in the oxidized state.
The platform enables the manufacture of site-specific ADCs without introducing impurities associated with the conventional reduction/oxidation procedure.
The in silico docking procedure identified sites that were experimentally shown to be able to shield the hydrophobicity exerted by the conjugated duocarmycin payload.
The resulting ADCs were less hydrophobic and had improved properties over randomly conjugated ones.

A single-step, selective reduction of the engineered cysteines significantly improves the efficiency of the manufacturing process and the quality of the resulting ADCs compared to a two-step reduction/oxidation protocol.

Coupling a hydrophobic moiety to an antibody introduces hydrophobic patches, rendering the ADC more hydrophobic than the parent antibody, leading to negative physicochemical properties and less favorable pharmacological profiles.
The following sites in Fab1 were found suitable for replacement by a cysteine residue: HC-41S, HC-89V, HC-110T, HC-152E, HC-153P, LC-40P, LC-41G, LC-165E and LC-168S.
Conjugation with a hydrophobic payload at the indicated positions does not lead to alterations in binding affinity and in vitro cellular cytotoxicity when compared to a randomly conjugated ADC.
All ADCs were inactive on target-negative cells indicating selective killing of tumor cells mediated by the target.
Having the sulfonyl-group ortho to the phosphine is critical for selective reduction, as meta- and para substitutions do not show selective behavior.
ADCs generated using the selective reduction protocol had a DAR of 1.8 and 1-2% HMW species, similar to the reduction/oxidation protocol, but differed markedly in the amount of half-antibody present.
The selective reduction protocol decreased the number of process steps by eliminating the need for the re-oxidation step using DHAA.
The progress of the reduction of the engineered cysteine using the selective reducing agent can be monitored using RP-HPLC, allowing for simple in-process control measurements.
In silico docking runs placed the linker-duocarmycin inside the cavity naturally present in the Fab part of an IgG antibody.
Conjugation of engineered cysteine sites with the linker-drug resulted in ADCs that were less hydrophobic than the corresponding random DAR2 conjugated species.
The hydrophobic payload is shielded from its surroundings by the Fab cavity, resulting in less overall hydrophobicity of the ADC.
HC-41C is the preferable site for cysteine mutation as it demonstrated a Relative Hydrophobicity (RH) of as low as 0.3.

Binding of the site-directed conjugated ADC to its target antigen was preserved and in vitro cell killing experiments showed these mutants were equally effective in killing cancer cells as their randomly conjugated counterparts.
An exploratory in vivo xenograft model employing target-expressing BT-474 cells showed an improved anti-tumor response for the site-directed conjugated ADC as compared to the randomly conjugated ADC.
The improved anti-tumor response is in line with a two-fold increase in exposure of the site-specific ADC as compared to the random conjugate.

findings.claim: The AI-2 quorum sensing induced heterologous protein expression system components (specifically evolved lsr promoters) were created using error-prone PCR (ePCR).
Promoter variants EP01rec and EP14rec exhibit enhanced protein expression.
The promoter variants EP01rec and EP14rec retained their ability to exhibit the LsrR-mediated QS switching activity.
EP01rec and EP14rec share a mutation (TGTGCAAT → TGTACAAT) located close to the CRPI sequence box, which is hypothesized to be important for increased lsr promoter strength.

Reverting the G→A mutation in the putative CytR-binding site (EP01rec_AG and EP14rec_AG) decreased the ability to grow at high tetracycline concentrations compared to EP01rec and EP14rec, confirming the mutation's pivotal role in increasing promoter strength.
EP01rec and EP14rec resulted in higher GFP fluorescence than their respective controls.
EP01rec$_{\mathrm{AG}}$ and EP14rec$_{\mathrm{AG}}$ achieved GFP expression levels comparable with the wild type $lsr$ promoter.

The single nucleotide found mutated in the putative CytR-binding site sequence (TGTGCAAT $\rightarrow$ TGTACAAT) in the strongest promoter mutants, EP01rec and EP14rec was important for increasing the strength of these promoters.
The gfp transcriptional levels found with the wild type $lsr$ promoter were lower than the levels found with EP01rec$_{\mathrm{AG}}$ and EP14rec$_{\mathrm{AG}}$.
A point mutation in EP01rec and EP14rec located close to the CRPI sequence is associated with the CytR binding site and increased lsr promoter strength.
EP01rec and EP14rec promoters preserved their switching character based on the presence of AI-2.
Demonstrating the full switching character of EP01rec and EP14rec, which are significantly stronger than the wild type, required a single copy number plasmid.
Promoters were selected that provided E. coli with higher tetracycline resistance over the native promoter when placed upstream of the tet(C) gene.
Several mutations were found in the binding sites of QS repressor, LsrR, among the fourteen clones identified.
Site-directed mutagenesis was used to restore all p-IsrR-box sites to the native sequence to maintain LsrR repression while preserving other mutations.
The sequences of the promoter variants suggest regulatory linkage between CytR (CRP repressor) and LsrR.
The evolved promoters improve upon the native system and exhibit advantages over synthetic QS promoters previously reported.
Most mutations in the evolved promoter library were concentrated near or along the 6-bp (AACAAT) and 9-bp (AAGATTAA) sequences of the p-lsrR-box.
Mutations within the p-lsrR-box in 12 of the 14 clones were presumably responsible for increased promoter strength by affecting LsrR repressor binding and promoting leaky expression.
12 out of 14 lsr operon promoter mutants showed increased strength related to mutations near or within the LsrR-binding site.
The p-lsrR-box sequence region is essential to the LsrR-binding site.
Nucleotides in the vicinity of the proposed LsrR-binding site are involved in controlling expression levels under the E. coli promoter.

findings.claim: A version of the Bell inequality which is insensitive to the crosstalk is proposed.
Experimental violation of the Bell inequality in solid-state qubits would be an important step towards practical quantum information processing by solid-state devices.
The authors propose a version of the Bell inequality which is not affected by crosstalk.
The CHSH inequality is a type of the Bell inequality usually used in experiments.
For the singlet state, the maximum Bell inequality violation requires that the detector axes for both qubits lie in the same plane.
When measurement fidelity asymmetry is similar for both qubits (F_1^a > F_0^a and F_1^b > F_0^b), the Bell inequality |S| ≤ 2 is stronger violated for positive S than for negative S.
If measurement fidelity asymmetries are opposite (e.g., F_1^a > F_0^a and F_1^b < F_0^b), it is easier to violate the Bell inequality for negative S.
The threshold for Bell inequality violation on the F_0-F_1 plane is an arc of the ellipse symmetric with respect to the line F_0=F_1 and centered at F_0=F_1=0.5.
The inequality in the symmetric crosstalk case is more restrictive than the original Bell inequality (1).
For fully asymmetric crosstalk, the modified inequality is less restrictive than the original Bell inequality (1).
Slight modification of the CHSH inequality (1) can make it insensitive to the crosstalk.
With this simple modification, the CHSH inequality becomes insensitive to the mechanism of the measurement crosstalk.
In the ideal case, the maximum violation of the Bell inequality (S = ±2√2) can be realized for any maximally entangled state.
For a maximally entangled state with local measurement errors, Bell inequality violation is possible when the fidelities satisfy (F1 + F0)/2 > 0.92.
Symmetric crosstalk does not change the threshold condition for the observation of the Bell inequality violation.
Crosstalk reduces the gap between the classical and quantum bounds, making observation of Bell inequality violation with a finite margin more difficult.
The detrimental effect of crosstalk can be eliminated by using only negative-result outcomes in the CHSH inequality.
Numerical simulations show the possibility of CHSH inequality violation with a significant margin without further improvement of phase qubit technology.
The modified Bell inequality for symmetric crosstalk is $-2 + 4p_{c} \leq \langle s \rangle \leq 2$.
Configurations of the qubit measurement directions in the pseudospin space lying within either horizontal or vertical planes are optimal in certain cases.
Measurement crosstalk affects both the classical inequality and the quantum result.

findings.claim: Tidal interaction can excite the f-mode oscillations of the star in generic eccentric orbits.
Numerical simulations show that most of the energy released in gravitational waves is transferred into f-modes, which are characterized by a wave-function free of nodes along the radial direction.
In barotropic equations of state, all g-modes degenerate to zero frequency.
General relativistic effects are expected to modify the results of oscillation frequencies for the f-mode by not more than 20 per cent.
The values of $\dot{L}$ are negligible with respect to $\dot{L}_{GW}$ and the induced rotation on the NS is also negligibly small.
For $x < 0.07$ the NS is safe from tidal braking.

The energy absorbed by the neutron star is very small compared to the orbital energy at moderate eccentricity values (e ≲ 0.6), hence such absorption will not alter in any significant way the chirping signal.

The energy absorbed by the neutron star sets oscillations that give rise to a time varying quadrupole, which generates gravitational waves with a significantly different pattern than those associated with the decaying orbital motion.
The amount of energy absorbed by the neutron star in a given mode depends on the overlap of the tidal force field with the displacement field of the mode.
The detailed features of the star oscillation bears invaluable information on its equation of state and density.
r-mode and g-modes have lower frequency values than the f-mode, and can therefore be excited at resonance in an elliptical orbit earlier in the inspiral phase.
For large eccentricity e > 0.7 absorption by NS as computed in this approximation is not negligible compared to GW emission.

findings.claim: A distinct optical pathway highlighting the cavity-mediated activation of nanoantennas is key for absorption enhancement.
Absorption dominates the extinction 1-R-T in the AuNS–PCGR hybrid system.

In the AuNS–PCGR hybrid system, the narrowband cavity acts as the “bright” resonance that communicates with the external radiation and mediates the activation of the “dark” broadband antenna resonance, opposite to the Fano interference underlying both EIT and EIA where cavity resonance is the dark mode.
The ultrasharp Lorentzian-lineshaped hybrid resonance is continuously tunable over a broad spectral range by scanning of the incidence angle.
The linewidth of the enhancement can be widely tunable.
The maximum power transferred to the antennas is attained under critical coupling.
The cavity mediates strong absorption enhancement of one order of magnitude, and the sharp resonance is spectrally tunable from visible to near-infrared ranges.
The PCGR-coupled AuNSs produce a large and narrowband absorption enhancement that is tunable across a broad spectral range compared to solitary AuNSs.

The occurrence of absorption enhancement in the hybrid system does not involve manipulation of the retardation phase shift or specific configurations of coupling and loss rates necessary for the EIA regime.
The hybrid resonance presents strong angle dependence derived from the phase matching condition of the PCGR mode, validating the cavity’s role in absorption amplification.
The $10\times$ enhancement of extinction 1-R-T mediated by an on-resonant cavity is in stark contrast to the abrupt suppression of absorption observed in plasmonic nanoantenna–WGM couplings.
The absorption directly calculated from power dissipation in the AuNS dominates the total extinction 1-R-T in the simulated optical properties.

The incidence angle dependent absorption and the average near-field intensity on the AuNS surface share identical evolution trend, as the transition rate for absorption of a photon is proportional to the electric field intensity.
The symbiotic relationship between the antenna and cavity modes departs from Fano interferences, indicating that a different modal interaction mechanism is responsible for cooperative enhancement.
Strong absorption is realized using a few nanoparticles, in contrast to several reported perfect absorbers where dissipation is distributed over an extended surface area.
The delocalized PCGR mode serves as a conduit of energy from the far field to the near field, accumulating strong optical energy to feed the antennas.

The profound reduction of resonance linewidth for cavity-coupled antennas is induced by effective “dilution” of plasmonic dissipation with a large lossless dielectric cavity, prolonging the lifetime of the hybrid mode.
Large absorption amplification is retained and continuously tunable across the 600 – 1000 nm wavelength range, even though the absorption of solitary antennas is weak at extended spectral ranges.
When the antenna frequency equals the cavity frequency, the Fano interference is always destructive.
When the antenna frequency is greater than the cavity frequency, the Fano interference is constructive at lower frequency but destructive at higher frequency.
When the antenna frequency is less than the cavity frequency, the asymmetry is reversed and the interference is constructive at higher frequency but destructive at lower frequency.
The spectrally tunable absorption enhancement of the PCGR–coupled nanoparticle makes it ideally suitable for applications like on-chip photodetectors and spectrometers.
Eq. (3) represents a narrowband absorption peak in the vicinity of the cavity mode, and its Lorentzian lineshape is maintained regardless of resonance frequency detuning.
The frequency shift and linewidth broadening of the hybrid eigenmode induced by nanoparticle coupling predicted by TCMT match exactly with the wellknown Bethe-Schwinger cavity perturbation theory.
As the density of AuNSs rises, the 1-R-T peaks first increase and then decrease, contrary to conventional wisdom that more nanoparticles induce higher absorption.

The cavity can be understood as a matching network for the antenna, as it manipulates the antenna’s radiative damping through mediating the external radiation, and suppresses the antenna’s absorptive damping through mode hybridization.
Larger AuNS density maps to larger total plasmonic–photonic coupling $\mu$, and results in larger absorptive damping rate thus broader resonance linewidths.

The maximum power transferred to the antenna is obtained via critical coupling (or conjugate matching), that is, matching the radiative damping (associated with PCGR $\mathcal{Q}$ -factor) to the absorptive damping (associated with AuNS density).

By using a high- $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Q}}$ cavity, the maximum absorption will be achieved with very few nanoparticles, so that each nanoantenna delivers a very large absorption cross section, enabling ultrastrong light–matter interaction at its hotspots.

Similar building blocks (AuNS and PCGR) can lead to drastically different coupling scenarios depending on the order of mode excitation, and an optical pathway enabling cavity-mediated excitation of an antenna is indispensable for a cooperative interaction.
Strong, spectrally tunable absorption enhancement was demonstrated in AuNSs mediated by a PCGR cavity mode.

The physics underlying cooperative plasmonic–photonic hybridization includes an optical pathway highlighting cavity-mediated excitation of the antenna and a balance between the cavity’s Q-factor and the antennas’ density.
The findings can be generalized to inspire the synergistic integration of different types of cavities and antennas.
A new avenue to sculpting enhanced light–matter interactions with on-demand linewidths, spectral detuning, and enhancement factors was opened up, complementary to the Fano interference framework.

The absorption enhancement is attributed to unique optical pathways where the narrowband cavity resonance channels energy between the external fields and the broadband antenna resonance, in contrast to typical Fano interactions.

findings.claim: B-scan-wise multi-focus averaging method reduces the noise caused by multi-scattering (MS) photons in an in vivo optical coherence tomography image.
The B-scan-wise multi-focus averaging method reduces MS noise even for unanesthetized in vivo measurement.

The multi-focus-averaging (MFA) method uses a cost-effective electrical tunable lens (ETL) to acquire multiple OCT volumes with different defocus positions, which are coherently averaged after computational defocus correction.
The complex-averaged image is referred to as a "B-MFA image".
The final B-MFA image is obtained by averaging the squared intensities of four complex images of the MS-reduced JM cross-section.
The B-MFA method can be applied to standard (i.e., non-polarization-sensitive) OCT.
In the deep regions, the B-MFA and MFA images show particles with higher contrast than the single acquisition and SFA images.

Inside the glass plate region, the B-MFA and MFA images have the lowest noise intensity, whereas the single acquisition and SFA images have the highest and intermediate noise intensities, respectively.
Standard OCT measurement noise has been mitigated in the SFA image because of the complex averaging, while both the measurement noise and MS signal are mitigated in the MFA and B-MFA images.
B-MFA exhibits lower signal intensity but higher contrast than single acquisition and SFA images in en-face views at deep depth.
B-MFA method reduces multiple scattering (MS) signal and improves image contrast.
B-MFA provides the sharpest image among the four methods at all three depth regions, indicated by the smallest information entropy.
B-MFA showed smaller information entropies compared to SFA and MFA, indicating higher image sharpness, with reductions that are not trivial given the small standard deviations.
B-MFA requires phase stability only within a frame.
The lower requirement for phase stability of B-MFA is an important advantage for in vivo measurement because sample motion can cause significant phase error.
B-MFA images exhibit more scattering particles than MFA images at the superficial region scattering layer due to the difference in 1-D and 2-D computational refocusing.
A computational refocusing method less susceptible to phase instability may be adopted for MFA or B-MFA to solve the refocus artifact problem.
In in vivo fish measurements, the MFA image showed lower signal intensity than the B-MFA image.
The SSRE of MFA is smaller than that of B-MFA for the in vivo measurement.
The B-MFA method has an advantage for in vivo imaging over the MFA method.
The B-MFA acquisition of a single cross-section is 6.5 times and 3 times shorter than the heart and respiratory periods of medaka fish, respectively.

findings.claim: Chameleon demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in image captioning tasks.
Chameleon enables an early fusion of different modalities to generate both text and image tokens through the same manner of autoregressive modeling.
Chameleon adds query-key normalization, post-normalization, denominator loss, and a lower learning rate to manage training instability, which incur an efficiency cost.
Chameleon outperforms Llama-2 in text-only tasks.
Chameleon fails to correctly identify the unusual aspect in the query image
Chameleon converts each image to a sequence of discretized tokens and trains over combined text-image token sequences
Chameleon is competitive with models such as Mixtral 8x7B and Gemini-Pro in text-only tasks.
Chameleon performs non-trivial image generation.
Chameleon matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, including Gemini Pro and GPT-4V, according to human judgments on a new long-form mixed-modal generation evaluation.
Chameleon is a family of mixed-modal foundation models capable of generating and reasoning with mixed sequences of arbitrarily interleaved textual and image content.
Chameleon uses a uniform architecture trained from scratch in an end-to-end fashion on an interleaved mixture of all modalities (images, text, and code).

By quantizing images into discrete tokens, Chameleon applies the same transformer architecture to sequences of both image and text tokens without the need for separate image/text encoders or domain-specific decoders.
Chameleon-34B was trained on 5x the number of tokens as Llama-2.
Chameleon-34B achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual question answering and image captioning benchmarks, outperforming Flamingo, IDEFICS and Llava-1.5.
Chameleon maintains competitive performance on text-only benchmarks, matching models like Mixtral 8x7B and Gemini-Pro on commonsense reasoning and reading comprehension tasks.
Chameleon-34B substantially outperforms strong baselines like Gemini-Pro and GPT-4V in human evaluation of mixed-modal long form responses.
Chameleon represents images, in addition to text, as a series of discrete tokens.
A core weakness of the Chameleon tokenizer is in reconstructing images with a large amount of text, which upper bounds the capability of the models for heavy OCR-related tasks.
To stabilize Chameleon-7B by controlling norm growth, it was necessary to introduce dropout after the attention and feed-forward layers, in addition to QK-norm.
Chameleon-34B required an additional re-ordering of the norms to stabilize training.
Chameleon-7B can also be stably trained without dropout when using norm-reordering, but QK-norm is essential in both cases.
For Chameleon-7B it was important to use both dropout and z-loss to achieve stability, while Chameleon-34B only required z-loss.

In the Chameleon inference pipeline, tokens must be inspected at each step (copied from GPU to CPU in a blocking fashion) to guide control flow because the decoding formulation changes depending on whether the model is generating images or text.
Chameleon performs well in Brainstorming, Comparison, and Hypothetical categories, but needs improvement in Identification and Reasoning.
Chameleon performs slightly better on text-only prompts, while Gemini+ and GPT-4V+ are slightly better on mixed-modal prompts.
Chameleon performs similarly to other baselines in many cases, making the relative evaluation challenging.
Compared to Gemini and GPT-4V, Chameleon is very competitive when handling prompts that expect interleaving, mixed-modal responses.
The images generated by Chameleon are usually relevant to the context, making the documents with interleaving text and images very appealing to users.
The APIs of existing multi-modal LLMs provide only textual responses, so it is preferred to compare Chameleon to other native mixed-modal models.
Chameleon-34B outperforms Llama-2 70B on 5/8 commonsense reasoning and reading comprehension tasks.
Chameleon outperforms LLaMa-2 across the board.
Chameleon-34B (2-shot) outperforms Flamingo and IDEFICS (80B, 32-shot) on COCO captioning.
Chameleon-34B (2-shot) matches Flamingo and IDEFICS (80B, 32-shot) on Flickr30k captioning.
Chameleon-34B-SFT outperforms other models on Flickr30k captioning.
Chameleon-34B (2-shot) matches Flamingo and IDEFICS (32-shot) on VQA-v2.
Chameleon-34B-MultiTask approaches the performance of IDEFICS-80B-Instruct and Gemini Pro on VQA-v2.
Chameleon-34B-MultiTask trails Flamingo-80B-FT, GPT-4V, and Gemini Ultra on VQA-v2.
Chameleon is competitive on image captioning and VQA tasks using fewer in-context examples and smaller model sizes.
Chameleon is an end-to-end dense model without any routing components, unlike Gemini which uses separate image decoders.
Chameleon's unified token space allows it to seamlessly reason over and generate interleaved image and text sequences without modality-specific components.

findings.claim: CoNT addresses bottlenecks that prevent contrastive learning from being widely adopted in generation tasks from three aspects: the construction of contrastive examples, the choice of the contrastive loss, and the strategy in decoding.
CoNT achieves new state-of-the-art on summarization, code comment generation (without external data) and data-to-text generation.
CoNT samples contrastive examples from its own predictions (e.g., through beam search algorithm) to alleviate the exposure bias problem.
CoNT uses a N-pairs contrastive loss which gives a fine-grained treatment to contrastive examples based on their sequence-level scores (e.g., BLEU).
CoNT directly incorporates the learned sequence similarity score from the distance function into the inference stage to find a better global configuration.
CoNT greatly improves conventional MLE baselines and significantly outperforms all previous contrastive generation models.
CoNT establishes new state-of-the-art results on summarization, code comment generation (without external data), and data-to-text generation.

On data-to-text generation and commonsense generation, CoNT achieves on-par performance with T5-large and T5-3B using only the base version of T5 while maintaining the efficiency of lightweight models.
Self-generated contrastive examples alleviate the model's exposure bias.
The approach creates high-quality hard negative examples that is known to be important in contrastive learning.
The inference objective in CoNT can be generalized to other contrastive learning methods as long as the vector representations for source and target sequence pair exist.
The design of CoNT can better make use of the learned similarity function compared to generalization to other contrastive learning methods.
CoNT is able to substantially improve the MLE baseline and clearly outperform all previous contrastive baselines by a large margin on WMT'16 Ro-En and XSum.
CoNT built on PEGASUS-large and CodeT5-base achieves new SOTA on summarization and code comment generation respectively.
CoNT shows superior performance over strong MLE baselines on data-to-text generation and commonsense generation.
The N-pairs contrasting samples generally works better than dividing all samples into predefined positive-negative categories.
CoNT is able to greatly outperform the large version of T5 even built on a T5-base model on Totto.
CoNT surpasses the large version of T5 in terms of CIDEr and SPICE metrics on CommonGen.
CoNT outperforms all baseline systems according to the average ranking in human evaluation.
N-pairs contrastive loss consistently outperforms InfoNCE
With $\alpha \in [0.3, 0.7]$, N-pairs contrastive loss can benefit target-source representation similarity, a sequence-level score in inference process, while InfoNCE cannot
Contrastive learning with self-generated hypotheses is more effective than using batch samples
CoNT focuses on sequence-level contrastive examples
CONT models an additional contrastive learning objective to provide a sequence-level supervision for auto-regressive neural text generation models.
CONT clearly beats all previous contrastive generation models and boosts the performance of state-of-the-art large models to a new level.
CONT practically does not have a negative impact on decoding speed.
The total training time of CONT is about 2~4 times more than that of a MLE based model.
Speeding up the training stage without losing accuracy is the next important step to improve CONT.
Totally using self-generated samples will double the training speed of the naive contrastive text generation method and will do not further boost the improvement in performance.
Increasing the number of contrastive samples will continuously boost the performance.
Opening the dropout module in the decoder during inference helps the performance for CoNT on WMT'14 En-De.
Using lexical matching metrics such as BLEU or ROUGE on CPU slows down training speed and decreases GPU utilization to 0.
Reducing the rate of self-generated samples to 50% results in 1.0 BLEU superior to the baseline while saving about 1.0 GPU seconds per iteration compared with totally using self-generated samples.
Early stop after 10k steps is enough to improve the MLE baseline by 0.8 BLEU but saving 3/4 training time.

findings.claim: The DDG-based PST method allows obtaining 3D local axis orientation in the Stokes space with only one single input polarization state, simplifying the imaging system setup and mitigating motion artifact.
The DDG-based PST method can reconstruct myocardial fiber orientations, specifically a typical helical-like myocardial fiber structure in the superficial tissue of the whole mouse heart.
The depth-resolved ability of the DDG-based PST method detected physiologic change deep within the cardiac wall.
Collagen organization of the skin can be extracted from living tissue using the DDG-based PST method.
The DDG-based PST method has the potential to guide skin incision placement by visualizing patient-specific RSTLs in vivo.
The DDG-based PST method can be used to extract depth-resolved collagen organization using the single input PSOCT system.
The current treatment of the DDG-based PST method neglects the dichroism (anisotropic scattering attenuation) of the sample.

Based on the PSOCT-based polarization state transmission model, the local axis orientation and local phase retardation can be derived using a DDG-based PST method combined with a set of 3D rotation using only one single polarization state.
The PSOCT based polarization state transmission model reveals the depth-dependent polarization state evolution of light backscattered within a birefringent sample
The proposed polarization state tracing method relies on a discrete differential geometric analysis of the evolution of the polarization state in depth along the Poincare sphere
The method can visualize depth-resolved myocardial architecture in healthy and infarcted rodent hearts (ex vivo)
The method can visualize collagen structures responsible for skin tension lines at various anatomical locations on the face of a healthy human volunteer (in vivo)
The measured optic axis maps agreed with expected values, demonstrating the validity of the proposed method to derive depth-resolved relative optic axis orientation.
Linear gradient changes in the fiber orientation angle along depth were detected in the healthy heart, consistent with prior histology studies.
In the infarcted tissue, collagen fiber disorder begins around 300 μm from the outer wall, where a linear gradient change in fiber orientation is no longer observed.
The preferential direction of the collagen fibers is consistent with the general directions of RSTLs.
The collagen orientation of glabella is orthogonal to the direction of traditional RSTLs.
In the papillary layer (~105 μm), collagen fibers form a loosened mesh with an alignment matched with the RSTLs.
In the reticular layer (~175 μm and 245 μm), multiple arrays of collagen fibers with different orientations form a tight meshwork.
The polarization state image can visualize the birefringent component embedded within the tissue with high contrast.
The DDG-based PST approach enables depth-resolved birefringent imaging that only requires one single input polarization state.

The DDG-based PST approach improves measurement accuracy by determining the local axis orientation in 3D Stokes space compared to previous work using a single input polarization state in the 2D QU-plane.

The DDG-based PST approach removes the requirement of known polarization states incident on the sample without introducing additional polarization modulation schemes, unlike methods using two input polarization states.
A transition between layers with distinct optic axes results in a false binormal vector at the transition position, which is an integrated result from both layers and can propagate error.
The 22 μm lateral resolution may not be sufficient for detecting minute changes in collagen organization.
It is difficult to observe the dynamics of the myocardial fibers of the whole heart during heart beating because there is a time delay induced by the point scanning protocol.
The differential geometry method alone can only determine the optic axis in a homogeneous sample rather than an inhomogeneous sample with varying optic axes.
In a homogeneous sample where layers share the same optic axis, the binormal vector is equal to the optic axis.

findings.claim: DENIS is a portable digital nanoparticle-enhanced plasmonic imager for rapid detection of inflammatory biomarkers.
The bioassay performed by DENIS is in a single step without signal amplification or washing procedures.
DENIS enables highly sensitive, quantitative and robust detection of PCT and CRP biomarkers.
DENIS enables ultrahigh detection sensitivities with limit of detection (LOD) down to 21 and 36 pg mL^-1 for PCT and CRP, respectively, and a wide dynamic range of at least three orders of magnitude.
PCT detection with DENIS shows performance equivalent to gold standard clinical assays in noninfectious SIRS and sepsis patients.
DENIS can perform rapid detection by recording video of the plasmonic sensor and analyzing the signals in real time.
The DENIS detection mechanism is based on a large-area Au-NHA device supporting SPR and localized surface plasmon modes.
DENIS achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 21 pg/mL for PCT and 36 pg/mL for CRP.
The PCT detection dynamic range of DENIS is three orders of magnitude, from approximately 21 to >1E4 pg/mL.
The sensitivity and dynamic range enabled by DENIS are similar to the performance of gold standard lab techniques.
DENIS does not require time-consuming amplification and washing steps or bulky readout equipment.
DENIS device is suitable for on-site operation due to portability, inexpensive off-the-shelf optical components, and lack of moving parts or complex microfluidic elements prone to clogging.
DENIS sensor chips and bioassay reagents can be stored in the fridge stably over weeks and do not require fluorescent tags, unlike previously reported optical detection schemes.

DENIS was validated with measurements of PCT and CRP biomarkers from sera of 34 individuals, including 18 sepsis patients, 11 noninfectious SIRS patients, and 5 healthy controls, providing consistent and robust performance at the level of gold-standard immunoassays.

In the sampled group, DENIS measurements of PCT levels showed performance equivalent to clinically validated assay in assisting classification between sepsis and noninfectious SIRS patients, with 94.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity.
DENIS enables rapid detection of PCT and CRP in blood serum using a nanoplasmonic mechanism involving single Au-NPs binding on Au-NHAs.
The DENIS device weighs less than 1 kg and is built of inexpensive components.
DENIS provides equivalent performance to gold-standard laboratory assays when deployed in hospital settings with samples from sepsis, SIRS, and healthy donors.
Identification of PCT levels using DENIS can be performed in less than 15 minutes, which is significantly faster than laboratory immunoassays.
The device provides accurate and robust performance equivalent to gold-standard laboratory tests.
The plasmonic imager can enable identification of PCT levels typical of sepsis and SIRS patients in less than 15 min.
Rapid and quantitative detection of PCT and CRP from blood serum of the selected 34 subject cohort assisted in discrimination of healthy and sick groups.
Samples with high (sepsis) and medium (noninfectious SIRS) PCT levels can be identified in 5 and 10 min, respectively, reducing the test time to under 15 min.
Au-NHAs exhibit extraordinary optical transmission (EOT) at its resonance wavelength, controlled by the period and geometry of the nanoholes, when illuminated in a collinear optical path.
The plasmonic resonance is locally distorted upon the binding of single Au-NPs, resulting in local suppression in the EOT, which enables detection of single NP-labeled molecules.
The plasmonic interaction with the Au-NHA allows for high-contrast imaging of surface-bound NPs in a simple bright field optical reader over large field of view directly inside complex samples.
The imaged data is not affected by the bulk sample background because the resonance transmission through Au-NHAs is strictly dependent on the surface localized field.

The contrast generated by a single particle is significantly above the noise level induced by the camera and the sample, therefore individual molecules binding can be robustly quantified in a digital way directly in complex media.
Single NPs can be distinguished on plasmonic images from NPs aggregates and sediment by the size and the shape of the plasmonic image spikes.
The dynamic range of the device for CRP measurements covers from 36 to 1E5 pg/mL.

The high sensitivity of the assay is enabled by a unique plasmonic mechanism that detects individual molecules on the Au-NHA surface through imaging of single Au-NPs, without complex signal amplification.
The detection is robust against background noise, nonspecific adsorption of proteins, and variations in optical properties of the serum, enabling reliable detection.

The sensor chips were fabricated in a robust wafer-scale cost-effective process using DUVL lithography, and functionalization was performed in a scalable way with microarray bioprinter that uses minimal amounts of antibodies.
The detection principle is not limited to proteins and can be extended to small peptides, DNA, or RNA, as long as a pair of complementary recognition elements is available.
A reliable detection is considered when the PCT signal's 95% lower confidence interval exceeds the background's upper confidence interval.

findings.claim: DISTFLASHATTN is a distributed, memory-efficient, exact attention mechanism with sequence parallelism.

DISTFLASHATTN proposes new optimization techniques to balance causal computation workloads and overlap computation to increase GPU utilization and reduce communication overhead for training long-context LLMs.
DISTFLASHATTN proposes a rematerialization-aware gradient checkpointing strategy that eliminates redundant forward recomputation of FlashAttention.
DISTFLASHATTN optimizes for both memory-efficient attention and causal language modeling.
By altering checkpointing positions, DISTFLASHATTN avoids the recomputation of memory-efficient attention kernels without introducing any numerical difference.
DISTFLASHATTN is a distributed memory-efficient attention mechanism that distributes the computation along the sequence dimension.
DISTFLASHATTN includes a load-balanced scheduling strategy for causal language modeling to reduce the computation bubble.
DISTFLASHATTN includes an asynchronous communication design that overlaps the communication into computation.
A new rematerialization-aware checkpointing strategy effectively cuts off the recomputation time in gradient checkpointing when using DISTFLASHATTN in long-context training.
DISTFLASHATTN supports training P times longer sequences with P workers compared to a single-worker FlashAttention.
DISTFLASHATTN communicates less volume on GQA models due to the reduction of size of keys and values.
DISTFLASHATTN achieves a higher speedup on LLaMA-GQA model compared to Megatron-LM.

DISTFLASHATTN presents novel system optimizations including load balancing for causal language modelings, overlapped communication with computation in the distributed attention computation, and a re-materialization-aware checkpointing strategy.
DISTFLASHATTN has demonstrated up to 2.01× speedup and scales up to 8× longer sequences, compared to the popular system, Megatron-LM with FlashAttention.
DISTFLASHATTN deletes remote key and value from HBM at the end of each iteration to prevent memory accumulation.

The proposed load-balancing schedule routes the extra attention computation of later tokens to idle workers, yielding twice the throughput of the unbalanced version.

A scheduling technique that overlaps communication and computation by pre-fetching tensors hides communication overhead inside computation time, resulting in a 1.32x end-to-end speedup compared to a non-overlapping version.
The recomputation of FlashAttention is unnecessary for its backward pass, and a novel gradient checkpointing strategy avoiding it results in a 1.31x speedup without numerical difference.

Previous gradient checkpointing strategy causes a redundant recomputation of the FlashAttention forward kernel.

It is worth pursuing the sequence parallelism paradigm when distributing the attention module.
The optimization effectively reduces the communication overhead by hiding the communication time inside the computation time.

findings.claim: Non-compliance of research activities with clinical trials, goals unrelated to the EPR effect, and lack of awareness of the impact of solid tumor structure and interactions on the performance of drug nanocarriers have intensified dissatisfaction with EPR-based approaches.

NPs loaded with chemotherapeutic drugs have shown enhanced efficacy in targeting tumor tissue compared to healthy tissue due to the increased permeability and retention of drugs in tumor tissue, a finding known as the enhanced permeability and retention effect
The EPR effect is a unique phenomenon of solid tumors related to defective vascular architecture, large gaps between endothelial cells, abundant vascular mediators, and impaired lymphatic recovery.
The EPR effect is a blood vessel phenomenon that heavily depends on tumour blood flow.
The EPR effect was first discovered by Maeda and colleagues in solid murine tumors.
Nanoparticle delivery to solid tumors via the EPR effect remains very poor despite many efforts.
The effectiveness of the EPR effect is highly variable due to the complex microenvironment of the tumor.

findings.claim: The Effective one-body approach maps the general relativistic two-body problem onto that of a test particle moving in an effective external metric.
Theoretical models for GW signals are built by combining post-Newtonian calculations, the effective-one-body formalism, and numerical relativity.
The Effective one-body approach defines, in a non-perturbative manner, the late dynamical evolution of a coalescing binary system of compact objects.

The ISCO values predicted by the Effective one-body approach respect the 'black hole limit' $J_{real}<GE_{real}^{2}/c^{5}$, implying the system does not need to radiate a lot of gravitational waves in the final coalescence before settling down as a black hole.
The effective one-body approach maps the complicated and badly convergent PN expansion of the dynamics of a two-body system onto a simpler auxiliary one-body problem.
The effective one-body approach predicts an ISCO which is more tightly bound than the usual test-mass-in-Schwarzschild one.

The transition from adiabatic inspiral to unstable plunge is predicted to occur for orbits more tightly bound than the innermost stable circular orbit in a Schwarzschild metric of mass $M = m_{1} + m_{2}$.
The binding energy, angular momentum and orbital frequency of the innermost stable circular orbit for the time-symmetric two-body problem are determined as a function of the mass ratio.
The effective metric is a deformation of the Schwarzschild metric with the symmetric mass ratio $\nu=\mu/M$ as the deformation parameter.
The construction is a non-perturbative way of re-summing the post-Newtonian expansion in the relativistic regime where $GM/(c^{2}|q_{1}-q_{2}|)$ becomes of order unity.
The construction defines a specific $\nu$-deformed innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO).

Superposing the gravitational reaction force $A^{\text{reac}}$ onto the “exact” deformed-Schwarzschild dynamics defines a dynamical system which is a good candidate for describing the late stages of evolution of a coalescing compact binary.
The 2PN truncation of the Damour-Deruelle equations of motion defines a time-symmetric dynamics derivable from a generalized Lagrangian.
The contact transformation removes the acceleration dependence of the harmonic-coordinate Lagrangian and transforms it into the ADM-coordinate ordinary Lagrangian.
The Newtonian-level non-relativistic energy depends only on the combination N = I_R + J, which is the famous special degeneracy of the Coulomb problem.
1PN and 2PN effects lift the special degeneracy of the Coulomb problem by bringing an extra dependence on J.
The function \mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{R}}(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{J}) describing the energy levels is a coordinate-invariant object.
The numerical values of the coefficients A, B, ..., F are coordinate invariant.

The naive identification of energy levels (Eq. 4.3) is unsatisfactory because it is impossible to simultaneously require that energy levels coincide modulo a shift, the effective mass equals the reduced mass, and the effective metric depends only on the real masses.

Introducing energy dependence in the effective mass or metric, as done in the quasi-potential approach of Todorov and coworkers, is unsatisfactory because it obscures the mapping nature and renders generalization to radiation damping difficult.

The requirement (4.12) is imposed by dimensional analysis when requiring $m_{0}=\mu + \mathcal{O}(c^{-2})$ because it is impossible to write correction terms $\mathcal{O}(c^{-2})$ in the link between $m_{0}$ and $\mu$ without energy dependence.
The role of the effective metric is to reproduce, at all orders in the coupling constant G, the interaction generated by exchanging gravitons between two masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
The “one-graviton-exchange” interaction depends only on the (Lorentz-invariant) relative velocity and corresponds to a linearized Schwarzschild effective metric in the test-mass limit $\nu\to0$.
It is physically natural to impose that the linearized effective metric coincide with the linearized Schwarzschild metric, i.e. that $\hat{b}_{1} = 2$.
The BC subsystem admits the unique solution $\alpha_ {1} = \frac {\nu}{2}$ and $\alpha_ {2} = 0$ when $\hat{b}_{1} = 2$.
The BC subsystem would admit no solution in $\hat{b}_{1}$ if $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=0$, proving that a non-trivial energy mapping $\mathcal{E}_{0}=f(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{real}})$ is needed.

The function $\varphi(s)$ of the Mandelstam invariant $s=E_{real}^{2}$ is the most natural symmetric function of the asymptotic 4-momenta $p_{1}^{\mu}, p_{2}^{\mu}$ of a two-particle system which reduces, in the test-mass limit $m_{2}\ll m_{1}$, to the energy of $m_{2}$ in the rest-frame of $m_{1}$.
The function $\varphi(s)$ corresponds to a linearized effective metric coinciding with the linearized Schwarzschild metric.

The two motivations for using the function $\varphi(s)$ (simplicity/symmetry and linearized metric coincidence) are not really independent because they correspond heuristically to saying that the “effective interaction” is the interaction felt by any of the two particles in the rest frame of the other particle.
The effective metric is a simple deformation of the Schwarzschild metric with deformation parameter ν.
The effective radial potential tends to 1 for $R \to \infty$.
The stable circular orbits are located at the minima of the effective potential.
The ISCO corresponds to the critical value $j_*$ of the angular momentum where the maximum and the minimum of the effective potential fuse together to form an horizontal inflection point.
The Schwarzschild-coordinate radius of the effective ISCO is lower than the standard Schwarzschild value $6GM/c^{2}$ corresponding to the total mass $M=m_{1}+m_{2}$.
The truncation of Einstein's field equations to a conformally flat spatial metric is not a good approximation for close orbits.
At the 2PN approximation, some numerically significant terms in the interaction potential come from the transverse-traceless part of the metric.
The assumption that stars are corotating has a significant effect on the location of the ISCO by adding spin-orbit and spin-spin interaction terms.
The prediction that the ISCO is only slightly more bound than in the test-mass limit is robust under the addition of higher PN contributions.
The sensitivity to $a_4'$ of the binding energy is only at the $\sim 3\%$ level for $a_4' = \pm 4$.
The sensitivity to the 4PN coefficient $a_5'$ is further reduced to the $\sim 0.6\%$ level for $a_5' = \pm 4$.

findings.claim: The evaluation dataset and metric are distinct entities in an evaluation framework.
The evaluation framework leverages embedding space distance and common training corpora to extract useful indirect anchors that can trigger copyrighted character generation.
MTEB unifies datasets from different embedding tasks into a common, accessible evaluation framework.
The evaluation framework considers both the elimination of similar output to copyrighted characters and the generated image's consistency with user input.
State-of-the-art image and video generation models can generate copyrighted characters even if the characters' names are not explicitly mentioned, sometimes with only two generic keywords.
Common mitigation methods, such as DALL·E's prompt rewriting, are insufficient alone and require supplementary strategies like negative prompting.
As few as two generic keywords associated with a character are enough to generate their image without mentioning their name.
An effective intervention strategy m should aim to minimize DETECT while maximizing CONS.
Prompting with a character's name (e.g., 'Mario') is referred to as Character Name Anchoring.
Generation using keywords or descriptions without the character's name is referred to as Indirect Anchoring.
The proposed method is a two-stage approach that first generates candidate descriptions and keywords, then reranks them to identify the most effective triggers.

Ranking keywords based on their co-occurrence with the character's name in the LAION corpus is the most effective method and could generate more characters than using a 60-word description when only 20 keywords are used.
Combining prompt rewriting and negative prompts is effective across all open-source models evaluated in alleviating copyright concerns.
The number of detected copyrighted characters is significantly reduced for all models when combining prompt rewriting and negative prompts.
The CONS scores remain mostly stable when combining prompt rewriting and negative prompts.
The combination of prompt rewriting and negative prompts is not perfect at stopping the generation of copyrighted characters.
Current mitigation strategies are imperfect, and there are still many instances where characters are generated verbatim.
The metrics proposed should not be treated as a universal optimization target.
Current mitigations are lacking and more should be done to assess compliance with one's policy.
Future work can leverage optimization-based approaches to identify more complicated indirect anchors.
Future work can explore improved mechanisms to identify user intent to generate copyrighted characters from prompts alone.
Future work can address additional broader types of similarly challenging visual content, like trademarks and broader sets of less-popular characters.
Metrics like consistency scoring and detection could be improved to better capture legally-relevant and human-centered notions of consistency and character similarity.
Leveraging the lessons provided in the work will improve the likelihood that rights are respected and reduce litigation risk for companies.
Asking for generic “copyrighted characters” in the prompt instead of specific characters results in higher agreement with humans.
GPT-4V with generic “copyrighted character” in prompt is still the best option
Indirect anchors (keywords and descriptions) trigger models to generate copyrighted characters like Mario.
Indirect anchoring is able to bypass the system guardrails and generate high-quality images that highly resemble the target copyrighted characters on DALL·E.
Adding character name as negative prompt is a very effective method to reduce recreating copyrighted characters when the character name is part of user input.
Both LLM-based and retriever-based detection methods achieve over 90% accuracy in identifying potential copyright issues in user inputs.
The LM-based detector slightly outperforms the retriever-based detector in accuracy.

FineWeb is a 15-trillion token dataset of text sourced from 96 Common Crawl snapshots.
FineWeb is sufficiently large to train a Chinchilla-optimal model with more than 500 billion parameters.
FineWeb's recipe involves a principled strategy for choosing and tuning filtering heuristics that helped produce a small set of effective filters out of over fifty candidate filters from past work.
FineWeb-Edu is a subset of 1.3 trillion tokens from FineWeb that was rated as highly educational by a custom classifier.
Models trained on FineWeb-Edu exhibit significantly better performance on knowledge- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks like MMLU and ARC.

FineWeb-Edu outperforms all other open datasets compared on the aggregate group of tasks

The FineWeb dataset has a relative overrepresentation of words that reflect hegemonic norms, such as 'man' and 'christian'.

GRITLM is the first model to unify text embedding and generation, and thus all text-based language problems, into a single model at strong performance.

GRITLM can act as both the retriever and reader in a single model, potentially simplifying joint optimization by using the next-token objective to penalize both irrelevant context and poor context use.
GRITLM does not require switching out biases, leverages instructions to handle asymmetric or symmetric use cases, and considers the full breadth of embedding and generative tasks.
GRITLM matches the performance of otherwise equivalent embedding-only and generative-only variants allowing us to unify the two streams at no performance loss.

No neutron star-black hole mergers were detected.
The results include approximately one gravitational-wave detection per 15 days of data searched.
The catalog reports 11 confident detections of GWs from compact binary mergers and a selection of less significant triggers from both observing runs.
The three searches provide largely independent analyses that allow for important cross-checks and yield consistent results.
The searches identified a total of ten BBH mergers and one binary neutron star (BNS) signal.
The catalog announces four previously unpublished BBH mergers observed during O2: GW170729, GW170809, GW170818, and GW170823.
The reanalysis of the O1 data did not result in the discovery of any new GW events, but GW151012 is now detected with increased significance.

The catalog lists 14 GW candidate events with an estimated false-alarm rate less than 1 per 30 days in either matched-filter analysis but whose astrophysical origin cannot be established nor excluded unambiguously.
Source properties such as masses and spins are extracted via Bayesian inference using theoretical models of the GW signal.
Updated parameter estimates for previously reported detections exploit refined instrumental calibration, noise subtraction for O2 data, and updated amplitude power spectral density estimates.
The nonobservation of GWs from a neutron star-black hole binary yields a stronger 90% upper limit on the rate.
The cWB search results are not used in the event selection process.
Any sample of events all of whose measured FARs are greater than 1 per 30 days is expected to consist of at least 50% noise triggers.
The improved FAR measurements for GW151012 are the most salient result of the reanalysis of O1 with the O2 pipelines; no new gravitational-wave events were discovered.

Of the marginal triggers presented in the catalog, nine have excess power from known sources of noise occurring during times when the matched-filter template that yields the trigger has a GW frequency within the sensitive band of the detectors.
For four of the cases with excess power from known noise sources, the observed instrumental artifact overlaps the signal region and possibly causes the marginal trigger.
Scattered light leads to excess power at low frequencies that appear in time-frequency spectrograms as archlike shapes.
When scattered light affects frequencies above the minimum frequency used in the analysis, scattered light transients can create significant triggers in matched-filter searches.
The marginal triggers 161217 and 170720 occur during periods of scattered light affecting frequencies up to 80 Hz with high-amplitude arches.
Investigations identified high-amplitude ground motion correlated with the scattering for triggers 161217 and 170720.
The marginal trigger 161217 occurs during a period of high-amplitude ground motion at Livingston caused by storm activity.
During the storm activity affecting trigger 161217, the Livingston detector is not able to maintain a stable interferometer for periods longer than 10 min.
The presence of intense scattering artifacts contributes to the unstable state of the interferometer and could account for the SNR of the marginal trigger 161217.
Within 20 s of trigger 170720, excess ground motion from earthquakes forced the Livingston detector to drop out of its nominal mode of operation.
Before the detector dropped out of the observing state for trigger 170720, the data are heavily polluted with scattering artifacts that could account for the SNR of the triggers.
Artifacts related to scattered light are also observed at Hanford at the time of trigger 170720.

For trigger 151012.2, light scattering does not introduce significant power above 30 Hz prior to the reported trigger time, and no power overlap was found, suggesting artifacts could not account for the observed marginal trigger.

For triggers 170208 and 170616, a slight overlap with excess power from scattering is observed, but after mitigation, the marginal trigger remains with similar significance, suggesting the scattering artifact could not have accounted for the SNR of the marginal trigger.
The presence of noise artifacts cannot account for the SNR of marginal triggers 170405 and 170630 because they are identified as significant after the removal of short-duration transients.
Trigger 170405 is in coincidence with a short-duration, high-amplitude noise transient at Hanford.
Trigger 170630 is in coincidence with a short-duration, high-amplitude noise transient at Livingston.
Posterior distributions for all GW events are consistent with originating from BBHs, apart from GW170817.

The component masses of the detected BH binaries cover a wide range from about 5M⊙ to about 70M⊙ and lie within the range expected for stellar-mass BHs.
Lower-mass systems are dominated by the inspiral of the binary, and the component mass contours trace out a line of constant chirp mass which is the best measured parameter in the inspiral.
For high-mass binaries, the total mass can be measured with an accuracy comparable to that of the chirp mass.

findings.claim: Generating English Wikipedia articles can be approached as a multi-document summarization of source documents.
Considering discourse relations among sentences is important in multi-document summarization.
Prior work on multi-document summarization has focused on extractive summarization, which selects sentences or phrases from the input to form summaries, rather than generating new text.
Scaling up RNN sequence-to-sequence approaches to multi-document summarization has not been successful due to lack of large datasets and RNN inadequacy in capturing complex discourse relations.
There has been limited application of abstractive neural methods to multi-document summarization, possibly due to the paucity of large, labeled datasets.
The combination of graphs and GCNs processes sentence relations across documents better than the vanilla RNN sequence models.
The GCN system significantly outperforms the commonly used baselines and traditional graph approaches such as Centroid, LexRank, and G-Flow.
The model improves upon traditional graph-based extractive approaches and the vanilla GRU sequence model with no graph.
The model achieves competitive results against other state-of-the-art multidocument summarization systems.
The proposed model shows a clear advantage over traditional graph-based extractive summarizers and a baseline GRU model that does not use any graph.
The proposed model resolves issues by breaking down summarization into salience estimation and sentence selection without an expensive decoder, and by utilizing sentence relation graphs.
Backward GRUs and bi-directional GRUs did not meaningfully improve upon forward GRUs.
The addition of Cosine Similarity Graph on top of the GRU clearly boosts the performance.
The addition of ADG from G-Flow gives a slightly better performance.
The system exceeds CLASSY04, the best peer system in DUC 2004, and Support Vector Regression (SVR), a widely used regression-based summarizer.
The system remains at a comparable level to RegSum, the state-of-the-art multi-document summarizer using regression.
The model works on sentence level, spotlighting sentence relations encoded as a graph.
PDG improves R-1 score by 0.82 over ADG
PDG provides a more informative guide to estimating the importance of each sentence
PDG converges even faster than “No Graph” and achieves the lowest training cost and validation cost amongst all methods
PDG has particularly strong representation power and generalizability
PDG corrects for ADG's discrete nature by coercing the average edge weight and node degree to be more diverse and smaller
Including sentence personalization scores in edge weight assignments of the PDG leads to a select number of edges gaining markedly large distinction
All the graph representations show positive correlation between the node degree and the salience score
Nodes representing salient sentences tend to have higher degrees in the PDG
PDG represents edges which connect nodes of sentences from different documents, in contrast with the traditional sequence model
The model can capture sentence relations across documents.
The model demonstrates improved salience prediction and summarization.
The model achieves competitive performance with current state-of-the-art systems.
Sentence relation graphs, particularly PDG, help to learn the salience of sentences.

Knowledge Inheritance (KI) is defined as the process of distilling knowledge summarized by an existing small PLM during pretraining to efficiently learn larger PLMs.
During domain adaptation, an already trained large PLM could benefit from multiple small PLMs of different domains under the KI framework.
In the scenario of Knowledge Inheritance (KI), since student models have larger capacities, the performance of teacher models is no longer an “upper bound” of student models.

KI is more data-efficient than self-learning, especially under low-resource settings where domain data is scarce.
Large PLMs can simultaneously absorb knowledge from multiple domains using KI, achieving improved performance on both domains compared to self-learning.
Knowledge Inheritance (KI) supports knowledge transfer over a series of PLMs with growing sizes.

findings.claim: LSOCI almost exclusively uses multiple scattering to image the vascular flux and is expected to access deeper structures for a given wavelength, in contrast to OCT scanning-based techniques.

In LSOCI, any fully polarized state of illumination can be used, but the contribution backscattered from the skin has to be projected onto the diametrically opposite polarimetric state in the Poincaré space before detection.
The polarimetric filtering in LSOCI results in the detection of the temporal variation of the spatially depolarized speckle field provoked by multiple scattering.

Conventional LSCI or similar techniques detect a large part of the first-order scattering, whereas LSOCI aims at removing this contribution to reveal the multiple scattering that occurs in deeper layers in the volume.

LSOCI measurements are semiquantitative because exact calculation of blood flux requires a priori knowledge of the speed distribution of red blood cells which is not available in practical applications.
LSOCI images reveal the underlying microvascular pattern and completely remove surface stripes visible in nonfiltered dynamic optical speckle images.
Fingerprints visible in nonfiltered images mostly disappear in LSOCI images, revealing a complex structure of anastomotic microvascular activity hot spots.
LSOCI spatial resolution reaches 80 μm in the system.
LSOCI signal is based on the decorrelation time of the speckle intensity distribution traducing movements of red blood cells.
LSOCI signal is not aimed at imaging the structure of tissues such as OCT and CM.
LSOCI signal is naturally extremely sensitive to submicromovements.
LSOCI allows observing structures as small as 80 μm in real time.
LSOCI is a simple full field and noninvasive technique that is eye safe and low cost.
The total laser speckle contrast index was proportional to the speed of the blood flow.
Polarimetric filtering prevents the contribution of surface scattering from reaching the camera and favors the detection of multiscattered photons from the deeper layers of the skin.
The process utilizes the temporal variation of the spatially depolarized optical speckle field generated by moving red blood cells when illuminated with fully polarized coherent light.
The contrast function C converges to an asymptote proportional to sqrt(tau/T) whenever T is large compared with the correlation time tau.
In VMAI measurement mode, 20 raw images with 50 ms integration times provide stable results.
Longer integration times are preferred in VMAI measurement mode to fulfill the requirement that T is larger than the decorrelation time $\tau_{cv}$.
Linear polarizers orthogonal to the incident polarimetric state suppress the specular component and tend to suppress all of the first-order scattering corresponding to the surface contribution.
Polarimetric filtering strongly decreases the response of the skin surface to the benefit of multiscattering generated in the volume, in the deepest layers of the skin.
The dynamic and relative stability of the measurements demonstrate the possibility of performing semiquantitative measurements.
VMAI exhibits a mean stability of 7% in spite of the cardiac cycle effect.

findings.claim: LSST is a dedicated telescope with an effective aperture of 6.7 meters and a field of view of 9.6 deg $^{2}$.
LSST will survey 20,000 deg $^{2}$ of the sky in six broad photometric bands, imaging each region roughly 2000 times over a ten-year survey lifetime.

The LSST survey data will be public with no proprietary period in the United States, with a goal to make it world-public.
The combination of LSST with contemporary space-based near-infrared (NIR) missions will provide powerful synergies in studies of dark energy, galaxy evolution, and many other areas.

The baseline LSST cadence will result in orbital parameters for several million moving objects, dominated by main belt asteroids (MBAs), with light curves and colorimetry for a substantial fraction of detected objects.

LSST will survey over half the celestial sphere for asteroids, get superb orbits, go tremendously faint, and measure precise colors, allowing measurement of light curves for thousands of TNOs.

LSST extends time-volume space a thousand times over current surveys.

LSST will characterize in detail active galactic nuclei (AGN) variability and new classes of transients, such as binary mergers and stellar disruptions by black holes.

LSST will provide a powerful new capability for monitoring periodic variables such as RR Lyrae stars, which will be used to map the Galactic halo and intergalactic space to distances exceeding 400 kpc.
LSST science programs are highly compatible in terms of desired data characteristics, allowing a single data set to serve most programs.

findings.claim: LVPruning employs cross-attention modules to compute the importance of vision tokens based on their interaction with language tokens, determining which to prune.
LVPruning can be integrated without modifying the original MLLM parameters, which makes LVPruning simple to apply or remove.
LVPruning is a method that dynamically reduces the number of vision tokens in MLLMs based on their relevance to the language context using lightweight cross-attention decision modules.
LVPruning can significantly reduce computational costs—up to a $62.1\%$ decrease in inference TFLOPs—by pruning as much as $90\%$ of vision tokens without substantially affecting model performance.
LVPruning allows for adjustable token pruning ratios during inference without retraining.
LVPPruning is designed for MLLMs that pass all vision tokens through an MLP connector into the language model.
LVPruning significantly reduces the inference cost while maintaining competitive performance.
LVPruning outperforms the state-of-the-art MLLMs on three benchmarks, while delivering competitive results on the others.
LVPruning outperforms nearly all benchmarks, with only a slight performance drop compared to BLIP2-14B in POPE(rad).
LVPruning effectively balances model efficiency with task performance.
LVPruning achieves superior performance with competitive inference FLOPs compared to state-of-the-art Q-former-based MLLMs.
LVPruning computes relevance scores for each vision token based on language tokens, progressively removing redundant tokens throughout the LLM.
LVPruning eliminates up to 90% of vision tokens by the middle layer, achieving a 62.1% reduction in FLOPs with only a ~0.45% average performance loss across nine multi-modal benchmarks.

findings.claim: MONOTRANS starts with a monolingual transformer trained with MLM, which is transferred to a new language by learning a new embedding matrix through MLM in the new language while freezing parameters of all other layers.
MONOTRANS is competitive with joint multilingual pre-training across standard zero-shot cross-lingual transfer benchmarks (XNLI, MLDoc, and PAWS-X).
The monolingual transfer approach can be made competitive with mBERT by learning second language-specific transformations via adapter modules.
MONOTRANS exhibits stability issues when learning language-specific position embeddings for Greek, Thai, and Swahili, where the second step occasionally fails to converge to a good solution.
MONOTRANS is competitive with joint learning
The basic version of MONOTRANS is 3.3 points worse on average than its equivalent JOINTPAIR model
MONOTRANS is competitive with the best joint variant, with a difference of only 0.6 points when we learn language-specific position embeddings.
MONOTRANS is competitive with JOINTMULTI and JOINTPAIR despite being multilingual at the embedding layer only
The gap between MONOTRANS and joint models is larger, but MONOTRANS still performs surprisingly well given the nature of the task
Adding adapters results in a MONOTRANS model that is comparable to the best joint system
The proposed approach is competitive with multilingual BERT on standard cross-lingual classification benchmarks and on a new Cross-lingual Question Answering Dataset (XQuAD).
The results contradict common beliefs of the basis of the generalization ability of multilingual models.
Deep monolingual models learn some abstractions that generalize across languages.
Neither a shared subword vocabulary nor joint multilingual training is necessary for zero-shot transfer.

Adding adapters to allow a transferred monolingual model to learn higher level abstractions in the new language significantly improves performance
Joint multilingual pre-training is not essential for cross-lingual generalization.
Monolingual semantic representations learned from non-English languages transfer to English to a degree.
The setting to transfer a monolingual model to other languages is suitable for incorporating new languages into an existing model without access to original data.
The work provides a baseline for multilingual lifelong learning.
Monolingual representations generalize well to other languages and can be transferred to a new language by learning new subword embeddings.
Monolingual models transferred at the lexical level perform comparably to state-of-the-art multilingual models on standard zero-shot cross-lingual transfer benchmarks.

findings.claim: For recombinant antibodies, especially therapeutic antibodies, slow, spontaneous, and non-enzymatic modifications (except N-linked glycosylation) may adversely affect the affinity, specificity, and function of the antibodies.

Challenges with bacterial cells include inclusion body formation, high endotoxin levels and, importantly for antibodies, the lack of correct posttranslational processing and modifications, in particular N-linked glycosylation.
Glycosylation is the post-translational modification of proteins through the addition of carbohydrates to amino acid side chains.
The existence of N-glycan at the N297 position of CH2 domain of each heavy chain enables reactive sites for conjugation with payloads through glycosylation.
The different MTDs of AGS-16M8F and AGS-16C3F may be due to differences in protein glycosylation
The vast heterogeneity of structures across glycosylation sites hinders the in-depth analysis of glycan changes specific to an individual protein within a complex mixture.
glycosylation of the protein corona plays an important role in maintaining the colloidal stability of nanoparticles and influences nanoparticle-cell interactions
The N-glycosylation motif (N-X-S/T) is frequently found in the CDRs of antibodies.
The amount and location of glycosylation affect protein disposition, including regulating receptor binding and Fc effector functions.
The MRM-based method for monitoring site-specific glycosylation in rMAbs is sensitive and specific.
Somatic hypermutation (SHM) introduces many N-glycosylation sequences to mature antibodies, although human germline variable genes contain few.
The MRM-based method can rapidly characterize over 130 distinct glycopeptides and determine the extent of site occupancy within minutes.

The lack of commercially available N-glycosylated standards precludes absolute quantitation, thus the quantitation of glycosylation is performed by relative comparisons of glycan/glycopeptide signals.
MRM is a robust and sensitive technique for the characterization of immunoglobulin G and for site-specific quantitation relative to the protein content.

The MRM method was refined to observe and quantify high and low abundant N-glycopeptides in both a protein- and site-specific manner directly from rMAbs without protein enrichment nor N-glycan release.
MRM was utilized to detect the conversion of asparagine to aspartic acid at the glycosylation site by releasing the N-glycans with PNGase F, which increases the peptide molecular weight by 0.984 Da.
The MRM quantitation methods enable rapid analysis of multiple glycoforms simultaneously within a run time of 10 minutes per sample.
Over 130 glycopeptide transitions were monitored to determine the site-specific glycosylation and the site occupancy for each rMAb drug.

A system-wide glycoproteomic analytical platform based on multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) was developed for the characterization of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies at the site-specific level, enabling quantitation of distinct glycoforms without glycan release and protein enrichment steps.

For absolute quantification of N-glycan site occupancy, product ions containing an asparagine (N) were selected for MRM, and the corresponding peptide with an aspartic acid (D) residue after N-glycan release was monitored.
Single transition monitoring in conjunction with dynamic MRM provides sufficient specificity as it both identifies the compound as a glycopeptide and enables quantitation.
Relative quantitation of protein glycosylation is provided by using absolute ion abundances due to the lack of available standards.
It is possible to compare abundances of glycopeptides from MRM signals to study the distribution of N-glycans in rMAbs.
The MRM method is rapid in profiling the N-glycome and provides glycoproteome details.
Dynamic MRM was used, and Delta retention time is the retention time window for the target transition.

Glycopeptide absolute ion abundances are greatly affected by protein concentration, necessitating a normalization method where signals are normalized to the abundance of a distinguishing peptide belonging to the parent IgG subclass.
Glycopeptides were identified using a library of glycan structures released from the same rMAb drugs.
Good separation of the IgG peptides was achieved within two minutes.
Glycopeptides eluted earlier than the peptides, resulting in higher sensitivity and less charge competition.
Glycopeptides from IgG3 and IgG4 contain the same amino acid residues and therefore could not be distinguished.
The established methods are effective in simultaneously determining N-glycan compositions, their sites of attachment, and site occupancy in commercial rMAb drugs.
The six rMAb drugs analyzed have similar glycopeptides but in different quantities, and all are highly glycosylated with N-glycan site occupancy of over 97%.
The methods developed in this study are rapid and highly specific.
The methods can be widely used to determine the protein-specific glycan profile in rMAbs and percent site occupancy during drug development and quality control.
The methods can be easily used to check batch-to-batch consistency, which is essential because the molecular heterogeneity of rMAbs will affect their stability and their potency.

Understanding the distributions of N-glycan structures at the site-specific level can provide more information on the activities of rMAbs and is beneficial in optimizing their clinical outcomes for different diseases.
