findings.claim: MUSE is a systematic, multi-faceted framework to evaluate six desired properties for unlearning algorithms.
Muse has successfully scaled up such a paradigm for text-to-image models of 3B parameters using 460M image-text pairs.
MUSE formally defines different unlearning scopes and corresponding metrics, resulting in a systematic six-way evaluation featuring both data owners' and deployers' expectations.
MUSE's evaluation uses a large-scale corpus of over 6 million tokens, separated into verbatim text and knowledge sets.
MUSE currently evaluates unlearning for language models using books and news articles.
MUSE disentangles several desirable properties of unlearning algorithms and finds that no existing algorithm is able to satisfy all of the data owner and deployer considerations.
Most unlearning algorithms remove verbatim and knowledge memorization but at the cost of utility preservation and do not effectively prevent privacy leakage.
Negative preference optimization (NPO) and task vectors are especially effective in removing verbatim and knowledge memorization.
Negative preference optimization (NPO) often permits privacy leakage.
Negative preference optimization (NPO) and task vectors induce a sharp drop in the utility of the model.
Negative preference optimization (NPO) and task vectors struggle with large forget sets and successive unlearning requests.
Unlearning algorithms generally fail to meet data owner expectations in preventing privacy leakage.
Currently feasible unlearning methods are not yet ready for meaningful usage or deployment in real-world scenarios.
Retraining from scratch is usually too costly in real world deployment, so the authors focus on evaluating approximate unlearning algorithms.

Prior evaluations on LM unlearning focus on performance of specific tasks like question answering, but these metrics do not faithfully reflect data owner expectations and real-world deployment considerations.
Data owners typically have three main expectations regarding the unlearned model: (C1) No verbatim memorization, (C2) No knowledge memorization, and (C3) No privacy leakage.
Privacy is quantified using the membership inference test, which detects if a specific datapoint was used to train the model (member), distinguishing it from non-training data (non-member).
The PrivLeak metric for a good unlearning algorithm should be close to zero, whereas an over/under-unlearning algorithm will get a large positive/negative metric.
Unlearning can fail to prevent privacy leakage via under-unlearning (loss not made large enough) or over-unlearning (loss made abnormally large).
All unlearning methods compromise the model's utility by 24.2% to 100%.
GA, GA_GDR, and NPO_GDR lead to complete utility loss, rendering the unlearned models practically unusable.
Most methods, such as GA_KLR, NPO_KLR, and WHP, unlearn the knowledge on D_U at the cost of utility.
Model utility decreases with the size of the forget set and achieves a minimum at the largest size.
Over- or under-unlearn can exacerbate privacy leakage.
Current unlearning methods successfully prevent the model's memorization of content at a significant cost to utility on data not intended for removal.
Current unlearning methods lead to severe privacy leakage and cannot sustainably accommodate successive unlearning requests or large-scale content removal.
The evaluation benchmark does not have a comprehensive study of how unlearning would impact the model performance for different user bases, especially underrepresented groups.
The results are not a criticism of the paradigm of machine unlearning, but a study of the potential downsides of existing methods and a call for better algorithms.

findings.claim: Model MoErging methods aim to recycle expert models to create an aggregate system with improved performance or generalization.

AdaMerging is an adaptive model merging method where it autonomously learns the coefficients for merging either on a task-wise or layer-wise basis, using entropy minimization on unlabeled test samples as a surrogate objective function to refine the merging coefficients.
A key component of MoErging methods is the creation of a router that decides which expert model(s) to use for a particular input or application.
Different MoErging methods are rarely compared to one another and are often validated in different experimental setups.
MoErging methods are distinct from MoE approaches that jointly train all the experts from scratch
Unlike merging methods that typically produce a static combination of models, MoErging methods adaptively combine models to improve performance on a per-query or per-task basis
MoErging is a new paradigm for decentralized model development that aims to recycle expert models trained asynchronously by distributed contributors.
Experts in MoErging are specialized models trained and shared by individual contributors who do not have access to one another’s compute or data.
Routing in MoErging aims to select and aggregate contributor-provided expert models to improve performance or generalization.
Most MoErging methods were developed over the past year or so, resulting in studies rarely discussing or citing one another.
The core trade-off in MoErging is between the routing utility gained from expert data and the practical limitations of data availability and privacy.
In the scenario where expert data is shared, the benefits of MoErging methods are recycling of the compute required to train the expert models and decentralized training.
Zero-shot MoErging methods inherently rely on the generalization capabilities of the pre-trained expert models and routing mechanism.
Without task-specific adjustments, the effectiveness of zero-shot MoErging methods can be limited in specialized downstream tasks.
Few-Shot MoErging methods adapt the model using few labeled examples, often via prompt tuning or fine-tuning.
Full dataset MoErging methods use fully labeled data for end-to-end fine-tuning, potentially maximizing performance given sufficient data, but increase data and computational costs.
Model MoErging averages all parameters except MLP layers, which may contain more task-specific knowledge.
Model MoErging upcycles MLP layers into an MoE by converting each expert's MLP to a task vector via subtraction of base model parameters.
Model MoErging performs routing by multiplying routing weights with expert MLP task vectors and adding them to the base MLP weight.
Model MoErging performs routing at the example level by taking the mean of all token-level routing weights.
Model MoErging does not require expert training data access but uses an unlabelled test dataset to learn the router by minimizing routing distribution entropy.
Model MoErging methods aim to receive contributions from more tasks of greater variety and may target a wider range of use cases.
While MoErging methods generally assume expert models are trained independently, multitask MoE methods can be considered an important baseline when expert data is shared.
While most MoErging methods do not explicitly target a continual learning setting, techniques for continual learning with MoEs could be applicable to MoErging methods.
Model merging aims to combine independently trained models that share an architecture into a single model that retains the individual models' capabilities.
Merging can be considered a non-adaptive way of aggregating independently trained experts and is therefore a reasonable baseline for many MoErging methods.
Very few of the surveyed MoErging methods are actually used in practice.
Many MoErging methods lack user-friendly software implementations, requiring technical expertise to apply.
It is often unclear which MoErging methods are applicable and/or optimal for a given use case.

Assumptions made by many MoErging methods, such as custom expert training procedures or sharing expert training data, make them inapplicable unless the standard practice of solely sharing expert parameters changes.
Developing robust theoretical frameworks for MoErging is a crucial direction for future work to formally understand properties and guide method design.
The lack of platforms that facilitate the various stages of a MoErging pipeline may hold back the promise of MoErging as a framework for collaborative learning.
Custom expert training procedures can allow for better integration of experts with the routing mechanism, potentially leading to a better model.
Standard training leverages existing fine-tuning methods and allows reuse of trained experts available online.
Standard training may necessitate more sophisticated routing and aggregation strategies to effectively utilize off-the-shelf expert models.
Private data methods are more broadly applicable and privacy-preserving, relying on open data sources and expert models for routing and aggregation.

Higher frequency per-Step routing maximizes nuanced input adaptation but becomes computationally expensive and potentially unstable, with the risk of early routing errors propagating to later routing decisions.
Lower frequency, Task-based routing prioritizes efficiency but assumes consistent expert needs across a task, potentially limiting adaptability for diverse task inputs.
Selecting the routing frequency involves trading off adaptability, computational efficiency, and the consistency of expert needs within and across inputs.
Sparse selection enhances efficiency by activating only the most relevant experts, which is crucial with large expert pools to avoid processing all experts.

findings.claim: The SQUID impedance provides a means of flux tuning the SAW resonator, as well as a cross-Kerr interaction between the modes.

Exploiting multiple modes in a quantum acoustic device could enable applications in quantum information in a hardware-efficient setup, including quantum simulation in a synthetic dimension and continuous-variable quantum computing with cluster states.
The interaction with the SQUID-shunted mirror gives rise to coupling between the more than 20 accessible resonator modes.
The coupling between resonator modes is exploited to demonstrate two-mode squeezing of SAW phonons, as well as four-mode multipartite entanglement.
The SQUID reflector gives rise to coupling of more than 20 modes due to the narrow free spectral range.
The device generates two-mode squeezed states between phonons in different SAW modes with a parametric drive.
Extending the pump scheme to four tones demonstrates multipartite entanglement between four acoustic modes.
The short wavelength of sound allows for a much denser mode spacing than in the purely electromagnetic case.
The IDT couples more effectively to the even modes, resulting in a lower $Q_{c}$.
The second term in the effective Hamiltonian contains both beam-splitter and two-mode squeezing interactions.
A beam-splitting interaction may be implemented by a parametric drive close to the difference frequency of the SAW modes.
Modulating near the sum frequency will induce two-mode squeezing between pairs of modes.
The parabolic dependence of the frequency on flux implies the electromagnetic mirror mode, and hence the effective coupling rate, are modulated at twice the pump frequency.
Two-mode squeezing arises as two photons from the pump tone are converted to one phonon each in modes symmetric around the pump.
Squeezing is observed below the pump-off level in all four mode pairs.
The ellipticity $R_e$ is well above unity for all four mode pairs and shows a diminishing trend with increased detuning.
The ratio of the standard deviation in the squeezed quadrature to the pump-off case, $R_p$, has a value $R_p < 1$ across the four mode pairs.
No correlations are observed outside the two-mode squeezed pairs.
The squeezing is estimated to be below the vacuum level if the modes are cooled below an effective temperature of 80 mK.
It is unlikely the effective phonon temperature exceeds the 80 mK bound, leading to a strong indication that squeezing below the vacuum is observed in the phonon field.
Negativity of the entanglement test for all bipartitions is a signature of full multipartite entanglement.
The entanglement significance is substantially higher for bipartitions where modes 3 and 4 appear in separate sets due to imperfect alignment of the equidistant pump comb with the mode structure.
The square lattice is a cluster state that can be used to implement universal quantum computation and can be generated from the Hamiltonian of Eq. (1).
Two-mode squeezing was demonstrated in a surface acoustic wave resonator, likely below the phononic vacuum level.
Fully inseparable multipartite entanglement of four resonator modes was observed by extending the scheme to a multitone pump spectrum and calibrated measurement chain.
The dense mode structure of the resonator enables multiplexing all modes to one measurement channel without analog frequency conversion.
The small on-chip footprint of the device (< 0.2 mm^2) contributes to scalability.
Pump strengths similar to loss rates limit the amount of squeezing and correlations that can be induced.
The device used to measure multimode correlations has an integrated transmon qubit, although it was not used for this experiment.
Modulating the reflector SQUID at a frequency corresponding to the free spectral range will induce nearest-neighbor hopping of phonons, giving rise to an effective lattice Hamiltonian.
The dispersive interaction between SAW modes and the mirror is small compared to the linewidth due to weak vacuum coupling strength.
Parametric excitation relies on strong pumping because the dispersive interaction is small compared to the linewidth.
The last term of the Hamiltonian $H'$ produces squeezing and beam-splitter interactions.
The final sum in the Hamiltonian $\tilde{H}$ is only over SAW modes $k$ satisfying the four-wave mixing criterion $\omega_{k} = 2\omega_{p} - \omega_{j}$.
The theoretical covariance matrix qualitatively reproduces the features of the measured data shown in Fig. 4(b).
A good estimate of $\sqrt{G}$ and $n$ allows reconstruction of the quantum statistics.
The measured two-mode squeezing is a signature of entangled SAW modes.
If the calibration underestimates the real added noise in the amplification chain, it implies more entanglement in the reconstructed multimode state because added noise obscures correlations.
Including higher frequency probe modes in the analysis renders the covariance matrix obtained unphysical by multiple standard deviations, presumably due to error in calibration.
In the two-mode quadrature histograms for the mode pair closest to the pump, squeezing is manifest in the Q+ - Q- histogram, while the other quadratures show amplified noise.

The H-IV sample exhibits a super-wide stopband in a certain range from 280 to 650 nm.

The large shift of the red edge of H-IV compared with the 245 nm sample is caused by the interaction between constituent homogeneous crystals with different PS sphere sizes, resulting in a mean sphere diameter much smaller than 245 nm.
Heterostructure sample H-IV enabled an additional 2.5-fold FL enhancement relative to the homogeneous 245 nm film because the super-wide stopband of H-IV can simultaneously match the E and the F.
With the widening of the bandgap, the heterostructure PCs can not only fully couple with the emission light but also gradually couple with the excitation light, especially the H-IV sample.

findings.claim: Particles are optically bound outside the focal spot by the back-scattered light and multi-channel light scattering, forming a dynamic optical binding network.

findings.claim: The sensing capability of plasmonic nanoparticles can be used to detect single atomic ions in aqueous medium.
The system's ability to discern permanent binding and transient interaction allows studying the different interaction kinetics of zinc and mercury ions.
Detection of transient interactions enables statistical confirmation that sensor signals originate from single ions.
Mercury ions amalgamate with gold, while zinc ions eventually turn into probes of highly localized surface potentials as ionic strength evolves.
The small surface area of nanoparticles imposes a severe restriction on sensor systems because individual molecules occupy surface fractions, rendering them insensitive upon full coverage.
The coupling between the NR and microcavity transduces the interaction of a zinc or mercury ion with the NR into a red shift of the WGM's resonance position.
Permanent interactions manifest as a step pattern in the WGM position trace, whereas transient interactions appear as fast changes that exhibit a spike pattern.
The detection of spike events at a pH of ~7 is only possible in solutions with an ionic strength of at least ~1 mM.
Magnesium, perchlorate, sodium, and chloride ions are excluded as sources for the detected events because spike rates did not exhibit scaling behaviour with their concentrations.
EDTA forms chelate complexes with zinc ions, which are not detected as they carry a negative charge and are thus repelled from the negatively charged tips of the NR
The disparity of detection rate constants is either because of a difference in the number of sensing sites or to an intrinsic difference in the ions' association rates
The similarity of the spike magnitude and length distributions found for both types of ions indicates similar levels of sensitivity for mercury and zinc

The resulting time resolution is not sufficient for the detection of freely diffusing ions in water as their root mean squared displacements for periods of 0.1 ms greatly exceed the dimensions of the NRs
An attractive force between the ions and NRs is required to confine the analyte ions inside the sensing sites long enough to allow for their detection
The necessity of additional electrolyte for the detection suggests that the attractive force is electrostatic
Below an ionic strength of 14.6 mM in the case of mercury and 18 mM in the case of zinc, spike events were observed exclusively.
The rates, magnitudes, and durations of ion-NR interaction events do not show a direct dependence on ionic strength.
At an ionic strength of 14.6 mM, both spike and step transitions in resonance position are observed for mercury ions.
At an ionic strength of 60 mM, step-type transitions occur predominantly for mercury ions.
The formation of stable bonds between mercury ions and gold nanorods is an irreversible process.
The binding process of mercury ions to gold nanorods without a reducing agent might result from the reduction of mercury ions by light-induced hot carriers followed by amalgamization.
The rate of spike recognition decreases as the number of observed steps increases.
The sites on the nanorods sensitive to transient interactions are identical to those sensitive to binding-type interactions.
The association rate constant for zinc is less than 0.1 times the association rate constant for mercury.
Irreversible bonds do not form between zinc ions and nanorods.
At an ionic strength of 16 mM, spike events are observed exclusively for zinc ions.
At a low ionic strength, the repulsive potential caused by the positively charged CTAB prevents ion-NR interactions and no spikes or steps are observed.

Above a 1 mM ionic strength, Debye screening of the CTAB layer allows the analyte ions to be confined temporarily by the attractive potential created by the NR's negative surface charge and spikes are observed.
At high ionic strengths, the Zn ions remain confined for longer in the local minima of $E_{pot}$ found along the NR's surface and the Hg ions bond permanently to the NRs.
At 18 mM ionic strength, an additional type of transient event is observed, described as extended intervals during which the resonance trace exhibits an increased noise amplitude.

As the ionic strength reaches values between 26 and 28 mM, the temporal characteristic of the ion–NR interaction transforms to sudden jumps between two states interspersed by intervals of different length.
The discrete behaviour observed between 26 and 28 mM indicates a relatively long and stable, but reversible, adsorption of a zinc ion to a NR sensing site.
Observing only two distinct levels in the nRPDs implies that the interaction was most probably limited to a single sensing site.
The duration of transient zinc ion interactions is strongly influenced by the local environment of each sensing site.
At 30 mM ionic strength, spike- and burst-type events of opposite sign are observed, with shifts in the resonance position occurring towards the shorter wavelength side.
Under 30 mM ionic strength conditions, ions remain mostly confined inside the sensing site, although they are prone to local environmental fluctuations causing small transient changes in position.
The positively charged CTAB bilayer creates a repulsive potential for positively charged zinc and mercury ions, preventing them from reaching the sensing sites at the NR ends.
Introduction of electrolyte causes negatively charged ions to form a layer around CTAB end groups, reducing repulsive force via Debye screening and allowing analyte ions to get closer to NR tips.
Spike-type events are observed at an ionic strength of about 1 mM, corresponding to a Debye length of approximately 9.5 nm.
Burst-type and binding-type interactions for zinc and mercury ions, respectively, are observed at an ionic strength in the range 15–20 mM.

findings.claim: Using real questions, a strong teacher model, and the bi-encoder architecture are all crucial to the success of QUIP.
Other design decisions (e.g., question generation decoding strategies) do not qualitatively affect the main findings, pointing to the stability of the QUIP approach.
QUIP's training objective directly encourages contextual representations to encode useful semantic information, namely information about what questions can be answered by each span.
QUIP's bi-encoder is trained to encode single passages rather than passage-question pairs, making it more transferable to tasks involving single passages.

QUIP learns to push each phrase's representation far away from those of questions the phrase does not answer; this ability to represent unanswerability is crucial for correctly handling some question-based prompts.
QUIP succeeds in paraphrase detection and NER by learning meaningful token-level contextualized representations for single passages.
QUIP's bi-encoder architecture enables a more efficient way to use question prompts in NER compared with a cross-encoder.
QUIP yields more reliable scores when questions are unanswerable in sentiment analysis compared with a cross-encoder.
BERTScore should pair well with QUIP because BERTScore uses token-level representations
QUIP representations are expected to contain rich entity type information because questions in QA often ask for entities of a specific type.
QUIP is hypothesized to recognize that unanswerable questions should receive lower scores because it is trained to make each span’s representation far away from those of questions it does not answer.
QUIP outperforms the other bi-encoder model baselines, and even a cross-encoder BERT-large model.
The RoBERTa cross-encoder models are better at QA, but will underperform QUIP on non-QA tasks.
QUIP improves substantially over RoBERTa on all four datasets, with an average improvement of .076 AUROC.
The improvement is greatest on the PAWS datasets; since these datasets cannot be solved by lexical features alone, QUIP representations must be much more contextualized than RoBERTa representations.
Training on Unsupervised QA data degrades performance compared to RoBERTa, showing that QUIP does not merely make word representations encode local context in a simple way.

The cross-encoder models also lag behind QUIP at paraphrase ranking, despite their higher QA accuracy; since the cross-encoders are trained to take passage-question pairs as inputs, their representations of single sentences are not as useful.
Having real questions, accurate answer supervision, and a bi-encoder student model are all crucial to the success of QUIP.

QUIP's basic recipe is stable to many small changes, including including in-batch negative passages, using argmax prediction of the teacher rather than soft labels, and using beam search to generate diverse answers followed by one high-likelihood question per answer.
QUIP uses question generation and knowledge distillation to improve over directly training on labeled data, which is the approach used by QuASE.
QUIP proposes leveraging question-based task descriptions to improve accuracy in zero-shot and few-shot settings, using the QA format as a model-building interface for non-QA tasks.
QUIP learns token-level representations and uses token-level supervision from extractive QA, rather than learning a single vector for a sentence.
QUIP pre-trained token-level contextual representations that are useful for downstream few-shot learning.
The key idea of QUIP was to use question-answer pairs to define what information should be encoded in passage representations.
QUIP representations are useful for standard NLP tasks in zero- and few-shot settings, including paraphrase detection, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis, across nine total datasets.
QUIP gives a 0.6 F1 improvement on WNUT, but has effectively the same accuracy on CoNLL when training on the full training dataset.
The representation of a phrase in a passage should encode all questions that the phrase can answer in context.
The bi-encoder's token-level representations are useful for non-QA downstream tasks without extensive (or in some cases, any) fine-tuning.
The single-model approach for generating question-answer pairs is simpler than prior approaches that use separate models for answer and question generation.
Attempts to mitigate question quality and diversity issues, such as using a two-stage beam search, did not noticeably change downstream results.
Freezing the encoder is often useful in practice, particularly for large models, as the same model can be reused for many tasks

The proposed initialization style is uniquely enabled by the bi-encoder QA model because it builds a single passage representation that can simultaneously answer questions corresponding to all entity types.
It would be unclear how to use a language model or a cross-encoder QA model similarly for this initialization, as they must perform a separate forward pass for each question.
Using the cross-encoder student QA model with the same prompts leads to worse performance than the biencoder.
Question answering can provide a viable interface for building models that perform non-QA tasks.
The objective of matching the cross-encoder teacher model encourages the bi-encoder to learn important features identified by the cross-encoder, even on questions that are not entirely well-formed.
The authors develop alternative methods for few-shot learning that use token-level representations and question-based prompts, distinct from converting tasks to language modeling problems.
Decreasing the learning rate from $5 \cdot 10^{-5}$ to $2 \cdot 10^{-5}$ improved the RoBERTa baseline on CoNLL.
Calibration did not improve results for LM-BFF or the cross-encoder QA student model.
The design decisions (concatenating passages, using hard labels, two-stage beam search) have a relatively minor impact on the results.

findings.claim: RA-DIT is a lightweight fine-tuning methodology that provides a third option by retrofitting any LLM with retrieval capabilities.

RA-DIT operates in two distinct fine-tuning steps: (1) one updates a pre-trained LM to better use retrieved information, while (2) the other updates the retriever to return more relevant results, as preferred by the LM.
RA-IT models offer even larger performance boost when applied to smaller LLAMA models (7B and 13B).
The most gain can be achieved when combining LM-ft and R-ft in the RA-DIT method, which outperforms the REPLUG baseline by 0.8 points on average.

RA-DIT conducts parallel retrieval-augmentation for multiple retrieved passages.

RA-DIT is a lightweight Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning framework that can effectively retrofit any pre-trained LLM with retrieval capabilities.
RA-DIT updates the LLM with retrieval-augmented instruction tuning to make better use of retrieved knowledge and ignore irrelevant or distracting information.
RA-DIT fine-tunes the retriever with supervision from the LLM to retrieve texts that can better help the LLM generate correct outputs.
RA-DIT achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero- and few-shot evaluations on knowledge intensive benchmarks.
By fine-tuning over tasks that require both knowledge utilization and contextual awareness, each stage yields significant performance improvements, and using both leads to additional gains.
Lightweight instruction tuning alone can significantly boost the performance of RALMs, especially in knowledge intensive scenarios.
Language models and retrievers, when optimized independently and then fused through instruction-tuning, can compete effectively with RALMs that have undergone extensive continuous pre-training.
Supplementing the instruction-tuning data with unsupervised text leads to additional performance gains for both language model and retriever fine-tuning.
Integrating in-context retrieval augmentation during fine-tuning adapts the LLM to better utilize relevant background knowledge to make a prediction.

findings.claim: RAIN operates without the need of extra data for model alignment and abstains from any training, gradient computation, or parameter updates.
RAIN eliminates the need for maintaining additional models and avoids storing gradient information and computational graphs, resulting in memory usage matching vanilla auto-regressive inference.
Naïve generate-evaluate-regenerate method (cherry-pick sampling or reject sampling) results in significantly lower efficiency compared to RAIN.
RAIN is learning-free and does not rely on human annotations or any form of labeled or unlabeled data.
Larger models using RAIN enjoy no performance-alignment trade-off and smaller time overhead.
RAIN is data-free, while RLAIF requires a prompt dataset for alignment.
RAIN enables search and rewind operations for self-alignment of frozen LLMs in the inference phase.
The search process in RAIN can be conceptualized as occurring on a tree, where each node represents a token set.
RAIN can be seamlessly implemented as a plug-in, which can conveniently integrate with existing auto-regressive language models.
RAIN appears identical to vanilla auto-regressive inference if one only looks at the outer loop.
RAIN represents an emergent capability related to model size.
As the model size increases, the performance improvement of RAIN over vanilla auto-regressive inference becomes more pronounced.
For small-scale models, RAIN slightly reduces helpfulness, but this gap reduces with large-scale models.
For adequately large models, RAIN does not hurt performance on other objectives.
RAIN consistently surpasses vanilla auto-regressive inference in both cases, a superiority amplifying with model scale.
RAIN diminishes white-box attack success rates by 14%, 45%, and 75%, and transfer attack success rates by 25%, 47%, and 24% for models with 7B, 13B, and 33B parameters, respectively.
RAIN shows potential in boosting adversarial robustness under the static LLM-ATTACKS.
The responses generated by RAIN are more truthful.
RAIN can be compatible with existing alignment techniques, further enhancing the truthfulness of aligned models.
RAIN enhance the performance of LLaMA 7B by 20%.
Compared to RLHF and RLAIF, which require additional data, the efficacy of RAIN is comparable, if not superior.
RAIN necessitates a higher computational cost.
With the 30B model, RAIN demonstrates significantly better performance than multiple rounds of random search.
RAIN employs the results of self-evaluation to guide its search process, leading to greater efficiency.
RAIN experiences an acceptable time overhead.
Although self-evaluation can have errors, RAIN still significantly improves the model's performance.
Compared to vanilla auto-regressive inference, RAIN demands on average a 4-fold time increase on the LLaMA models for the HH dataset.
RAIN integrates self-evaluation of models and rewind functionalities into generation.
RAIN helps maintain or enhance the safety of well-aligned models like Vicuna and LLaMA-2 70B.
Frozen LLMs are self-alignable via RAIN without the use of additional data or further training.
Compared to standard auto-regressive inference, RAIN demands a longer yet acceptable inference time.
Employing RAIN for data generation and subsequently fine-tuning the model using this generated data can expedite the process by transferring additional inference overhead to the finetuning phase.
By integrating self-evaluation and rewind mechanisms, unaligned LLMs can directly produce responses consistent with human preferences via self-boosting.
The self-annotation and finetuning process utilized in works like RLAIF and Self-Alignment can be omitted for alignment.
LLMs' feedback quality is on par with human feedback.
The visit count of a candidate token set is positively correlated with its average value.
The time overhead shrinks w.r.t. the increased safety of the models.
When used during the inference phase, frozen LLMs are capable of generating responses that are aligned with human preferences.

findings.claim: REFA is a new alignment framework that proposes probabilistic control on a structural token that controls termination.
REFA's core innovation is a new class of regularizers that operate directly on the probability of the End-of-Sequence (EOS) token.
The token-level intervention in REFA provides a principled solution to the URSLA shortcut, ensuring genuine quality improvements.
REFA unlocks a versatile mechanism for managing the alignment-efficiency tradeoff, enabling practitioners to fine-tune models that adhere to specific token budgets.
REFA is a new alignment framework that proposes probabilistic control on a structural token that governs termination.
REFA is designed to leverage the full spectrum of available data by operating on sets of preferred and rejected responses.
The core innovation of REFA is a new class of regularizers that operate directly on the probability of the End-of-Sequence (EOS) token.
REFA achieves state-of-the-art results in iterative, on-policy alignment, reaching a 60.29% win rate on AlpacaEval2 with Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
REFA is a reference-free, multi-preference alignment method.
REFA introduces a novel approach to fine-grained control via an End-of-Sequence (EOS) probability regularizer.
REFA aims to synthesize the strengths of SimPO, InfoNCA, and MPO within a single, coherent, reference-free framework that also solves the URSLA shortcut.
REFA-InfoNCA can be suboptimal for alignment because it may require the model to continue assigning non-trivial probability to undesirable responses.
REFA-Dynamic uses a group-contrastive loss that generalizes the Bradley-Terry model to sets of responses in a reference-free setting.
The REFA-Dynamic loss is minimized as the probabilities of all rejected responses approach zero.
REFA-Dynamic offers a theoretically superior objective compared to distribution matching.
W-REFA is particularly effective in off-policy experiments.
Unweighted REFA-Dynamic shows strong performance in on-policy settings where reward model noise is a greater concern.
REFA introduces a novel approach of fine-grained, token-level intervention to address length-based reward hacking, unlike prior methods that apply sequence-level normalization or regularization.

By identifying and solving the subtle failure modes introduced by length normalization itself, REFA not only achieves more robust alignment but also provides a practical framework for managing the inference-time budget.
REFA-Dynamic is designed to be robust and is particularly effective in on-policy and iterative settings where reward model scores may be noisy or less calibrated.

The core idea of REFA-Dynamic is to use the reward signal to partition responses into positive and negative sets, and then optimize a contrastive objective on the model's length-normalized probabilities, while simultaneously regularizing the model's termination behavior to prevent the URSLA shortcut.
W-REFA is designed for scenarios, such as off-policy training, where fine-grained and reliable reward scores are available.
W-REFA allows the model to prioritize more informative examples, defined as those with rewards far from the mean.

The cross-entropy objective in REFA-InfoNCA provides a positive gradient push to all responses with a non-zero target probability, regardless of their quality, encouraging the model to waste capacity on low-quality responses.

The objective in REFA-InfoNCA creates 'gradient conflicts' among high-quality responses, as each is incentivized to increase its own probability at the expense of all others, hindering their collective improvement.
The REFA-Dynamic loss resolves gradient conflicts among positive responses by moving from a sum of individual objectives to a single, group-contrastive term.

In REFA-Dynamic, partitioning responses into positive and negative sets and treating them asymmetrically (positives in numerator, negatives only in denominator) prevents the model from directly promoting low-quality responses.
For the REFA-Dynamic loss, the gradient for any negative response is strictly positive, while the gradient for a positive response is negative.
The stationary point of the REFA-Dynamic loss is achieved only as the probability of all negative responses approaches zero.

Under the URSLA principle, any length-normalized objective that penalizes negative responses (like REFA-Dynamic) creates a perverse incentive for the model to shorten negative responses to increase their per-token uncertainty and satisfy the loss.
The gradient of the simplified REFA-Dynamic loss w.r.t. $s_y$ is $p_y^{model} - p_y^{pos}$ if $y \in Y^+$ and $p_y^{model}$ if $y \in Y^-$.
To decrease $L_{\mathrm{REFA - dynamic}}(\theta)$, the model must increase $\pi_{\theta}(y|x)$ for $y \in Y^{+}$ and avoid increasing $\pi_{\theta}(y|x)$ for $y \in Y^{-}$.

Given two responses with similar average token probabilities, if one is shorter, it typically has a higher probability, incentivizing shorter responses as a shortcut to reduce $L_{\mathrm{REFA - dynamic}}(\theta)$.

Length normalization introduces a failure mode called the URSLA shortcut, where models learn to satisfy the alignment objective by prematurely truncating low-quality responses rather than learning from their semantic content.
Viewing generation as a sequential decision-making process, the EOS token acts as the transition to a "terminal state" in the MDP, making it a uniquely powerful point of intervention.
Token-level control on the EOS token directly counteracts the URSLA shortcut and transforms output length into a controllable parameter.
Robust control of length-based reward hacking requires moving beyond the sequence level to intervene directly on the model's termination logic at the token level.
Models can learn to shorten negative responses to satisfy the loss.
The Targeted Regularizer counteracts the URSLA shortcut by penalizing premature termination.
As $\lambda$ increases, the average token count decreases, and the entire length distribution shifts towards shorter and precise outputs.

findings.claim: Reversed-phase ion pair high performance liquid chromatography (RP-IP HPLC) was used to identify a class of impurity formed through lipid:mRNA reactions that are typically undetectable by traditional mRNA purity analytical techniques.
RP-IP HPLC retains selectivity to variations in mRNA hydrophobicity due to sequence or chemical modifications, unlike CE which is driven by size and charge.
The RP-IP HPLC profile of adduct species varied in retention times across different chemistries likely based on size and hydrophobicity of the adducted lipid structure
In RP-IP HPLC assays, relative UV intensity of the LP peak is correlated with relative mass, consistent with a constant rate of reaction on the single base level.
A correlation between relative mRNA integrity (including the adduct as an impurity) and protein expression was found when assessed using RP-IP HPLC
Only combinations including the ionizable lipid resulted in significant adduct formation with mRNA by reversed phase-ion pair high performance liquid chromatography (RP-IP HPLC).
The RP-IP HPLC adduct profiles of mRNA extracted from the binary system and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) with the same ionizable lipid show the same qualitative peak profile.

Adduct formation in a binary reaction with a highly reactive lipid evaluated by RP-IP HPLC at 1 day, 2 days, and 7 days shows increased tailing likely corresponding to the accumulation of multiple adducts per mRNA molecule.
A positive correlation was observed, with more adduct at longer mRNA lengths, for mRNA-LNP and corresponding binaries assessed by RP-IP HPLC.
RP-IP HPLC provides specificity and sensitivity to detect adducted mRNA molecules, which are otherwise difficult to identify due to the low rate of modification.
RP-IP HPLC can detect even single adduct events on intact mRNA, whereas in contrast, even purified LP is not distinguished by the conventional CE methodology.

It is critical that formation of these mRNA-lipid adducts are examined during formulation design, clinical evaluation, and commercialization by using appropriate RP-IP HPLC methodologies to ensure there is no loss in mRNA integrity.
RP-IP HPLC is able to resolve aldehyde species differing only by a short alkyl chain, highlighting the selectivity of the RP-IP HPLC method to detect minute differences on the intact mRNA molecule.
This study highlights the need for advanced methods such as RP-IP HPLC to ensure the quality, consistency, and efficacy of any pharmaceutical product.

findings.claim: Live cell imaging of mitochondrial ATP dynamics is a powerful tool to evaluate metabolic flexibility and heterogeneity at a single-cell level.

Different cell types, including cancer cells, show specific mitochondrial ATP responses.
Subcellular ATP signals are used to assess metabolic activity and flexibility at the single-cell level.
Mitochondria dynamically supply ATP for glucose phosphorylation in a variety of cancer cell types.
The hexokinase-dependent process of mitochondrial ATP supply for glucose phosphorylation is reversed upon the removal of glucose or other hexose sugars.

Mitochondrial ATP levels in aged MEFs were less affected by glucose removal but clearly reduced by cell treatment with oligomycin, indicating enhanced oxidative phosphorylation in senescent MEFs.
Mfn2 ablation modifies the metabolic setting of cells in favor of oxidative phosphorylation.

The SAIL-7B model can steadily utilize the helpful information among the search results.

SAIL addresses RALM limitations by employing real-world search engines, introducing a search result denoising process capable of filtering out distracting information, and incorporating instruction fine-tuning.

SAIL demonstrates its superiority in broader applications, including instruction following for chatbots, fact and fairness checking, all of which benefit from access to up-to-date information retrieved from real-world search engines.

findings.claim: The SAMMR method does not need to extract the dispersion coefficients or use the metric functions.
The SAMMR method affords a better performance for axial resolution and the signal-to-noise ratio in vis-OCT systems compared to previous methods.
The proposed SAMMR method requires only a single arbitrary measurement of mirror reflection to extract the phase delay caused by the material dispersion imbalance, involving no mirror movement.
The proposed SAMMR method demonstrates a better performance for axial resolution and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the vis-OCT system compared with the previous methods, i.e., TSIF and TSMMR.
The proposed SAMMR method only compensates for dispersions caused by the instrument itself and requires the measurement of mirror reflection before taking the images.
SAMMR method requires only a single measurement of a mirror reflection with arbitrary OPD within the imaging depth.
The SAMMR method provided a PSF of better symmetry than that of the TSMMR method.
The symmetry metric indicates the better symmetrical property of PSF calculated by the SAMMR method.
The linear amplitude of PSFs with different dispersion compensation methods demonstrates the best performance of the SAMMR method.
The proposed SAMMR method provides both the highest SNR and the smallest FWHM of PSF compared to TSIF and TSMMR methods.
The SAMMR method extracts material dispersion-induced phase delay ($\phi_{D}$) and uses it to compensate for dispersions in B-frames.
SAMMR method provides the PSF with the best symmetrical property compared to TSIF and other phase-based methods when additional dispersion is introduced.
SAMMR method provides the dispersion-compensated PSF with the highest SNR, the smallest FWHM, and the best contrast compared to the other two methods.
SAMMR method achieves comparable FWHM and contrast in both cases with and without additional dispersions in the vis-OCT system.

The SAMMR method avoids the translation and tilting of the mirror in the reference arm by requiring only one measurement of the mirror reflection, thereby improving dispersion compensation performance.
Directly using the SAMMR method on a spectral interferogram caused artificial peaks in the resulting A-line.
The observations verified the effectiveness and robustness of the SAMMR method for dispersion compensation in the vis-OCT system.
SAMMR method eliminates potential phase errors caused by limited mechanical accuracy of the translational stage in the TSMMR method and tilting of optical alignment in the reference arm.
SAMMR method provided an ultrahigh axial resolution of about 1.5 μm in vis-OCT imaging.
The robustness of SAMMR was validated through effective compensation of additional material and higher-order (more than third-order) dispersions in the vis-OCT system.
The effectiveness and genericity of SAMMR were demonstrated in an 800 nm SD-OCT system.
SAMMR method is only applicable in OCT systems where measuring the mirror reflection in the sample arm is possible.
SAMMR method only compensates for material dispersion in the OCT interferometer, not dispersion induced by the sample itself.
SAMMR method assumes material dispersion is the same in the full field of view (FOV) of the sample arm due to single measurement of PSF with a normally incident laser beam.
The SAMMR and TSMMR methods offered greater improvements in the sharpness and SNR of images when compared with the TSIF method.
The SAMMR and TSMMR methods show sharper images using the TSIF method.
SAMMR and TSMMR methods can compensate for all higher-order dispersions, unlike other tested methods.
The symmetrical property, SNR, FWHM, and contrast of PSF could be further improved using phase-based TSMMR and SAMMR methods.
TSMMR and SAMMR methods are phase-based and consider higher-order (>3rd order) dispersion, while TSIF method only considers up to the third-order dispersion.
Removing residual DC signal by moving an average window helps avoid potential artificial peaks in A-lines.
Dispersion-compensated fingertip images show significantly sharpened tissue structure with improved contrast compared to original images.
Dispersion-compensated onion images clearly delineate finer cell wall structures compared to original images.
Sharpened cell wall structures with improved SNR values are indicated by spiculate peaks along the imaging depth in a representative A-line.
Imaging the sample at the corner of FOV leads to a different dispersion compared to the measurement in the middle of the FOV due to tilted light beam in the scan lens.
Future work aims to develop a digital dispersion compensation method not requiring mirror reflection measurement, capable of compensating for sample dispersion and spatially dependent dispersion.

findings.claim: SELF-RAG enhances an LM's quality and factuality through retrieval and self-reflection.

SELF-RAG trains a single arbitrary LM that adaptively retrieves passages on-demand, and generates and reflects on retrieved passages and its own generations using special tokens, called reflection tokens.
SELF-RAG outperforms ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat on Open-domain QA, reasoning and fact verification tasks.
SELF-RAG shows significant gains in improving factuality and citation accuracy for long-form generations relative to ChatGPT and retrieval-augmented Llama2-chat.
SELF-RAG improves an LLM's generation quality, including its factual accuracy without hurting its versatility, via on-demand retrieval and self-reflection.
SELF-RAG provides citations for each segment with its self-assessment of whether the output is supported by the passage, leading to easier fact verification.

SELF-RAG enables a customizable decoding algorithm to satisfy hard or soft constraints defined by reflection token predictions, allowing flexible adjustment of retrieval frequency and customization of models' behaviors to user preferences.

SELF-RAG significantly outperforms pre-trained and instruction-tuned LLMs that have more parameters and widely adopted RAG approaches with higher citation accuracy on six tasks, including reasoning and long-form generation.
SELF-RAG outperforms retrieval-augmented ChatGPT on four tasks, Llama2-chat and Alpaca on all tasks.
SELF-RAG enables retrieval on demand and selection of the best possible model output via fine-grained self-reflection, making it widely applicable and more robust and controllable.
SELF-RAG processes passages in parallel and filters out irrelevant ones through self-reflection, without relying on external models at inference.
The self-reflection mechanism in SELF-RAG evaluates other aspects of the model output quality including factuality.
SELF-RAG trains an arbitrary LM to learn to generate fine-grained self-reflection and customizable inference.
SELF-RAG trains the target LM on task examples augmented with reflection tokens from a critic model offline, with a far lower training cost compared to RLHF.
Reflection tokens in SELF-RAG enable controllable generation at inference, while RLHF focuses on human preference alignment during training.
Other works use general control tokens to guide LM generation, while SELF-RAG uses reflection tokens to decide the need for retrieval and to self-evaluate generation quality.
SELF-RAG is a framework that enhances the quality and factuality of an LLM through retrieval and self-reflection, without sacrificing LLM's original creativity and versatility.
SELF-RAG processes multiple passages in parallel to generate each segment.
SELF-RAG uses its own generated reflection tokens to enforce soft constraints or hard control over the generated task output.
SELF-RAG enables an arbitrary LM to generate text with reflection tokens by unifying them as next token predictions from the expanded model vocabulary.
SELF-RAG significantly reduces training costs compared to PPO by computing critique offline and inserting them into the training corpus.
SELF-RAG tailors an LM with no additional training.
SELF-RAG demonstrates a substantial performance advantage over supervised fine-tuned LLMs in all tasks and outperforms ChatGPT in PubHealth, PopQA, biography generations, and ASQA (Rouge and MAUVE).
On the bio generation task, SELF-RAG 7B and 13B models outperform the concurrent method CoVE, which iteratively prompts Llama2_65B to refine output.
SELF-RAG obtains the best performance among non-proprietary LM-based models on all tasks.
On ASQA, SELF-RAG shows significantly higher citation precision and recall than all models except ChatGPT.
SELF-RAG bridges the performance gap in citation precision, even outperforming ChatGPT.
SELF-RAG gains are not solely from training data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the SELF-RAG framework.
Training an LM with No Retriever or No Critic models largely contributes to the performance gain of SELF-RAG.
Human annotators find SELF-RAG answers are often plausible and supported by relevant passages with higher S&P scores on short-form PopQA.

SELF-RAG trains an LM to learn to retrieve, generate, and critique text passages and its own generation by predicting the next tokens from its original vocabulary as well as newly added special tokens, called reflection tokens.
SELF-RAG enables the tailoring of LM behaviors at test time by leveraging reflection tokens.
SELF-RAG significantly outperforms LLMs with more parameters or with conventional retrieval-augmented generation approaches.
SELF-RAG can still generate outputs that are not fully supported by the citations.
SELF-RAG significantly less frequently generates answers that are not included in the provided evidence compared to Alpaca 30B, Llama2-chat 13B, and Alpaca.
When retrieved passages are not relevant, SELF-RAG generates ISREL=Irrelevant, indicating that the following answers may not be factually grounded.
Generating reflection tokens makes the LM controllable during the inference phase, enabling it to tailor its behavior to diverse task requirements.
Reflection tokens are categorized into retrieval and critique tokens to indicate the need for retrieval and its generation quality respectively.
Reflection tokens are inserted offline into the original corpus by a trained critic model, which eliminates the need to host a critic model during training, reducing overhead.
The critic model is supervised on a dataset of input, output, and corresponding reflection tokens collected by prompting a propriety LM (i.e., GPT-4).

findings.claim: SKILL-IT obtains 36.5 points higher accuracy than random sampling on the LEGO synthetic in the continual pre-training setting.
SKILL-IT reduces the validation loss on the target skill by 13.6% versus training on data associated with the target skill itself on the Natural Instructions dataset in the fine-tuning setting.

Applying the skills framework to continually pre-train a 3B-parameter LM on the RedPajama dataset achieves higher accuracy on the LM Evaluation Harness with 1B tokens than the baseline approach of sampling uniformly over data sources with 3B tokens.
Skill-stratified sampling is static and does not incorporate the ordering as training proceeds, resulting in oversampling skills that may be already learned early on in training.
SKILL-IT prioritizes prerequisite skills and skills that are not yet learned.
For the complete graph, the SKILL-IT algorithm reduces to stratified sampling.
For a skill set with an empty graph, the SKILL-IT update rule reduces to sampling proportional to each skill's validation loss.
SKILL-IT outperforms baselines that do not use skills as well as skill-stratified sampling.
Both skill-stratified sampling and SKILL-IT are able to significantly reduce loss on all skills, but the former is slower.
SKILL-IT outperforms skill-stratified sampling by initially allocating more weight to prerequisite skills and eventually allocating more weight to skills that are learned more slowly.
On the addition synthetic with k = 3, SKILL-IT converges to near-zero validation loss faster than the baselines on skills 1 and 2.
SKILL-IT results in the same validation loss of 0.01 as training only on the target skill in 38.1% fewer steps on LEGO.
SKILL-IT converges to a validation loss of 0.01 in 59% fewer steps required to do so when training only on the target skill on addition.
SKILL-IT improves validation loss on Spanish question generation by 5.3% over just training on the respective target skill.
SKILL-IT improves validation loss on Stance Detection by 13.6% over just training on the respective target skill.
The skill-stratified sampling approach uses the ordered skill set to identify prerequisite skills, but does not exploit them dynamically.
A significant portion of the improvement over training only on the target skill comes from identification of prerequisite skills through the learned graph in the skill-stratified sampling method.
SKILL-IT is able to improve performance with finer-grained dynamic weighting on prerequisite skills.
SKILL-IT outperforms uniform sampling over the data sources when continually pre-training a 3B parameter model on RedPajama.
SKILL-IT achieves higher accuracy with 1B additional tokens than uniform with 3B additional tokens.

SKILL-IT focuses on understanding how skills are related to each other and induce some order in how LMs learn by explicitly modeling skill graph structure, which is important for data-efficient LM training.
SKILL-IT studies how to select data for learning one or many skills at the mixture level for LMs instead of the instance level.
SKILL-IT finds that embedding-based heuristics do not fully identify skills.
SKILL-IT utilizes a curriculum defined over a skills graph, which does not necessarily align with training on easiest to hardest skills.
SKILL-IT finds in synthetics that feature similarity does not always recover skills.
SKILL-IT incorporates the skills graph into a dynamic sampling algorithm, looks more broadly at skills rather than tasks, and characterizes when using the skills graph improves model performance.
SKILL-IT outperforms random sampling by 3.2% on average across skills in the Natural Instructions continual pre-training experiment.
SKILL-IT initially allocates more weight to skill 2 and less to 1, 3, 4, 5 in the LEGO pre-training experiment.
SKILL-IT allocates more weight to skill 2 in the addition pre-training experiment because it has an edge to skill 1.
SKILL-IT allocates very little weight to skill 3 in the addition pre-training experiment because it is learned faster than the other two skills.
In the addition pre-training experiment, SKILL-IT eventually puts more weight on skill 1, the hardest skill, before converging to uniform sampling.
SKILL-IT outperforms random and skill-stratified sampling on average for the LEGO synthetic experiment on the 1.3B model.
SKILL-IT outperforms random and skill-stratified sampling on average for the Natural Instructions pre-training experiment on the 1.3B model.
SKILL-IT initially allocates more weight to skill 2, which has an edge to skill 1, while allocating little weight to skill 3 which is learned quickly.
SKILL-IT puts more weight on the harder skill 1 before converging to uniform sampling when all losses roughly approach 0.
SKILL-IT on average still outperforms random and skill-stratified sampling when skills graph is learned on a 125M parameter model and used for data selection with a 1.3B model.
SKILL-IT initially allocates more weight to skill 2, but eventually puts more weight on skills 4 and 5 before converging to uniform sampling when all losses converge to near 0.
SKILL-IT on average still outperforms random and skill-stratified sampling even though the edges used by SKILL-IT are not derived from the larger model.
Both the graph and the online dynamics of SKILL-IT are important for its performance.
Simple baselines, including using a static graph and no graph perform similarly to SKILL-IT on average across all skills on the Addition dataset.

findings.claim: Single-Molecule Kinetic Fingerprinting combined with aptasensors permits high-accuracy discrimination of ligand bound and ligand-free states, resulting in zero background.
The detection limits achieved by Single-Molecule Kinetic Fingerprinting are superior to recently reported aptasensors.

Single-molecule kinetic fingerprinting provides a unique approach to probe the dynamic behavior of aptamer-ligand binding processes, allowing for high-accuracy discrimination between analyte bound and apo states of single aptasensor molecules.
The programmable dynamics of the hairpin enables fine-tuning of the hybridization kinetics of the fluorescent probe, rendering the acquisition time sufficiently flexible to optimize discrimination.
The hybridization kinetics of the short ssDNA probe is highly sensitive to the number of base pairs formed with, and thus the secondary structure of, the nucleic acid target.
The method allows for the absolute discrimination between the ligand bound and ligand-free states by discriminating the binding kinetics of the short probe.
High sensitivity was achieved because the ligand-free state can be confidently screened out based on its distinct kinetics.
The stochastic switching of fluorescence signals between bound (ON-) and unbound (OFF-) states is attributed to the binding and dissociation of the fluorescent probe.
The change in hairpin accessibility directly reflects the binding of a single analyte molecule, provided that ligand dissociation is sufficiently slow.

The standard deviation in the number of binding and dissociation events per aptasensor molecule is expected to increase only as the square root of the number, implying that signal acquisition time can be prolonged to distinguish states with distinct probe binding kinetics to arbitrarily high accuracy.
No background peak was observed in the presence of ligand, implying that all aptasensors are occupied under the concentration of ligand used.
The diffusion-driven fluorescent probe binding provides resistance against photobleaching as the probe is continuously exchanged with bulk solution.
The hairpin with a higher stability requires a shorter acquisition time than that with a lower stability for good separation of the bound and ligand-free states.
The rate constant of hairpin opening and closing is 100- to 800-fold faster than that of binding of the short fluorescent probe.
The ratio of k_on,b and k_on,f is a function of K_eq,H, whereas the ratio of k_off,b and k_off,f is close to one and independent of K_eq,H.
For all nucleic acid constructs, the ligand bound and ligand-free states can be discriminated within 20 min.

A hairpin with a longer stem yields limited accessibility for the fluorescent probe in the absence of analyte and a larger change in the hybridization kinetics of the fluorescent probe upon ligand binding, rendering the time needed to resolve the Poisson peaks shorter.
Using single-molecule kinetics fingerprinting, background signal due to sensor leakage is completely excluded.
A hairpin with a shorter stem yields more single-molecule counts that more quickly resolve the Poisson peaks.
The sensitivity of the adenosine aptasensor is superior to some recently reported aptasensors.
No other nucleosides, including guanosine, cytidine, and thymidine, gave a significantly higher signal than the blank for the adenosine aptasensor.
The LODs of acetamiprid and PCB-77 are superior to recently reported biosensors.
The leakage of the aptasensor was suppressed by sorting single-molecule time traces by their kinetic probing behavior.
Three analytes were detected with remarkable sensitivity.

The SDSBEC can operate with E_R far below ℏ, whereas the best-developed approaches to superconducting, hot vapor, and color center magnetometers are limited to E_R ≳ ℏ.
With a 87Rb SDSBEC, the authors demonstrated E_R = 0.075(16)ℏ, a factor of 17 improvement over the best previously reported.
The single-domain, ultracold two-body interactions allow the system to escape the coherence vs. density trade-off that imposes an energy resolution limit on traditional spin precession sensors.

findings.claim: Socratic Models (SMs) are a modular framework in which multiple pretrained models may be composed zero-shot via multimodal-informed prompting to exchange information and capture new multimodal capabilities without finetuning.
In Socratic models (SMs), the composition is pre-determined and fixed for each task.
Socratic Models are competitive with state-of-the-art zero-shot image captioning and video-to-text retrieval.

Socratic Models enable new applications such as answering free-form questions about egocentric video, engaging in multimodal assistive dialogue with people by interfacing with external APIs and databases, and robot perception and planning.
Socratic Models (SMs) is a modular framework in which new tasks are formulated as a language-based exchange between pretrained models and other modules, without additional training or finetuning.

SMs are quantitatively competitive with zero-shot state-of-the-art on standard benchmarks including image captioning on MS COCO, contextual image captioning on Concadia, and video understanding with video-to-text retrieval on MSR-VTT.
SMs enable new capabilities across applications such as open-ended reasoning for egocentric perception, multimodal assistive dialogue, and robot perception-driven planning.
SMs can answer free-form questions about first-person videos by assembling video into a language-based world-state history and performing open-ended text-prompted tasks about that history.
The Socratic Models framework proposes to compose multimodal pretrained models through language, without requiring training.
Socratic Models can be a strong alternative for applications in which data is less available or more expensive to obtain.
Socratic Models (SMs) is a framework in which multiple large pretrained models may be composed through language (via prompting) without requiring training, to perform new downstream multimodal tasks.
SMs substantially outperform the zero-shot state-of-the-art ZeroCap
SMs do not perform as well as methods such as ClipCap which are directly finetuned on the training set
SMs 3-shot exceeds the performance of MAGIC which finetunes the text generator on the training set's unpaired captions
SMs outperform the task-specific prior best method, Kreiss et al. [17], on Concadia test split
Socratic Models sets a new zero-shot state-of-the-art on MSR-VTT
SMs offer a zero-shot alternative to perform egocentric perceptual tasks without training on large domain-specific datasets
The SMs-based approach formulates video understanding as reading comprehension, re-framing “video Q&A” as a “short story Q&A” problem
SMs with VLM, Web Search, and LM prompting can enable multimodal dialogue applications such as guiding a user through online recipe steps and providing assistive visuals via video search.
Socratic Models is a modular framework that leverages structured dialogue (i.e., via prompting) between multiple large pretrained models to make joint predictions for new multimodal tasks.

SMs leverage the commonsense knowledge already stored within foundation models pretrained on different domains of data (e.g., text-to-text, text-to-images, text-to-audio), which may include Internet-scale data.
SMs can adapt pre-existing foundation models to capture new multimodal functionalities zero-shot without having to rely on additional domain-specific data collection or model finetuning.
SMs retain robustness to distribution shifts, which is known to deteriorate after finetuning.
No model training was used to create the demonstrated results of Socratic Models.
In the Socratic Models system for egocentric perception, it is necessary to use a third baseline VLM paired with a strong LM to generate pseudo ground truth instead of the VLM being evaluated.

Upon correcting the evaluation protocol (i.e., increasing the number of associated captions per video to 20), R@1 for Portillo-Quintero et al. [67] improves to 58.0, and SMs improve on top of that with LMs and ALMs to 60.7 R@1 zero-shot.
Socratic Models can provide meaningful results for complex egocentric tasks without any model finetuning.
Socratic Models can reconcile the complementary strengths of pretrained foundation models to address egocentric perception difficulties through contextual reasoning.
Socratic Models generates Socratic image summaries of individual video frames which are concatenated with timestamps to form an event log used as context for a language model.
Socratic Models generally produces more relevant captions for a larger portion of the egocentric examples compared to state-of-the-art image captioning models.
Socratic Models can produce reasonable captions without additional training on domain-specific data.
Socratic Models can perform open-ended multimodal-informed completion of text prompts conditioned on egocentric video, generating compelling answers to open-ended reasoning tasks.
The answers generated by Socratic Models may inherit undesirable characteristics from component models, such as an LM being overconfident even when wrong.
Tasks such as summarization, open-ended Q&A, forecasting, corrections, and video search can be subsumed under the same unified language-based system for multimodal reasoning using Socratic Models.
The accuracy of answers and explanations in the Socratic Models system is largely conditioned on whether the necessary information can be found within the world-state history.
The quality of language-based reconstructions of videos (e.g., via key frame sampling and captioning) is central to the approach of Socratic Models.

Socratic Models can perform simple retrieval of events (recall questions) and provide natural language responses including negative answers, expanding beyond standard video search which might only return nearest neighbor video frames.

A common failure mode for temporal reasoning questions in Socratic Models is that the system tends to over-count, especially as a reaction to false positive VLM detection results that get surfaced into the world-state history.
Socratic Models can answer questions about cause and effect relationships between events, conditioned on that all the events appear in the world-state history.
Socratic Models with LMs enables generating more semantically interpretable descriptions of future events, conditioned on multimodal information.

findings.claim: In Striped Attention, each device has a subset of tokens distributed uniformly throughout the sequence instead of contiguous subsequences.
Striped Attention permutes the sequence so that every device always operates on a discontinuous subset of tokens distributed approximately uniformly throughout the original sequence.
Striped Attention ensures that approximately half of the query/key interactions on each device will be inhibited by the causal mask.
Striped Attention is an exact attention algorithm that exploits the permutation equivariance of the core attention computation to ensure the internal permutation does not affect the final output.
Striped Attention is able to take advantage of the structure of causal attention to save time on every iteration, unlike Ring Attention.

findings.claim: The pharmacokinetics and distribution of h-α-Gal A mRNA encoded protein in WT mice demonstrated prolonged half-lives of α-Gal A in tissues and plasma.
Single intravenous administration of h-α-Gal A mRNA to Gla-deficient mice showed dose-dependent protein activity and substrate reduction.
Repeat i.v. administration of h-α-Gal A mRNA showed a sustained pharmacodynamic response and efficacy in Fabry mice model.

These studies across species demonstrate preclinical proof-of-concept of systemic mRNA therapy for the treatment of Fabry disease and this approach may be useful for other lysosomal storage disorders.

A single intravenous (i.v.) administration of h-α-Gal A mRNA in Gla-deficient mice showed a dose-dependent restoration of h-α-Gal A activity with concomitant depletion of lyso-Gb3 in plasma and tissues (liver, kidney, heart, spleen).
lyso-Gb3 concentrations in plasma and tissues were significantly reduced 6 weeks after a single i.v. injection of h-α-Gal A mRNA in Fabry mice.
Repeat i.v. administration (every other week and monthly) of h-α-Gal A mRNA in Fabry mice demonstrated significant substrate reduction (lyso-Gb3 and Gb3) in a dose-dependent manner.

Administration of h-α-Gal A mRNA every other week in WT NHPs demonstrated sustained functional α-Gal A protein in plasma after each dose, with the absence of an immune responses to the protein encoded by the mRNA.
These preclinical proof-of-concept studies indicate that systemic mRNA therapy could be a potential treatment for Fabry disease.
Repeat i.v. administration of h-α-Gal A mRNA did not induce immune responses in these mice, as no notable change in anti-h-α-Gal A antibody levels was detected.

Significant h-α-Gal A activity accumulation was observed in the EOW group dosed with 0.5 mg/kg of h-α-Gal A mRNA compared to the group receiving a single dose, demonstrating no neutralizing anti-α-Gal A antibody development.
Efficacy in Fabry mice receiving h-α-Gal A mRNA EOW is equivalent to monthly dosing at 0.5 mg/kg irrespective of the substrate evaluated (i.e., Gb3 or lyso-Gb3).

h-α-Gal A encoded by exogenously administrated h-α-Gal A mRNA has a prolonged plasma and tissue half-life, resulting in greater clearance of heart and kidney substrates than published data using ERT, combination therapy of ERT/CT, and some gene therapy.
Long duration (up to 6 weeks) of substrate reductions in tissues and plasma were observed after a single injection.
Multiple administrations to non-human primates confirmed safety and translatability.

Therapeutic proteins made from exogenously administered mRNA in the body may mimic the endogenous target protein more closely than recombinant proteins, such as ERTs, which are manufactured from CHO, human, or plant cell lines.
mRNA treatment produces transient protein levels, while avoiding genomic integration and the off-target risks of gene therapy or gene editing therapy.

Preclinical studies demonstrated restoration of functional human methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (hMUT) and human porphobilinogen deaminase (hPBGD) in the liver by systemic mRNA treatment with corresponding amelioration of disease in animal models of MMA and AIP, respectively.
The half-lives of h-α-Gal A in liver, heart, and kidney were more than 100 h.
Persistent h-α-Gal A activity was observed in liver, heart, and kidney tissues throughout the study (160 h after dose).
h-α-Gal A protein was found to localize in liver tissue lysosomes of the Fabry mice
h-α-Gal A activity was dose responsive in liver, kidney, heart, spleen, and plasma
Kidney and heart isolated from low and mid dose group mice did not have significant reduction in substrate compared to untreated control (eGFP group)
h-α-Gal A staining remains detectable in heart and liver 42 days after a single administration
Enzyme h-α-Gal A activity was detectable in plasma, heart, and liver tissues at day 28 after dose
Lyso-Gb3 levels did not return to baseline levels by completion of the study (84 days or 12 weeks after dose)
IHC analysis of liver samples demonstrated a dose-responsive increase in h-α-Gal A by protein staining in the liver with a rank order of 0.5 mg/kg EOW > 0.5 mg/kg monthly > 0.2 mg/kg EOW.
Liver enzymes remained within normal reference ranges after one or four consecutive i.v. administrations of h- $\alpha$ -Gal A mRNA in NHPs.
Administration of h- $\alpha$ -Gal A mRNA did not induce an immune response in NHPs, as indicated by no increase trend in serum anti- $\alpha$ -Gal A antibody levels.
Exogenously administered mRNA packaged in bio-degradable LNPs is taken up by the liver, translated into h-α-Gal A, secreted into circulation, and targeted to lysosomes via endocytosis.
The extended circulation time of h-α-Gal A relative to agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme) and agalsidase alfa (Replagal) allows for better tissue distribution.
h-α-Gal A produced in liver from administered mRNA distributes to heart, kidney, and spleen.
In the Fabry mouse model, lyso-Gb3 substrate was maximally reduced for 4-6 weeks after a single dose and remained below baseline through 12 weeks.

Enzyme levels in tissues correlate with the dose level and frequency of administration of LNP encapsulated mRNA.
Repeated mRNA administration to Fabry mice or NHP did not result in anti h-α-Gal A antibody production, indicating improved tolerability to the human protein produced in the murine liver.
mRNA administration results in the production of functional h-α-Gal A in liver, which is secreted into the circulation and taken up by distal tissues such as kidney, heart, and spleen

findings.claim: Dropping the encoder module in T-D reduces model parameters by almost half for a given hyper-parameter set.
In T-D, error signals are propagated from both input and output time-steps during training because the model is forced to predict the next token in the input as well as the output.
For monolingual text-to-text tasks, redundant information is re-learned about language in the encoder and decoder of T-ED, which allows for easier optimization in T-D.
T-D exhibits easier optimization with longer sequences.
In T-D, when generating the next token, attention from both the input sequence m and the output sequence y are considered due to the self-attention of the Transformer.
T-DMCA allows processing sequences 3x in length over the T-D model.
The Transformer-Decoder (T-D) could learn and improve up to L = 4000 before running out of memory on 16GB GPU RAM.
T-DMCA modifications allowed training up to L = 11000 with continued performance improvements.
The T-DMCA model does statistically significantly better on all linguistic quality dimensions except non-redundancy, where tf-idf performs about as well.

T-DMCA performs better on American Actors than Diseases, probably because of the prevalence of the former (and biographies) in Wikipedia compared to the latter in our training set for our single, global model, whereas Sauper & Barzilay likely benefit from the category-specific templates.
On average T-DMCA ROUGE-1 scores are higher than Sauper & Barzilay (2009) but do worse on the less common and somewhat specific disease category.
The T-DMCA model offers a respectable alternative to the Wikipedia version and is more succinct while mentioning key facts.
Generating English Wikipedia articles can be approached as a multi-document summarization of source documents.
The model can generate fluent, coherent multi-sentence paragraphs and even whole Wikipedia articles.
When given reference documents, the model can extract relevant factual information as reflected in perplexity, ROUGE scores and human evaluations.
The authors describe the first attempt to abstractively generate the first section (lead) of Wikipedia articles conditioned on reference text.
A decoder-only modification of the Transformer architecture performs better in the case of longer input sequences compared to recurrent neural network (RNN) and Transformer encoder-decoder models.
In the current work, neural abstractive models are trained in the multi-document regime with Wikipedia, where input and output text are generally much larger with significant variance.
The current dataset has a ROUGE-1 recall score of 59.2, compared to 76.1 and 78.7 for other summarization datasets, showing it is the least amenable to purely extractive methods.
The task is treated as a sequence transduction problem from very long input sequences to medium output sequences.
Memory-compressed attention layers are able to exchange information globally on the entire sequence, unlike local attention layers which only capture local information within a block.
Optimizing for perplexity correlates with increased ROUGE and human judgment for the task of generating Wikipedia articles.
The best abstractive model more than doubled the ROUGE-L F1 metric compared to extractive-only methods.
The MoE-layer helped performance by adding model capacity at high L, dropping log-perplexity from 2.05 to 1.93 at L = 11000 with 128 experts.
As perplexity decreases, model outputs improve in terms of fluency, factual accuracy, and narrative complexity.
The model with access to reference documents inserts factual information in the generated article.
