findings.claim: Maleimide chemistry for cysteine linkage has chemical instability in plasma, including a retro-Michael reaction which results in premature loss of the drug-linker from the ADC.
RETRO obtains comparable performance to GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile despite using 25× fewer parameters.
RETRO features document reading via nontrivial modifications that require further training to the LM architecture, while using an off-the-shelf frozen BERT retriever for document selection.
A major challenge with the use of the maleimide-based strategy is its susceptibility to the premature release of payload through the retro-Michael reaction in the presence of blood thiols.
Succinimide or maleimide hydrolysis improves the stabilities and potencies of ADCs by preventing elimination reactions through retro-Michael reactions.
RA-DIT is a lightweight Retrieval-Augmented Dual Instruction Tuning framework that can effectively retrofit any pre-trained LLM with retrieval capabilities.
RETRO changes the decoder-only architecture to incorporate retrieved texts and pretrains the language model from scratch.
RETRO introduces a new attention mechanism which takes many pre-encoded text chunks independent of query x and simultaneously incorporates them in intermediate spaces.
RETRO introduced the idea of training an LM on top of a frozen retriever.
Hydrolysis of the thiosuccinimide ring prevents the retro-Michael elimination.
After fine-tuning, RETRO performance translates to downstream knowledge-intensive tasks such as question answering.
RETRO modifies an autoregressive LM to attend to relevant documents via chunked cross-attention, thus introducing new parameters to the model.
Hydrolysis converts the succinimide-thioether into succinic acid, which could help to prevent the retro-Michael reaction by firmly binding the conjugate to be thiol-stable.
RETRO predicts tokens based on an order of magnitude more data than what is typically consumed during training.
A new strategy developed by Lahnsteiner and coworkers to overcome the retro-Michael exchange is the formation of a stable 6-membered ring via transcyclization of the succinimide-thioether ring.
Pre-trained transformers can be rapidly RETROfitted with retrieval to achieve good performance.
The performance gain of RETRO remains constant with model scale and is comparable to multiplying the parametric model size by ~10x.
The gain of RETRO increases with the size of the retrieval database and the number of retrieved neighbours on the C4 validation set, when using up to 40 neighbours.
At evaluation, RETRO can be used without retrieval data (RETRO[OFF]), bringing limited performance degradation compared to baseline transformers.
The performance of RETRO comes from both explicit neighbour copying and general knowledge extraction.
None of the methods mentioned (BlenderBot 2.0, Guided Transformer) are designed to model arbitrary text sequences, in contrast with RETRO.
RETRO shares components with kNN-LM and DPR in that it uses frozen retrieval representations.
RETRO models longer sequences than QA examples; this requires to reason at a sub-sequence level, and to retrieve different documents for the different chunks of a sequence.
Similar to FID, RETRO processes the retrieved neighbours separately in the encoder, and assemble them in the chunked cross-attention.
RETRO differs from REALM, that prepends retrieved documents to the prompt.
In RETRO, retrieval is done during the whole pre-training process, and is not simply plugged-in to solve a certain downstream task.
Retrieval models such as RETRO exacerbate privacy issues by being able to directly copy training data.
RETRO outperforms the baseline at all model sizes on all datasets.
The smallest gains are for Curation Corpus, where RETRO only slightly outperforms the baseline.
The retrieval model (RETRO) outperforms the baseline on all test sets and outperforms Jurassic-1 on a majority of them, despite being over an order of magnitude smaller.
Overall, RETRO 7.5B outperforms Jurassic-1 and Gopher on a majority of the test sets.
On the dm_mathematics and ubuntu_irc subsets, the RETRO model does not outperform the 7B baseline and underperforms Jurassic-1.

findings.claim: Thin slab photonic crystals have a bandgap only for TE polarized, guided waves.
Electromagnetic band structure can produce either an enhancement or a suppression of spontaneous emission from two-dimensional (2-D) photonic crystal thin films.
Light extraction enhancement arising from Zone folding or Bragg scattering of the photonic bands is probably the more important effect than Purcell enhancement.
Angle resolved photoluminescence from inside the photonic crystal gives a direct spectral readout of the internal 2-D photonic band dispersion.
Periodic patterned semiconductor films prevent light trapping by using reciprocal lattice vectors to Bragg scatter all internal light into the escape cone near the origin of k-space.
The 2-D photonic band structure is dominated by the light cone, representing modes that can couple to external plane waves in the glass substrate.
There is no forbidden band at any frequency above the light cone.
Spontaneous emission is far more enhanced into the allowed bands within the light cone (case B) than at other light cone frequencies (case A) due to long interaction time with the thin film.
Spontaneous emission at cases B and D is very strong, while at cases A and C it is unenhanced.
By rescaling the photonic crystal lattice constant, leaky conduction band modes (case B) can be tuned to overlap the material emission band, producing enhanced spontaneous emission.
The overall effect of the photonic crystal is a competition between enhancement factors versus nonradiative recombination, which is net favorable for external spontaneous emission.
The benefit from improved light extraction efficiency is probably far more important than the Purcell effect for light emission from 2-D photonic crystals.

The Purcell effect changes the rate of spontaneous emission and helps in competition with nonradiative recombination, while light extraction competes with parasitic light absorption to influence overall efficiency.
In good quality materials with internal quantum efficiency close to 100%, there is not much further internal efficiency improvement to be expected from the Purcell effect.
The Purcell effect could lead to an increased modulation speed for telecommunications applications.
Photonic crystal voids expose edges of the active region that suffer from nonradiative surface recombination, necessitating Purcell enhancement to compensate.

In photonic crystals where voids do not penetrate all the way through the active region, both Purcell enhancement and surface recombination are probably nearly absent, but extraction enhancement remains.
A photonic crystal film surface patterned by blind voids might turn out to be optimal for LED efficiency because the extraction benefit is accompanied by no nonradiative recombination penalty.
In a thin symmetric waveguide similar to an unpatterned thin film on glass, the spontaneous emission rate is about 20% lower than in bulk InP.
The zero-point electric energy is about twice as concentrated within the semiconductor backbone relative to the volume of the unpatterned film because voids represent about half the total area.
The large effective volume of the band modes is almost exactly compensated by the increased effective degeneracy number g, producing a Purcell enhancement factor similar to that of a nanocavity.
The dominant influence for increased spontaneous emission output in photonic crystals is extraction by Bragg scattering into the escape cone.
A periodic structure scatters coherently, which might be a faster mechanism for coupling out light than a random scatterer, competing more effectively against parasitic optical absorption.
The spectrally integrated extraction enhancement is composed of a minor Purcell effect and a substantial extraction improvement by Brillouin Zone folding, essentially Bragg scattering.
The formula predicts a spectrally integrated extraction enhancement by about a factor ten, related to the material Q_m.

The Weight-Ensembling Mixture of Experts (MoE) module can dynamically integrate shared and task-specific knowledge based on the input sample.
The Weight-Ensembling MoE module is designed to segregate shared information and task-specific knowledge.
The Weight-Ensembling MoE module can be viewed as a dictionary look-up operation where routing weights select task vectors from the dictionary matrix.
WEMoE consistently demonstrates superiority over SOTA methods across the majority of tasks.
The performance of the merged WEMoE model shows an upward trend with an increase in the number of training steps and converges rapidly, reaching a high accuracy level in just 200 steps.
WEMoE (l = 2) consistently achieves the highest performance on the clean test set and most of the distorted test sets.
In scenarios where there is a significant loss in image quality, such as pixelation, WEMoE (l = 2) might overfit some specific tasks, resulting in a performance decline.
WEMoE (l = 0) tends to exhibit more stability in performance under conditions of significant image quality loss, attributed to its lower parameter count making it less prone to overfitting.
The performance of WEMoE (l = 0) is comparable to AdaMerging.
The influence of different learning rates is not significant, suggesting that WEMoE is insensitive to the learning rate parameter.
When l = 0, WEMoE corresponds to a partial implementation of AdaMerging, with the scaling factor $\lambda$ fixed at 0.3.
Weight-Ensembling MoE generates input-conditioned weights and infers through the MLP modules only once, unlike Ye & Xu (2023) which passes the input through each expert.
Identifying and separating shared knowledge and task-specific knowledge, and then dynamically integrating them, can mitigate the parameter interference problem to a great extent.
When both attention and MLP weights are up-scaled separately, the performance is significantly improved across most tasks, surpassing the other two methods.
MLPs may contain more task-specific information, making them an ideal target for the routing mechanism.
If the routing network were applied to both MLPs and attention weights, it would result in increased computational load and memory usage, and the marginal performance gain might not warrant the cost.
The performance of the merged model is relatively stable with respect to the scaling coefficient $\lambda$ of the task vector.
The router tends to allocate a greater weight to the task vector corresponding to the source task of the input sample.
Routers are able to effectively identify the expert with the highest performance depending on the input feature and assign a higher weight to it.
The key innovation of the approach lies in the proposed MoE design, which offers the ability to dynamically integrate shared and task-specific knowledge based on input.
Shallow-layer routers show no clear correlation between routing weight allocation and the source task of the input sample.
Deep-layer routers show a pronounced correlation between weight allocation and the source task of the input sample, favoring the task vector corresponding to the input sample's source task.
Shallow-level features are insufficient to distinguish between different tasks and predominantly contain shared information.
Deep-level features contain more task-specific information.
Applying Task Arithmetic to merge parameters of shallow-level MLPs and constructing MoE exclusively in deep-level MLPs can reduce inference cost overhead while maintaining performance.
At the first layer, the router assigns almost all samples to Cars.
From the 6th layer onwards, the router assigns the highest weight to the correct task for the majority of samples.
The router at the 6th layer is the first to exhibit a clear correlation between routing weight allocation and the source task of the input sample.

The proposed data selection methodology utilizes image-text correlation and model perplexity to evaluate and select data of varying quality.

The approach maps data quality into a two-dimensional space based on the distinct distribution of image-text correlation and model perplexity, allowing for the selection of data based on their location within this distribution.
The two-dimensional space can be used to construct multi-stage subsets of varying quality to facilitate curriculum learning.
The multiple training strategy utilizes a minimal amount of data while maintaining data quality diversity, significantly enhancing the model's fine-tuning performance.
The results emphasize substantial enhancements in five commonly assessed capabilities compared to using the complete dataset.
The proposed method constructs a representation space using clip score and model loss as two-dimensional coordinates to categorize data quality by distribution.

Clip score reflects how well the image features correspond to the text features, allowing identification and selection of high-quality data where the image and text are closely related.
The loss produced by the model reflects the difference between the target text and the model's internal preferences, and a higher loss makes the learning process more challenging for the model.

LLM2Vec is an unsupervised approach that transforms pre-trained decoder-only LLMs into universal text encoders using three steps: enabling bidirectional attention, masked next token prediction, and unsupervised contrastive learning.
LLM2Vec does not require any labeled data and is highly data- and parameter-efficient.
LLM2Vec-transformed models outperform strong encoder-only models by a large margin on word-level tasks such as chunking, named-entity recognition, and part-of-speech tagging.
LLM2Vec-transformed models set a new state-of-the-art for unsupervised models on the Massive Text Embeddings Benchmark (MTEB), with the best model reaching a score of 56.8.
Adapting via MNTP improves performance for all models and tasks in LLM2Vec-transformed models.
Transforming a model with LLM2Vec leads to improved performance over the strong Uni + weighted mean baseline for all models.
LLM2Vec with MNTP and SimCSE is much more sample-efficient and crucial in compute or data-constrained settings.
LLM2Vec-transformed models reach better performance earlier in training
The observation that LLM2Vec-transformed models reach better performance earlier is consistent across all three models
LLM2Vec is much more computationally efficient than Muennighoff et al. (2024) as it requires only parameter-efficient fine-tuning and 1000 gradient steps.
LLM2Vec outperforms Springer et al. (2024) without inducing any additional computational overhead at inference time.
LLM2Vec is a strong unsupervised approach to transform any decoder-only LLMs into a (universal) text embedder.
Applying LLM2Vec to Mistral-7B achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on MTEB among unsupervised approaches.
When combining LLM2Vec with supervised contrastive fine-tuning, Meta-LLaMA-3-8B achieves SOTA performance among approaches that train only on publicly available data (as of May 24, 2024).
LLM2Vec is a promising solution for low-resource and compute constrained scenarios due to its simplicity, compute and sample-efficiency.
The LLM2Vec methodology is language-agnostic and can be easily extended to other languages using just unstructured text collections.
Weighted mean works the best for causal (i.e., Uni) models, while mean pooling performs the best for LLM2Vec approach.

findings.claim: The IceCube Event Catalog of Alert Tracks (ICECAT-1) contains detailed information on key parameters of 275 neutrino events detected between 2011 May 13 and 2020 December 31.
The IceCube Event Catalog of Alert Tracks (ICECAT-1) contains 275 track-like neutrino events that retroactively pass the alert criteria from 2011 to 2020.
The cascade sample is not part of the catalog in this paper.
The Gold stream has a higher signal purity than the Bronze stream.
Signalness is calculated after event selection to grade alerts and is not explicitly used in alert selection.
The GFU selection results in only the highest-energy events (hundreds of TeV) being selected.
The majority (86%) of the alerts issued by IceCube fall under the GFU selection.
The 10 yr catalog includes 72 GFU Gold and 164 GFU Bronze events.
The high-energy starting event (HESE) selection for alerts includes only starting tracks, track-like events that have the neutrino interaction vertex inside the fiducial volume of the detector.
The HESE selection technique efficiently rejects the atmospheric muon background.
The expected number of signal events can change up to ~15% when using a spectral index of 2.19 instead of 2.37.

The observed rates of alerts from the Gold and Bronze channels are compatible with expectations when considering Poisson fluctuations, as well as the uncertainties in the astrophysical neutrino spectral parameters and the background modeling.
The follow-up reconstruction yields an improved angular reconstruction over the initial alert.
The calibration of the change in log-likelihood is especially sensitive to the optical properties of the ice.
The neutrino event selection used in this catalog is designed to select astrophysical event candidates that are likely to provide well-reconstructed directions on the sky.
The number of coincidences between neutrino alerts and sources in the five catalogs is consistent with the median expectation due to chance.

Spatial correlations between neutrino alerts and sources from other catalogs are not evidence for definitive association because the observed number of correlations is consistent with accidental correlations.
Dedicated follow-up studies using the light curves of the closest sources to each alert are encouraged.
The correlation of IceCube alerts with sources from very high energy gamma-ray and X-ray catalogs is consistent with chance expectation.

Several events from previous catalogs do not meet the selection criteria used for this real-time alert selection because automated event selections cannot supply sufficient information to issue alerts automatically.

Capability calibration is defined by establishing the model's query-level expected accuracy as the precise target for confidence estimation.

findings.claim: MixDA uses a two-stage algorithm where the first stage trains domain-specific adapters with masked language modeling objectives on unlabeled data.

MixDA decouples the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of the Transformer architecture into two parts: the original pre-trained FFNs to maintain the old-domain knowledge and novel domain-specific adapters to inject domain-specific knowledge in parallel.
In the first stage of MixDA, a mean-square-error auxiliary loss is added to maintain similarity between the domain adapter's output representations and the base model's feedforward network.
MixDA adopts a mixture-of-adapters gate to fuse the knowledge from different domain adapters dynamically.
In the second stage of MixDA, all domain adapters are added to the model and always activated.

MixDA employs a two-stage adapter-tuning strategy that leverages both unlabeled data and labeled data: i) domain-specific adapter on unlabeled data; followed by ii) the task-specific adapter on labeled data.
In the second stage of MixDA, MLP-sigmoid gates following the domain adapters control the weight to aggregate their outputs.
MixDA can be seamlessly plugged into the pretraining-finetuning paradigm.
In the second stage of MixDA, the aggregated output is fed through a newly-introduced task adapter.
MixDA achieves superior performance on in-domain tasks (GLUE), out-of-domain tasks (ChemProt, RCT, IMDB, Amazon), and knowledge-intensive tasks (KILT).
Training in the second stage of MixDA freezes the base model and domain adapters, and updates the gates and task adapter.
Further analyses demonstrate the reliability, scalability, and efficiency of MixDA.
Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters (MixDA) decouples FFNs into original pre-trained FFNs to maintain old-domain knowledge and novel domain-specific adapters to inject domain-specific knowledge in parallel.
MixDA demonstrates superior performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.
MixDA scales well to the increasing number of domains.
MixDA adds only a small number of parameters per domain.
The domain adapter in Mixture-of-Domain-Adapters is a feedforward network specifically designed for domain knowledge, unlike mixing different designs of adapters.

findings.claim: The MI attack achieves high attack accuracy against a classifier model and an LSTM-based language model.
The MI attack is a cheaper membership inference attack on text-generative models that does not require knowledge of the target model or expensive training of shadow models.
The paper investigates MI attacks on word embeddings and their applications in classification and text-generation under label-only (black-box) access.
The MI attack on text-generative language models does not require knowledge of the target model or expensive shadow model training.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding exploits the property that good word embeddings capture semantic relationships and consider words adjacent in training data as semantically close.

Membership Inference on Word Embedding works in a realistic setting where the attacker does not have knowledge of or sample access to the exact training data distribution, unlike Song and Raghunathan (2020).
Membership Inference on Word Embedding on text-generative language models does not require knowledge of the target model or expensive shadow model training, unlike previous work.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding transfers through LSTM-based language models where the trained embedding layer is not based on Word2Vec.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding is expected to generalize to other large transformer-based models for which shadow model training would be highly costly.

Membership Inference on Word Embedding is query-efficient because it uses a curated list of word pairs, substantially reducing the number of queries to the model compared to Song and Shmatikov (2019).
Membership Inference on Word Embedding cannot be trivially mitigated by limiting the number of queries made to the model.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding considers the question of what kind of sensitive information an adversary can learn given black-box access to a model that uses embeddings as its first layer.

The security notion of Membership Inference on Word Embedding can apply to membership of substrings of specific length, emails/documents, or users' collections without assuming all users' emails/collections have the same number of words.
In Membership Inference on Word Embedding, the adversary does not have access to any auxiliary labeled data.
In Membership Inference on Word Embedding, the adversary does not need sample access to the exact training distribution of the target model; access to a similar distribution can be sufficient.
Relaxing the assumption on the adversary's knowledge makes the Membership Inference on Word Embedding attack stronger.
The analysis of Membership Inference on Word Embedding shows that the attack is successful for input data drawn from real datasets.
In Membership Inference on Word Embedding attacks that use thresholds, the authors specify exactly how the thresholds would be computed.
The text-generative model attack in Membership Inference on Word Embedding has the advantage that it doesn't require a threshold.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding exploits the property that a good embedding is expected to capture semantic relationships between words.
Membership Inference on Word Embedding combines the semantic relationship property with the assumption that words adjacent/close in training data will be semantically close.
Word embeddings are vulnerable to black-box membership inference attacks under realistic assumptions.
Membership inference leakage persists through classification and text-generation applications even when the embedding layer is not exposed to the attacker.
Membership inference attacks in the context of word embeddings and their effect in other NLP tasks are relatively unexplored.
The grey-box attack model is strictly less general than the black-box attack model because score-based attacks cannot be applied when the model only exposes the predicted label.

The proposed attack exploits the property that good embedding functions preserve semantic meaning, by finding special word pairs that are not semantically close generally but appear significantly closer in the embedding space if the attacker's data was used in training.
The attack achieves success rates of above 90% in doing membership inference attack against word embeddings.
The leakage from word embedding is transferable to classification and text-generation NLP tasks.
The security experiment allows for implementation by varying the parameters of the experiment, such as access to distributions, target model types, and training on a subset of the data.
If the target model is a word embedding, the input to the security game is a word and the output is an embedding vector.
If the target model is a text generative model, the input to the security game is a text sequence and the output is the predicted next word.
Training the model on a random subset of each user's data makes the attacker's task more difficult because the attacker does not know which subset will be used.
The dimension of the model representation is very large for machine learning models to handle when using all words in the dictionary.
The attack has two phases: a preparation phase without interaction with the target model and an interactive query phase.
The attack identifies pairs of words whose distance significantly changes upon including the target dataset.
Due to unique properties of LASSO regression, the final linear model is sparse, meaning the attacker only needs to query a few words.
Controlling the $\lambda$ parameter changes the number of pairs of words that have non-zero weight in the linear combination.
Changing $\lambda$ can also change the generalization of the attack to unseen models.
The attack works better with larger target datasets.
The attack reaches a plateau after 200 shadow models.

findings.claim: Carlini et al., 2023 discloses that training data extraction and MIAs are both feasible for diffusion models.
An adversary can perform a training data extraction attack to recover individual training examples by querying the language model.
Larger models are more vulnerable than smaller models to the extraction attack.
Training data extraction attacks aim to reconstruct verbatim training examples rather than just representative 'fuzzy' examples.
Training data extraction attacks are more dangerous than model inversion attacks because they can extract secrets such as verbatim social security numbers or passwords.
Training data extraction attacks have been limited to small LMs trained on academic datasets under artificial training setups or settings with a priori knowledge of the secret.
Training data extraction attacks are often seen as theoretical or academic and are thus unlikely to be exploitable in practice
Training data extraction attacks are practical
The authors focus on k-eidetic memorization with a small k value because it makes extraction attacks more impactful.
Training data extraction reduces to membership inference: predicting whether each sample was present in the training data.
Extraction attacks are practical even when the data contains a given sequence only a few times.
Extraction attacks are practical and efficient, and can recover hundreds of training examples from a model, even when they are contained in just one training document.
The attack can extract hundreds of verbatim text sequences from the model's training data.
The attack is possible even though each of the above sequences are included in just one document in the training data.
Large language models memorize and leak individual training examples.
The proposed method extracts verbatim sequences from a language model's training set using only black-box query access.
Certain worst-case training examples are memorized even if training examples do not have noticeably lower losses than test examples on average.
The attack ranks samples highest based on an abnormally high likelihood ratio between the target model and a separate reference model.
In the best attack configuration, 67% of candidate samples are verbatim training examples.
The adversary's objective is to extract memorized training data from the model.
The strength of an attack is measured by how private (formalized as being k-eidetic memorized) a particular example is.
Stronger attacks extract more examples in total (both more total sequences, and longer sequences) and examples with lower values of k.
The goal is to study the ability of LMs to memorize data generally, not to create an attack that can be operationalized by real adversaries to target specific users.
The memorized content extracted can be generated through honest interaction with the LM.
The authors recovered a person’s full name, address, and phone number from the training data.
Disclosing that the vulnerability exists allows a malicious actor to perform these attacks on their own to recover personal information.
The benefits of publicizing these attacks outweigh the potential harms.
If the perplexity is low, the model is not very “surprised” by the sequence and has assigned on average a high probability to each subsequent token in the sequence.
Maintaining a high temperature throughout the generation process would likely cause the sampling process to randomly step off the path of a memorized output.
A higher temperature causes the model to be less confident and more diverse in its output.
Sampling conditioned on Internet text is the most effective way to identify memorized content.
The method can extract the entirety of the MIT, Creative Commons, and Project Gutenberg licenses.
While 604 memorized examples have been extracted, many of these could likely be extended to much longer snippets of memorized content.
The memorized content is highly dependent on the model’s context.
In the right setting, orders of magnitude more extraction is feasible than when the context is just slightly suboptimal.
None of the 273 extracted samples found using Internet conditioning can be reliably reproduced when using the same prefix initially provided to GPT-2 that produced this sample.
Nearly all extracted samples can be reproduced with high probability if the entire sequence of data up to (but not including) the beginning of the memorized content is provided.
The work vastly underestimates the true amount of content that GPT-2 memorized because simple prompts are used.
Larger models memorize significantly more training data; even hundreds of millions of parameters are not enough to memorize some of the training points.
Improvements in LM performance with model size come at the cost of decreased privacy.

findings.claim: Queries generated through Self-Instruct exhibit limitations in diversity and complexity.
Applying SELF-INSTRUCT to vanilla GPT3 demonstrates a 33% absolute improvement over the original model on SUPER-NATURALINSTRUCTIONS.
Applying SFT to Llama-13b with self-instruct results in a considerable decline in MMLU performance (from 42.5 to 30.3) and Codex-Eval performance (from 26.6 to 13.4).
The performance of SELF-INSTRUCT on SUPER-NATURALINSTRUCTIONS is on par with InstructGPT_001, which was trained with private user data and human annotations.
Tuning GPT3 with SELF-INSTRUCT outperforms using existing public instruction datasets by a large margin, leaving only a 5% absolute gap behind InstructGPT_001.
SELF-INSTRUCT provides an almost annotation-free method for aligning pretrained language models with instructions.
SELF-INSTRUCT starts with a small seed set of tasks as the task pool.
In SELF-INSTRUCT, random tasks are sampled from the task pool and used to prompt an off-the-shelf LM to generate new instructions and corresponding instances.
SELF-INSTRUCT filters low-quality or similar generations before adding them back to the initial repository of tasks.
The data resulting from SELF-INSTRUCT can be used for the instruction tuning of the language model itself to follow instructions better.
SELF-INSTRUCT is a semi-automated process for instruction-tuning a pretrained LM using instructional signals from the model itself.
The iterative SELF-INSTRUCT process on GPT3 leads to about 52k instructions, paired with about 82K instance inputs and target outputs.

SELF-INSTRUCT refers to the pipeline of generating tasks with a vanilla pretrained language model itself, filtering the generated data, and then conducting instruction tuning with this generated data in order to align the LM to follow instructions better.
SELF-INSTRUCT brings in additional gains when combined with the SUPERNI training set.
SELF-INSTRUCT models show consistent improvement in instruction-following ability as the size of generated data grows, but this improvement almost plateaus after 16K instructions.
SELF-INSTRUCT is task-agnostic and generates new tasks (instructions along with instances) from scratch, unlike recent works that generate instructions of a task given a few examples.
Most self-training methods assume a specific target task as well as unlabeled examples under it; in contrast, SELF-INSTRUCT produces a variety of tasks from scratch.
SELF-INSTRUCT can be viewed as a form of “knowledge distillation” where the source and target of distillation are the same, i.e., a model's knowledge is distilled to itself.
Finetuning GPT3 on the SELF-INSTRUCT dataset leads to a 33% absolute improvement on SUPERNI over the original GPT3.
Tuning GPT3 with SELF-INSTRUCT outperforms using existing public instruction datasets by a large margin.
Tuning GPT3 with SELF-INSTRUCT performs closely to InstructGPT $_{001}$ .
SELF-INSTRUCT may help bring more transparency to what happens “behind the scenes” of widely-used instruction-tuned models like InstructGPT or ChatGPT.
SELF-INSTRUCT inherits limitations from LMs, specifically tail phenomena where gains are skewed toward frequent uses and minimal in low-frequency contexts.
The majority of gains by SELF-INSTRUCT are likely skewed toward tasks or instructions that present more frequently in the pretraining corpus.
SELF-INSTRUCT might show brittleness with respect to uncommon and creative instructions.
SELF-INSTRUCT might work best for larger models due to its dependence on inductive biases extracted from LMs.
The iterative algorithm of SELF-INSTRUCT may have unintended consequences such as the amplification of problematic social biases.
The instruction and instance input does not have a strict boundary in many cases.
To encourage the diversity of the data format, instructions that do not require additional input (i.e., X is empty) are allowed.
Input-first approach can generate inputs biased toward one label, especially for classification tasks.
Pretrained LMs can achieve instance generation to a large extent when prompted with instruction-input-output in-context examples from other tasks.
The top 20 most common root verbs and their top 4 direct noun objects account for 14% of the entire set of generated instructions.
A decent number of new instructions were generated which do not have much overlap with the seed instructions.
Most of the generated instructions are meaningful, while the generated instances may contain more noise.
Even though the generations may contain errors, most of them are still in the correct format or partially correct, which can provide useful guidance for training models to follow instructions.
Future work can benefit from improving the quality of generated data by using human annotators or training a reward model to select better generations
When evaluating on SUPERNI, the model's performance gain plateaus earlier at around hundreds of instructions.
The early plateau on SUPERNI may be due to the fact that the new generated data is distinct from typical NLP tasks in SUPERNI.
The findings in the paper demonstrate the importance of diverse instruction data.
The algorithm has difficulty in producing balanced labels, which reflects the models' prior biases.

findings.claim: Dragon Skin (Smooth-On Inc.) and air-brushing are used for fabrication of a 3D phantom that mimics the appearance of a real organ under multiple imaging modalities.

The fabricated phantom is the first 3D, hollow bladder phantom with realistic normal and multi-stage pathology features suitable for endoscopic detection using white light cystoscopy (WLC), optical coherence tomography, and blue light cystoscopy.
The flexibility of the material and technique allowed for the representation of a wide range of diseased tissue states, ranging from inflammation (benign) to high-grade cancerous lesions.
The authors introduce Dragon Skin and air-brushing as a new material and new strategy, respectively, for the fabrication of complex disease-mimicking optical phantoms.
The resulting phantom mimics subsurface features of the bladder that are visible to OCT, features visible with traditional WLC, and fluorescently-labeled lesions visible with BLC.
The fabrication process presented is the first to permit arbitrary 3D form factors while including diseased states that span the range of benign and pre-cancerous to muscle-invasive cancer.
In the single-scattering assumption limit appropriate for OCT measurements, attenuation of the amplitude of the interferometric signal follows Beer's law.
Airbrushing for extended periods of time (more than ~5 seconds) led to non-linear results in thickness due to changing air pressure.
The relationship between total air-brushing time and average thickness of Dragon Skin follows a linear trend on both smooth and textured surfaces.
The linear fit for the relationship between spray time and thickness is nearly identical for smooth and textured surfaces.
Intrasample variation in layer thickness is higher for thinner samples.
The variation in layer thickness on a smooth surface and a textured surface are almost indistinguishable.
Pre-cancerous dysplastic lesions manifest as a thickening of the urothelium, appear flat under WLC, and do not exhibit fluorescent contrast under BLC.
Carcinoma in situ (CIS) manifests as a combined urothelium and lamina propria layer and is only distinguishable with subsurface imaging techniques like OCT.
Inflammation does not disrupt the layered structure of the bladder tissue, making it distinguishable from CIS using OCT.
T1-staged tumors exhibit a combined urothelium and lamina propria layer, protrude more deeply into the bladder wall, and lack a clear demarcation with the subsequent muscularis propria layer.
T2-staged (and higher) cancers are classified as muscle-invasive carcinomas and lack well-defined layers or horizontal structure.
The attenuation coefficients of the phantom exactly match the average value previously reported for bladder tissue.
The three distinct layers of healthy bladder tissue are accurately mimicked by the phantom.
The resulting papillary tumors are composed of a single layer, which is not representative of the actual composition of papillary tumors.
It is impossible to create a phantom that perfectly matches the color of tissue for all patients.
The vasculature in the phantom appears slightly fluorescent due to the red Sharpie dye.
Judicious choice of a different red pigment can avoid the fluorescence problem in the future.
The material and techniques can be generalized for developing other large-scale organ phantoms such as for the stomach.

findings.claim: The construction of the spherical inclusion phantom allows more repeatable fabrication compared to previous susceptibility inclusion phantoms.
The spherical inclusion phantom provides a way to experimentally explore streaking artifacts and susceptibility underestimation in terms of their dependence on image acquisition parameters.

The phantom provides benefits over previous multi-compartment phantoms with cylindrical geometry, including no compartmental barrier materials, reproducible geometry, analytical phase solution, and elimination of background phase due to air-phantom boundary.
Formalin cross-linking and water-proof surface coating effectively blocked water diffusion between the compartments to preserve the phantom's integrity.

Factors that limit the agreement between phantom phase images and theoretical prediction include air bubbles trapped at gel interfaces, imperfect magnet shimming, and the susceptibility of external materials such as the phantom support hardware.
Non-tissue-mimicking materials, such as air bubbles and structural barriers for compartmental separation, can cause phase errors and should be minimized.
Compartmental shapes with known analytical dipolar field solutions are beneficial for validation of phase measurement, a pre-requisite of susceptibility reconstruction.
Thin cylindrical or elongated ellipsoidal shapes embedded in a larger cylindrical container have been frequently used for validation phantoms.
Some authors have used thin plastic or latex balloons to contain the inner-compartment materials in order to minimize the compartmental barrier material.

Other authors have constructed a gel inclusion phantom where the inner materials were cut from thin cylindrical agarose rods and positioned inside a background gel in a semi-random fashion; in this case no structural barrier was used but the orientation of the cut pieces was uncontrolled.
Previous phantoms' designs were not conducive to good control of the compartmental geometry, necessary for reproducible research.
Predominantly cylindrical or elongated geometry chosen for the inner compartments could limit experiments to imaging on primarily transverse planes with respect to the compartments' long axis.
Phase images in the longitudinal planes are sensitive to air bubbles/pockets that are prone to form at the top of the elongated compartments.
A phantom that can be imaged in any scan plane is desirable for volumetric susceptibility imaging validation because susceptibility-induced phase maps are strongly orientation dependent.
The spherical shape of the overall phantom served to eliminate bulk background phase caused by the air-phantom boundary.
The spherical inner compartments produced 3D phase variation according to a known analytical solution.
The beneficial features of the spherical phantom hold regardless of the phantom's physical orientation in the magnet bore or the scan plane choice.
The MRI phase shift inside a uniformly magnetized sphere is zero.
The gradient echo image phase inside a uniformly magnetized sphere vanishes.
Inside a small homogeneous sphere embedded in a larger sphere, the MRI phase shift is zero.
warm gelatin solution did not melt the congealed gel compartments because of the formalin cross-linking
Water diffusion across the boundaries was suppressed effectively.
Signal voids caused by air bubbles are visible on the surfaces of the spheres.
The measured phase is close to zero within the inclusion spheres.

The phase around the inclusion spheres displays the characteristic dipolar field patterns with relatively large positive values along the main magnetic field direction, and negative values in the perpendicular directions.
The intensity of the phase variation increased from inclusion 1 to 3, in the order of increasing iron concentration and in good agreement with theoretically modelled phase.
The measured phase map was contaminated by air bubbles, contact with the phantom stand, and slowly-varying background magnetic field left uncompensated by shimming.
The rates increase approximately linearly with the concentration.
Deviation from linearity is likely attributed to errors in controlling the small volumes of the iron oxide solutions.
The particles act as a strong transverse relaxation agent, while affecting longitudinal relaxation relatively weakly.
For all the inclusions, the transverse relaxation rates and the effective transverse relaxation rates are very close.

The closeness of transverse and effective transverse relaxation rates reflects homogeneous $B_{0}$ field inside the inclusions, to suppress inhomogeneous spin dephasing, which is a direct consequence of the spherical phantom geometry.
Water diffusion across compartmental boundaries could be a contributing factor to susceptibility changes.
The proposed phantom appears well-suited for cross-sectional comparative studies.
Longitudinal, absolute susceptibility studies may require more work to improve the phantom's stability.
Susceptibility maps indicated no evidence of iron settlement at the bottom, or blurring at the spherical boundaries.
More surface defects formed at the inclusion boundaries in the later-day data.
Repeated cooling and warming could have stressed and possibly cracked the compartmental boundaries.
Sodium azide could be more effective than the preservative used here for storing the phantom at room temperature.
The outer sphere theoretically eliminates background B0 inhomogeneity caused by the air-phantom susceptibility boundary.

findings.claim: ADC values for both diffusion times were lower in Phantom B than in Phantom A.
The intracellular volume fraction f_i is significantly higher for phantom B than for phantom A.
Fixing D had the greatest effect on the f_i CoV for phantom A, reducing it by a factor of 1.3 compared with fitting all parameters.

The low CoV of mean $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ values in phantom A and the maximum difference post-immersion being less than half a micron suggest that the phantom microstructure shows little variation over 6 months.

The microstructural modelling suggests that phantom B has a higher $f_{i}$ than phantom A, which is consistent with the observed lower ADC in phantom B, as ADC is expected to decrease as intracellular volume fraction increases.
The biomimetic tumor tissue phantom is stable over a period of 10 months.
ADC values were stable with coefficients of variation less than 5%.
Microstructural parameters showed greater variability with coefficients of variation up to 13%.
There is evidence of bias in sphere size estimates.
The phantom consists of a collection of approximately spherical, micron-scale hollow polymer spheres, which mimic cells.
A single Rician probability density function (PDF) was appropriate for ADC fitting because the signals used were not averaged.
The phantom's microstructure consists of extended clumps of spheres rather than a packing of discrete idealized spheres.
Median ADC values at the two diffusion times were significantly different (P < 0.001), with a mean percentage difference of 16%.
Fixing D had little impact on the percentage of voxels near constraints for R and f_i, showing that fixing diffusivity did not improve precision.

The similarity in post-immersion $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ values for the two phantoms provides evidence of the repeatability of the construction process, in that samples with comparable sphere sizes can be generated.
SEM characterization demonstrates the stability of both phantoms, and also shows that the sphere size is appropriate for mimicking tumor cells.

The aggregation of spheres is not ideal in that such a structure is not generally considered in the types of microstructural model the phantom is designed to validate, where tissue is modeled as a collection of individual spherical cells.
The aggregation may better reflect biological tissue, where cell adhesion plays an important role in forming and maintaining tissue structure.

The current phantom clearly oversimplifies the tumor microenvironment, as structures such as cell nuclei, collagen fibers, and blood vessels are not mimicked, nor are different cell populations, such as tumor and immune cells.

The observation of a higher ADC at a lower diffusion time provides evidence of hindered and/or restricted diffusion in the phantom, consistent with the dependence of ADC on diffusion time that has previously been observed in biological tissue in general and in tumor tissue specifically.

These findings, along with the observation that the multi- $G$ , multi- $\Delta$ data are well described by a microstructural model, demonstrate that this phantom more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previous phantoms.

Using the biomimetic phantom in multi-center studies could enable a more comprehensive validation of DW-MRI, enabling comparison of ADC time-dependence, and microstructural estimates, between scanners.

The fact that this is a water-based phantom is advantageous for multi-center studies, as the phantoms could be distributed dry and immersed in water on-site, which is more practical than using phantoms immersed in organic solvents.
The CoVs of less than $5\%$ indicate that ADC repeatability in the phantom is very good, and provide evidence that the phantom remains stable over 10 months.
As PLGA is known to degrade over time, it is expected that the phantom will eventually become unstable, potentially limiting the extent to which it can be used as a long-term test object.

The time-dependence of extracellular diffusion is expected to be weaker in three-dimensional geometries, such as the sphere packings considered in the present work, than in the two-dimensional geometries relevant to axonal packings.
Excluding the Δ = 45 ms data reduced R, bringing the estimate closer to the SEM R_o, though a bias still remains.
The opposite trend was observed for f_i when excluding longer diffusion times, suggesting that exchange is not the dominant effect on f_i estimates.
The sCT data suggests that f_i is overestimated, not underestimated, from the microstructural model.
Simulations indicate that if T2 is higher inside than outside the spheres, all model parameters are overestimated, with the magnitude of the bias increasing as the T2 difference increases.
A limitation of the comparisons between modalities is that different sections of the bulk phantom have been used for sCT, SEM and MR.
The phantom exhibits time-dependent diffusion and signals are well described by a microstructural model.
The phantom more closely reflects diffusion in tissue than previously used free-diffusion phantoms.
Microstructural estimates were found to be more variable than ADC measurements.
There is evidence of bias in $R$ and $f_{i}$.

findings.claim: The tissue-mimicking phantom is an essential tool for evaluating biomedical optical systems, and it can also be used for the standardization of optical imaging techniques.
The IAD method successfully quantified the optical properties of the fabricated phantoms.
The phantom was employed to assess the imaging depth limitation of a hyperspectral imaging system.
The paper presents a protocol for performing computations using the inverse adding-doubling (IAD) method to measure the optical properties of the created phantoms.

A protocol created a phantom with optical properties similar to esophagus and stomach tissues, specifically absorption coefficients of 0.1–2.5 cm⁻¹ and reduced scattering coefficients of 0.5 - 20cm⁻¹ at 550 nm.
Agar concentration determines the stiffness of the phantom
Intralipid $20\%$ emulsion and Nigrosin are used to adjust the scattering and absorption features of the phantom, respectively
IAD measurement showed increased reduced scattering coefficients with an increase in the intralipid concentration
Intralipid does not change the absorption property of the phantom
Absorption coefficients were increased as the Nigrosin concentration increased
There was a rapid decrease in the reduced scattering coefficients between the Nigrosin concentration of 3.1 μg/mL and 4.7 μg/mL
High Nigrosin concentration might affect the quantification accuracy of the scattering property
Thick phantoms result in higher light extinction, making it difficult to measure accurate spectral features of the underlying target.
Measuring unscattered light is significant to obtain accurate calculation of the optical properties.
The IAD method successfully quantified the optical properties of phantoms that are consistent with intralipid and Nigrosin concentrations.
Combining the proposed protocol with 3D printer technology can significantly increase its applicability.
The 3D printer provides a mold that can mimic complex biological structures such as vessel networks, allowing the technical evaluation of optical systems under actual biological tissue conditions.
Combining 3D printer technology and fluidic channels enables the assessment of functional imaging capabilities such as blood flow and oxygen saturation monitoring.

findings.claim: The glass-based imaging phantom provides controlled levels of scattering and absorption with excellent optical homogeneity, long-term stability and reproducibility.
Most tissue-mimicking phantoms simulate flat regions of healthy tissue.

Silica beads and polymer microspheres exhibit well-controlled particle size and refractive index, allowing the prediction of scattering levels of tissue-mimicking phantoms based on Mie scattering theory.
Inorganic glass offers excellent long-term stability combined with the ability to induce absorption and scattering in the glass matrix.
Absorption in the glass-based imaging phantom is induced by doping the glass with nickel ions that mimic hemoglobin absorption.

Scattering in the glass-based imaging phantom is achieved by in-situ formation of crystals in the glass upon heat treatment, which provides a homogenous distribution of scattering species in the glass matrix.
The high homogeneity, reproducibility and long-term stability of the glass samples demonstrate their excellent suitability for use in tissue-mimicking phantoms.
The absorption of glass in the visible spectrum is commonly achieved by doping metal ions or forming metal or semiconductor nanoparticles in the glass matrix.

It is difficult to adopt the method of incorporating white metal oxide particles (e.g. TiO2) for the fabrication of glass-based phantoms as these metal oxide particles are easily dissolved in a glass melt.
The scattering species formed in the glass matrix were sodium barium phosphate ($\mathrm{NaBaPO}_4$) crystals.
The amount of $\mathrm{BaO}$ and $\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_5$ is considered to limit the growth of the crystals in the glass matrix.

A second heat treatment at $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is necessary to enlarge the crystal size and, in this way, to increase the scattering level in the glass matrix to sufficient level for the fabrication of glass-based phantoms.
The absorption of the glass samples is not affected by the in-situ formation of the crystals in the glass matrix.
The nickel-ion doping does not affect the scattering, i.e. the in-situ formation of the crystals in the glass matrix.
The reduced scattering coefficient can be independently controlled by varying the parameters of the second heat-treatment, regardless of the amount of nickel-ion doping in the glass matrix.
The average size of crystals in the glass matrix increases with extended heat treatment durations while the total crystal phase portion is retained, aligning with the Oswald ripening mechanism.
Lithium disilicate glass ceramics demonstrate the capability of forming spherical Li3PO4 crystals in the glass matrix.
The small size of scattering crystals formed in the glass matrix leads to Rayleigh scattering rather than Mie scattering, which is more prevalent in tissue.
Sodium leaching has been observed in the glass, particularly in humid environments, attributed to the high sodium content in the glass matrix.
The use of 3D printing of fused silica glass enables the development of 3D printed glass-based phantoms with complex and high-resolution structures.
Samples #1 and #2 showed negligible scattering because they were not subjected to heat treatment for in-situ crystal formation.
Samples #3 - #10 presented both absorption and scattering because they were subjected to heat treatment.
The coefficient of variation (CV) is defined as the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean value of the attenuation.
The absorption is approximately proportional to the concentration of nickel ions in the batch of glassmaking raw materials.
The absorption level of the glass sample can be controlled by varying the amount of nickel oxide in the raw material.

The average crystal size is significantly enlarged when the sample was subjected to the heat-treatment at $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in comparison to the sample treated at $650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for 10 hours.
If larger crystal sizes are required to induce higher scattering, a second heat-treatment at $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is necessary for the crystal growth.
The crystal phase portion did not change with longer duration of the heat treatment at $750^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Long heat treatment at $650^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ only leads to the formation of small crystals that cause low level of scattering, which is insufficient to mimic many types of human tissues.
The average crystal size has the dominating effect on the reduced scattering coefficient.
The glass samples exhibit a high level of homogeneity of both scattering and absorption with a CV value below 2% over the entire measurement range in the visible spectral region.
The glass samples can be fabricated with a high degree of inter-batch reproducibility in absorption and scattering levels with a CV value below 2%.
The glass samples maintain stable scattering and absorption levels over one-year-equivalent room-temperature conditions with a CV value below 4%.
Nickel ions doped into the glass induce absorption similar to hemoglobin, with levels controlled by varying nickel oxide content.
Crystals formed in-situ in the glass upon heat treatment induce scattering similar to human tissues.
Absorption and scattering levels in the glass phantom can be independently controlled because nickel ions do not affect crystal formation and crystals do not induce absorption.
The glass samples exhibit excellent optical stability, homogeneity, reproducibility, and long-term stability.
Glass samples are robust and remain intact without cracking or breaking during measurements and tests under normal handling conditions.
The absorption spectrum of nanoparticle-doped glasses is affected by the concentration and morphology of the nanoparticles, which can be tuned by adjusting ion quantity and heat-treatment conditions.
Modifying nanoparticle size allows shifting the absorption peak, potentially enabling the mimicking of other tissue chromophores such as bilirubin.

findings.claim: Erasing the heralded information after the interference has been measured recovers the interference pattern, implementing a delayed-choice quantum erasure.
A quantum eraser scheme investigates whether it is possible to recover an interference pattern suppressed by which-path information by erasing that information.

The proposed quantum eraser scheme uses surface acoustic wave (SAW) phonons, implementing the process by constructing a two-phonon entangled state where the second phonon marks the which-path information.

The slow propagation of the “herald” phonon is exploited to delay the which-path information detection after detection of the result of the interferometric process, allowing for a delayed-choice quantum erasure.

The experiment successfully completed a quantum eraser protocol using an acoustic Fabry-Perot interferometer, demonstrating delayed-choice quantum erasure where erasure occurs after interference result registration.
Omitting the heralding step yields a clear interference pattern in the interfering half-quanta pathways.
Including the heralding step suppresses the interference pattern.
Changing the relative phase of the two intermediate states makes the paths interfere constructively or destructively, resulting in a phase-dependent modulation of the first qubit's final state.
When $\varphi = \pi$, the interference is constructive, and the qubit energy is transferred to the acoustic channel, leaving the qubit in $|g\rangle$.
The modeled maximum of the f-e decay has a 50 MHz misalignment compared to measurements.
Generating the herald destroys the interference pattern.
Even if the heralding phonon is not captured and detected via $Q_{2}$, the interference is not recovered because $Q_{1}$'s state is irremediably coupled to the herald and thus to the environment.
Simply tracing out $Q_{2}$'s state will not recover the interference pattern; measurements of $Q_{1}$ must be conditioned on measurements of $Q_{2}$.

The amplitude reduction in conditional measurement is partially accounted for by a model including losses and finite coherence time, with remaining discrepancy attributed to decoherence during measurement.
The construct enabled demonstration and exploitation of two-phonon entanglement, opening the door to two-phonon interferometry, acoustic Bell tests, and phonon coherence length measurements.
Phonon heralding can be used to mitigate propagation losses in future acoustic experiments and implement high-fidelity acoustic quantum state transfer and remote entanglement.

findings.claim: MKQA supplies the widest range of languages to date for evaluating question answering.
MKQA is challenging even in English, but especially in low-resource languages.
MKQA selects 10k realistic English queries from the Natural Questions dataset and human translates them into 25 additional languages and dialects.

MKQA replaces NQ's passage embedded answer spans with high-quality, language- and retrieval-independent answer annotations, linked directly against Wiki-data entities and a limited set of well-defined value types.
MKQA's grading procedure ensures labels are sufficient to evaluate any QA method, including knowledge graph and generative approaches.
Less than 4% of answers in MKQA are rendered incorrect by geographical and cultural context.
MKQA covers 26 languages and dialects from 14 language family branches.
MKQA is the largest and most linguistically diverse open-domain QA evaluation set currently available.
MKQA is innately more challenging than Natural Questions due to the multi-stage re-annotation process.
MKQA verifies its questions are predominantly geographically invariant, so answers will not change due to geographical or cultural factors.
MKQA answers are predominantly entities (42.2%) or atomic answers such as dates, binary, or numbers with units.
MKQA's definition of unanswerable is based on the ability of a human to find a succinct answer to a question on the web.
MKQA provides higher answer coverage (67.58%) as opposed to the TyDi language average of 38%.
MKQA does not expect an answer to be derived from a single source document.
MKQA addresses both academic and practical requirements for a wide and diverse question answering benchmark by covering a large number of diverse language families and having significant reach.
The Wikidata IDs provided for a large portion of gold answers allow these answers to be further localized into Wikipedia languages beyond those in MKQA.

The 'unanswerable' definition in MKQA yields more challenging evaluation because correctly answering questions is on average harder than learning when to abstain, and many difficult questions unanswerable in NQ are answerable in MKQA.

The primary benefit of defining Unanswerable as queries without short answers is that it enforces the retrieval-independent annotations property of MKQA, since long answers have an unbounded number of correct answer strings.
On English alone, the best system receives an F1 score of only 52.3% on MKQA, which is less than the same methods achieve on Natural Questions and TriviaQA.
Unanswerable examples in MKQA are easier than the unanswerable examples in Natural Questions, as the model maintains higher performance at all No Answer confidence thresholds.
The most challenging questions migrated from unanswerable in Natural Questions to answerable in MKQA, shifting the unanswerable distribution from 63% to 32%.
For Korean and Arabic, the best F1 score on MKQA is only 6% higher than the lower bound score of 32.42% obtained from predicting exclusively "unanswerable".

MKQA's properties, including geographical invariance, language-parallel questions, retrieval-independent annotations, and linguistic diversity, set it apart from existing resources in terms of annotation quality, difficulty, and flexibility to evaluate new approaches.
The answer resolution step enables disambiguation of homonyms and collection of valid answer synonyms/aliases for more robustly measuring annotator agreement and prediction accuracy.
For Simplified Chinese, the resulting data quality (answer acceptance rate of 89%) is still within an acceptable range.
The property of 'retrieval independent annotations' is currently not used in any other multilingual QA benchmarks except XQA.
Translation followed by English DPR outperforms the Elastic-search multilingual sparse retrievers.
Multilingual retrievers, English state-of-the-art retrievers, and generative QA models all fail to overcome the bottleneck of collecting relevant passages in multilingual open-retrieval QA.
XLM-R outperforms M-Bert, and Translate-Train outperforms Translate-Test and Zero Shot.
Existing transfer learning methods have significant deficits to overcome for low-resource multilingual QA to match English performance.

findings.claim: TYDI QA questions are written by people who want to know the answer but don't know it yet, and data is collected directly in each language without translation to provide a realistic information-seeking task and avoid priming effects.
TYDI QA is the first public large-scale multilingual corpus of information-seeking question-answer pairs.
The data collection procedure for TYDI QA is model-free and translation-free.
TYDI QA enables the community to reliably draw conclusions aligned with people's information-seeking needs while exercising systems' ability to handle a wide variety of language phenomena.
TYDI QA presents a model with a question along with the content of a Wikipedia article, and requests that it make two predictions: Passage Selection Task and Minimal Answer Span Task.
TYDI QA annotators were encouraged to ask about anything interesting that came to mind, no matter how unrelated, whereas QuAC annotators were requested to ask about a particular entity.
TYDI QA requires reasoning over lengthy articles with an average size of 5K–30KB
A substantial portion of questions in TYDI QA (46%–82%) cannot be answered by their article
Full documents allow TYDI QA to embrace the natural ambiguity over correct answers, which is often correlated with difficult, interesting questions

TYDI QA is intended to help bridge the gap between descriptive linguistics and computational linguistics datasets by including examples of linguistic phenomena typically not found in English and potentially problematic for NLP models.
TYDI QA displays a more balanced distribution of question words compared to SQuAD
Measurements on English are treated as a useful means of debugging rather than a goal of the TYDI QA task
TYDI QA GOLDP task provides compatibility with existing code for SQuAD, XQuAD, and MLQA
TYDI QA has substantially lower lexical overlap compared to MLQA and XQuAD
TYDI QA exhibits substantially lower lexical overlap between questions and answers compared to MLQA and XQuAD.
Non-English languages in TYDI QA show overall lower lexical overlap.
The lower lexical overlap in TYDI QA is evidence of a more complex relationship between questions and answers.
F1 scores remain low on the TYDI QA gold passage dev set despite lacking several core challenges of TYDI QA (e.g. no long articles, no unanswerable questions).
Progress on the TYDI QA dataset is more likely to generalize on the breadth of linguistic phenomena found throughout the world's languages by targeting a typologically diverse set of languages.
The Passage Selection Task requires returning the index of the passage that answers the question or NULL if no such passage exists, given a list of passages.
The Minimal Answer Span Task requires returning the start and end byte indices of the minimal answer span, YES/NO for yes/no questions, or NULL if a minimal answer is not possible.
The task formulation reflects that information-seeking users do not know where the answer will come from and it is not always obvious whether the question is answerable.
Datasets where question writers saw the answer are mostly solved, whereas datasets whose question writers did not see the answer text remain largely unsolved.
Unseen answers provide a natural mechanism for creating questions that are not answered by the text.
Approaches that rely too heavily on the availability of high-quality machine translation will fail to generalize across the world's languages.
The diversity of languages with little parallel training data allows researchers to make more reliable conclusions about how well their models will generalize across languages.
NULL-related errors in the dataset are entirely false positives, failing to find answers that exist.
NULL-related errors occur in a variety of article lengths, from under 1000 words through large 3000-word articles.
NULL errors cannot be attributed to long articles alone; alternative causes such as difficult or subtle question-answer matching should be considered.
Scores cannot be compared across languages because each language has unique questions, varying Wikipedia content quality/amount, and annotator quality.
The authors recommend studying the interaction between morphology and question-answer matching.
The authors recommend evaluating the effectiveness of transfer learning for languages with and without parallel data.
The authors recommend studying the usefulness of machine translation in question answering for data augmentation and as a runtime component.
The authors recommend studying zero-shot QA by explicitly not training on a subset of the provided languages.
The authors believe that a deeper understanding of the data itself will be key and encourage further linguistic analyses.
The authors invite others to create compatible datasets for other languages, noting that no single effort will be sufficient to cover the world's languages.
For many languages, the content required to answer questions has not been written down, creating a paradox where cross-language retrieval is necessary but parallel data for translation is lacking.
Question answering is well-suited for evaluating multilingual models.
Avoiding data collection procedures reliant on translation and multilingual modeling greatly mitigates the risk of sampling bias.

findings.claim: It is possible to construct a functional antibody library using low, non-combinatorial synthetic CDR diversity.

Non-combinatorial synthetic CDR diversity design is a viable approach to the construction of antibody libraries, and the design principle may have certain advantages that include highly nature-like sequences and the avoidance of undesirable sequence motifs.
A semi-synthetic human scFv library with pre-defined synthetic diversity in all six CDRs was designed and constructed, with each CDR having a low diversity of fewer than 10,000 unique sequences.
The library consists of antibody clones with highly nature-like CDR sequences and the occurrence of the post-translational modification motifs is minimized.
Multiple unique clones with nanomolar affinity could be isolated from the library against a number of target antigens.

The library was designed to have predetermined CDR sequences with non-combinatorial diversity that dutifully mimic natural CDRs with somatic hypermutations but without many of potential PTM-prone motifs.
The sequence between two adjacent framework regions is identified as CDR.
The CDR sequences of the library contain only small numbers of mutations from the human germline CDR sequences and are highly similar to the CDR sequences of natural human antibodies.

Highly similar distribution patterns were found among the CDR-H3s of natural human antibodies, the simulated repertoire, and the constructed library, demonstrating the nature-likeness of the library CDRs.
The occurrence of undesirable PTM motifs in the CDRs was much lower than in natural human antibody CDRs, with exceptions for CDR-H1 and CDR-L2.
A majority of the isolated clones were of lambda light chain class.

The dissociation constants obtained were comparable to those from other previously reported antibody libraries and typical hybridoma-derived antibodies, supporting the validity of the non-combinatorial CDR design approach.
The panning process did not appear to significantly alter the percentage of the designed CDR sequences or the average number of mutations per CDR residue.
The mutation frequency in framework regions (FRs) decreased after the panning selection.
Asp-Gly and Asn-Gly sequences were completely eliminated from the CDRs and CDR-framework region (FR) junctions.
Cysteine and methionine residues were removed from the CDR design.

The predefined, non-combinatorial CDR design approach allows greater diversity of CDR1s and 2s compared to the Tiller et al. approach, but grafting CDR sequences with different germline origins onto a single framework potentially introduces unnatural CDR-FR junction sequences.
The much lower diversity in CDR3s of the semi-synthetic library may have a negative effect on the performance of the library.

Sub-stoichiometric coupling efficiency during oligonucleotide synthesis produces shorter and/or out-of-frame CDR sequences, which are more likely to occur in longer CDRs, resulting in the enrichment of short CDR sequences in the final library.

The antibody library does not necessarily have CDRs with large diversity derived from random combination at the nucleotide or codon level, and CDRs with pre-defined, non-combinatorial sequence diversity can be combined to generate a highly functional antibody library.

The total diversity of the antigen combining site is more important than CDR-H3 diversity, and the relative importance of CDR-H3 in antigen binding is probably more of a result, rather than a cause, of the evolution of the large CDR-H3 diversity by VDJ recombination.

The enrichment of the binders against the standard antigens such as lysozyme and EpCAM seemed to be slower than other libraries of comparable diversity, and as many as four rounds of panning were required to obtain moderate numbers of binders.
The limited diversity of the CDRs and the relative scarcity of mid- to long-length CDR-H3 may have contributed to the slower enrichment of binders.
The resulting library with approximately 10^9 individual clones was successfully panned against a number of antigens and yielded multiple clones with dissociation constants in nanomolar range.
