findings.claim: Speckle-modulating OCT (SM-OCT) can obtain speckle-free OCT images, but it seriously reduces the imaging sensitivity and time resolution.

Speckle-modulating optical coherence tomography (SM-OCT) can be used to acquire an unlimited number of uncorrelated speckle patterns and effectively remove speckle noise without degrading the resolution of the image.
The proposed deep-learning-based speckle-modulating OCT effectively removes OCT speckle noise without reducing OCT sample-arm input-light power and temporal resolution.
Averaging M measurements in SM-OCT decreases speckle noise by a factor of $\sqrt{M}$.
Speckle-modulating OCT makes progress in removing speckle noise but badly reduces OCT sample-arm input-light power and temporal resolution.
SM-OCT removes speckle noise, evidenced by the reduction of speckle noise being inversely proportional to the square root of M (number of compounded images).
In SM-OCT imaging, the pixel value distribution becomes narrower with increasing averages and resembles a Poisson distribution, unlike the Rayleigh distribution in conventional OCT.
Beads were more easily detected in SM-OCT images compared to OCT images after as few as 10 averages.
SM-OCT yielded a more accurate representation of the structure of the sample than OCT.
SM-OCT is capable of rendering in vivo images that approach histological detail by removing the significant contribution of speckle noise.
SM-OCT provided major improvement in image quality in all three spatial dimensions, revealing fine structures masked by speckle noise in OCT.
The intrinsic axial resolution of SM-OCT is uncompromised, demonstrated by a 2 μm-thick horizontal line.
SM-OCT outperformed alternative speckle reduction methods with respect to speckle noise reduction, while those methods smoothed fine features at the cost of structural detail.

SM-OCT enabled the observation of the lamellar structure of the corneal stroma and clear boundaries between various layers of the cornea in a live mouse, which conventional OCT was unable to resolve due to speckle noise.
SM-OCT provided particularly well-resolved individual layers of the retina in a live mouse, allowing the outer plexiform layer and the external limiting membrane to be readily distinguished.
SM-OCT enabled the detection of fine structures in human fingertip skin, including sweat ducts, dermal papillae, and tactile corpuscles (Meissner's corpuscles).
SM-OCT can remove speckle noise without compromising resolution, as evidenced by the revelation of cellular structure and striation of the tactile corpuscle.
SM-OCT retinal imaging of a human volunteer resulted in enhanced delineation of various retina layers, particularly in the three nuclear layers and differentiation between outer retina layers.
SM-OCT is a low-cost, robust and simple modification to existing OCT systems.
SM-OCT is able to reduce a potentially unlimited amount of speckle originating from the turbid sample itself in addition to speckle caused by a turbid object placed in the optical path.
SM-OCT obtains an unprecedented number of 100 independent speckle patterns, which could be extended without compromising resolution.
An object cannot move more than a few microns while frame averages are acquired in the current SM-OCT implementation.
SM-OCT implementation is best suited for SDOCT systems where the full spectrum is captured simultaneously.
Phase and speckle variance methods, such as those used in Doppler OCT and OCT angiography, will encounter additional variations owing to the movement of the diffuser in SM-OCT.
SM-OCT is expected to enable superior diagnostic capabilities compared to conventional OCT because of its ability to reveal anatomical features that are otherwise hidden by speckle noise.
Potential clinical applications of SM-OCT include early detection of epithelial cancers, evaluation of tumour margins, early detection of retinal diseases and internal diagnostics.

The significant reduction of speckle noise by SM-OCT facilitates further OCT image enhancement and image-based calculations including measurement of the attenuation coefficient, blur-deconvolution for extended depth of field and improved segmentation of structures such as retinal layers.
SM-OCT would enable a more precise fit owing to the removal of speckle noise.

Increasing the number of compounded images does not lead to an inherent degradation in resolution because each image is acquired at the same angle, sample position and set of illumination wavelengths.
Moving the diffuser too fast can induce multiple phase changes during the acquisition time of a given A-scan, resulting in OCT fringe washout and a decrease in signal intensity.
This is the first time that the tactile corpuscle has been clearly observed in the intact skin of a live human.
The ability to scramble the phase inside the voxel is limited by the PSF of the lenses in the 4f imaging system.
The benefit of speckle noise removal significantly outweighs the reduction in lateral resolution because speckle removal ultimately allows detection of fine structural details.
Significant speckle reduction can be achieved with as few as 10 averages.
For time-domain OCT and swept-source OCT, continuous movement of the diffuser during acquisition may pose challenges because of fringe washout.
It may be beneficial to synchronize the movement of the diffuser so that it moves only in between frame or A-scan acquisitions for time-domain and swept-source OCT.

To obtain a high-resolution speckle-reduced volume and angiography of the same volume, the sample should be scanned once with a moving diffuser and a second time with the diffuser either static or removed from the optical path.
Deviations from the ideal diffuser axial location resulted in power and resolution losses and impeded the speckle reduction effect.

The roughest diffuser (1,500 grit) reduced the OCT signal and the lateral resolution more than the other diffusers, but it achieved the best qualitative performance in terms of speckle removal and appearance of fine anatomic detail in tissue.
LG NRs were used because their scattering-to-absorption ratio is higher compared to conventional gold nanorods and because their scattering peak is in the infrared.

Dynamic contrast images are completely free of speckle noise and have remarkably high contrast.

Dynamic contrast OCT might fulfill the 20 years old promise of optical biopsies by OCT.

findings.claim: The optical spring effect is a radiation-pressure-induced change in stiffness of the “mirror spring”
The in-phase component of the radiation pressure force causes a change in the mechanical oscillator's rigidity, known as the optical spring effect.
The sensing resolution of cavity optomechanical spring sensing scales with the effective mechanical Q of OMO in addition to the optical Q.
Cavity optomechanical spring sensing enhances sensing resolution by six orders of magnitude, sufficient for single-molecule detection.
A peak shift appeared when feedback cooling was applied due to the phase not being precisely 90 degrees, which is called the optical spring effect.
Cavity optomechanical spring sensing can enhance sensing resolution by a factor of Q_m^eff compared with conventional approaches.
Cavity optomechanical spring sensing does not rely on external sensing elements like plasmonic nanoantennas and utilizes the entire effective sensing area of a whispering-gallery microcavity.
The optical spring sensing principle dramatically enhances sensing resolution by orders of magnitude compared with conventional approaches.
The strong optical spring effect from the optomechanical coupling results in an OMO frequency sensitively dependent on the laser-cavity detuning.
The observed OMO frequency shifts induced by particle bindings are purely transduced from the optical spring effect.
The demonstrated optical spring sensing principle can be applied for other physical sensing applications such as inertial sensing, electromagnetic field sensing, and gas sensing.
The effective sensing area of a whispering-gallery microcavity is more than five orders of magnitude larger than that of plasmonic devices.
Every 1-fm cavity resonance wavelength shift induced by a particle binding event can be transduced to an OMO frequency change of about 1.5 kHz.
The demonstrated approach is more than $10^{4}$ times higher resolution than a conventional microcavity sensor with the same optical quality factor.
The demonstrated approach is about 50 times higher resolution than that achieved with an optical Q of $10^{8}$ at a visible wavelength.
The harmonics of the OMO vary proportionally with the OMO fundamental frequency and can be applied for particle sensing.

At larger bead radii (50 and 85 nm), experimental values are smaller than theoretical predictions because the optical Q starts to degrade at a large bead size.
The impact from cavity Q change counteracts that from the cavity resonance wavelength shift, leading to a smaller shift of OMO frequency.
In protein sensing experiments, excessive noises from unwanted molecules were significantly reduced, resulting in a detection noise level close to the DPBS background noise.
The observed signals were protein binding induced.

The minimal detectable OMO frequency shift in current devices is primarily limited by the laser frequency jitter.
Adoption of a fine laser frequency locking circuitry can improve the sensing resolution by ~100 times to around δλ/λ0 ~ 10^-14.
Employing a visible laser can increase the optical Q to above 10^8, improving sensing resolution by more than one order of magnitude.
Incorporating a plasmonic structure can enhance the cavity resonance shift.
Future improvements would enable detecting small molecules and atoms with a mass down to sub-Dalton level in cryogenic environment.
Controlling the motion pattern of the coherent OMO may function as a unique paradigm to study and control the mechanical properties of molecule binding and unbinding.
The Allan deviations of higher order harmonics increase almost proportionally to that of the fundamental oscillation tone, indicating that the SNR would not be improved on the higher order harmonics.

kNN-LM approach requires storing the representations for each token in the corpus, which is an expensive requirement even for a small corpus like Wikipedia.

kNN-LM was not fine-tuned for downstream tasks, perhaps because it is unclear how to adapt the retrieval mechanism: a kNN can only use examples labeled for the target task—during fine-tuning, this precludes LM examples, which contain the desired world knowledge.
kNN-LM retrieves a set of tokens and interpolates between the LM's next token distribution and kNN distributions computed from the retrieved tokens at inference.
kNN LM interpolates a parametric LM token distribution with a retrieved token distribution, without the need for additional training.
kNN-LM extends a pre-trained LM by linearly interpolating its next word distribution with a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) model.
Scaling approaches for alleviating the storage requirement of kNN-LM to large corpora remains an open challenge.
kNN-LM requires access to internal LM representations to compute the kNN distribution, which are not available for black-box LMs such as GPT-3.
kNN LM interpolates the original LM's softmax token distributions with retrieved token distribution without additional training.
The nearest neighbors in kNN-LM are computed according to distance in the pre-trained embedding space and can be drawn from any text collection, including the original LM training data.
kNN-LM allows rare patterns to be memorized explicitly, rather than implicitly in model parameters.
Using kNN-LM with the same training data for learning prefix representations and the kNN model improves performance, suggesting the prediction problem is more challenging than previously appreciated.
Using $L^{2}$ distance for FAISS retrieval results in better performance for kNN-LM compared to inner product distance.
kNN-LM substantially outperforms existing work on WIKITEXT-103
Gains from kNN-LM are additive with the related but orthogonal continuous cache
kNN-LM works well in multiple domains
A kNN-LM trained on 100M tokens with a datastore of 1.6B tokens already outperforms the LM trained on all 3B tokens.
kNN-LM allows a single model to be useful in multiple domains by simply adding a datastore per domain
Using the input to the final layer's feedforward network as the key function achieves the largest improvement in kNN-LM performance.
kNN-LM is most helpful for examples containing rare patterns such as factual knowledge, names, and near-duplicate sentences from the training set.
Interpolating the memorizing LM (no dropout) with the original LM improves validation perplexity by only 0.1, whereas kNN-LM improves it by 1.9.

kNN-LM improves performance because the Transformer learns a good representation function, and kNN-LM allows memorizing training data while retaining an effective similarity function, unlike implicit memorization which hurts generalization.
kNN-LMs can significantly outperform standard language models by directly querying training examples at test time
The nearest neighbors are computed according to distance in the pre-trained LM embedding space
The approach allows for effective domain adaptation by simply varying the nearest neighbor datastore without further training
The model is particularly helpful in predicting rare patterns, such as factual knowledge

Adding out-of-domain data to the datastore makes a single LM useful across multiple domains without further training.
The model is particularly helpful for long-tail patterns, such as factual knowledge, which might be easier to access via explicit memory.

findings.claim: Llama 3 delivers comparable quality to GPT-4 on a plethora of tasks
Integrating image, video, and speech capabilities into Llama 3 via a compositional approach performs competitively with the state-of-the-art on image, video, and speech recognition tasks
Llama 3 is a dense Transformer with 405B parameters and a context window of up to 128K tokens.
Llama 3 was pre-trained on a corpus of about 15T multilingual tokens, compared to 1.8T tokens for Llama 2.
The flagship Llama 3 model was pre-trained using $3.8 \times 10^{25}$ FLOPs, almost $50 \times$ more than the largest version of Llama 2.
The flagship Llama 3 model has 405B trainable parameters and was pre-trained on 15.6T text tokens.
Smaller Llama 3 models trained for much longer than compute-optimal perform better than compute-optimal models at the same inference budget.
Llama 3 uses a standard dense Transformer model architecture with minor adaptations rather than a mixture-of-experts model to maximize training stability.

Llama 3 adopts a post-training procedure based on supervised finetuning, rejection sampling, and direct preference optimization as opposed to more complex reinforcement learning algorithms that tend to be less stable and harder to scale.
The flagship Llama 3 model performs on par with leading language models such as GPT-4 across a variety of tasks.
Smaller Llama 3 models are best-in-class, outperforming alternative models with similar numbers of parameters.
Llama 3 delivers a much better balance between helpfulness and harmlessness than its predecessor.
Llama 3 models can answer questions in at least eight languages, write high-quality code, solve complex reasoning problems, and use tools out-of-the-box or in a zero-shot way.
The two-step scaling law prediction slightly underestimates the final performance of the flagship Llama 3 model.
With the described optimizations, Llama 3 can be pre-trained on sequences of 8K tokens without activation checkpointing.
About 78% of unexpected interruptions during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training were attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues.
For Llama 3, the effective training time achieved was higher than 90% while supporting automated cluster maintenance.
Increasing the percentage of non-English data during pre-training improves the multilingual performance of Llama 3.
Llama 3 is trained on more complex tasks compared to Llama 2, suggested by an increase in the average length of prompt and response.
Rejection sampling did not result in observed gains in tool benchmarks for Llama 3.
A knowledge probing technique is developed that takes advantage of Llama 3’s in-context abilities.
Llama 3 pre-trained language models are very robust to changes in MCQ labels and to the structure of the few-shot prompt labels.
Llama 3 pre-trained language models, in particular Llama 3 405B, are robust to answer order and prompt format.
Llama 3 8B and 70B variants outperform other models of similar sizes on general knowledge tasks
Llama 3 405B model outperforms GPT-4 and Nemotron 4 340B on general knowledge tasks
All Llama 3 variants outperform comparable models on IFEval
Llama 3 models demonstrate perfect needle retrieval performance, successfully retrieving 100% of needles at all document depths and context lengths.
Llama 3 models achieve near perfect retrieval results on Multi-needle.
Llama 3 405B and 70B models either match or surpass other models on various tasks in the ZeroSCROLLS benchmark.
The Llama 3 405B model outperforms all others on En.QA and En.MC in InfiniteBench.
Llama 3 variants perform the best on Nexus compared to their counterparts
Llama 3 8B and 70B models outperform other models in their category on API-Bank by a significant margin
Llama 3 405B and 70B models perform competitively on BFCL and are close second in their respective size class
Llama 3 has new capabilities that lack sufficient external benchmarks in terms of breadth and depth.
Llama 3 does not have significant susceptibilities in generating malicious code or exploiting vulnerabilities.
Larger Llama 3 models generate more insecure code and code with a higher average BLEU score.
Llama 3 does not outperform commonly used, traditional non-LLM tools and techniques in identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities.
Llama 3 70B and 405B fail to effectively use network reconnaissance information to gain initial access to the vulnerable machine.
Attempts to execute exploits and post-exploit actions were entirely unsuccessful for Llama 3 70B and 405B.
There is no significant uplift in performance related to usage of the Llama 3 model in CBRNE attack planning scenarios.

findings.claim: MetaICL outperforms a range of baselines including in-context learning without meta-training and multi-task learning followed by zero-shot transfer.
The gains of MetaICL are particularly significant for target tasks that have domain shifts from the meta-training tasks.
Using a diverse set of the meta-training tasks is key to improvements in MetaICL.
MetaICL approaches (and sometimes beats) the performance of models fully finetuned on the target task.
MetaICL outperforms much bigger models with nearly 8x parameters.
MetaICL is complementary to human-written instructions, and the best performance can be achieved by combining both approaches.
MetaICL tunes a pretrained language model on a large set of tasks to learn how to in-context learn, evaluated on strictly new unseen tasks.
Finetuning the model in the MetaICL data setup leads to better in-context learning by learning to recover task semantics from examples.
MetaICL allows learning new tasks from k examples alone without relying on task reformatting or task-specific templates.
MetaICL experiments use 142 NLP datasets from Ye et al. (2021) and Khashabi et al. (2020).
MetaICL consistently outperforms baselines including LM in-context learning without meta-training and multi-task learning followed by zero-shot transfer.
MetaICL enables the model to recover the semantics of the task in context during inference even when the target does not share similarities with meta-training tasks.
MetaICL often gets close to or beats the performance of models trained with supervised finetuning on the target datasets.
MetaICL performs as well as models with 8x parameters.
MetaICL without any templates is better than recent work using human-written natural instructions.
The best performance is achieved by combining MetaICL with human-written natural instructions.
MetaICL achieves substantial improvements even with smaller LMs by explicitly training on an in-context learning objective.
MetaICL effectively learns semantics of a new task with no manual effort, significantly outperforming zero-shot transfer methods.
MetaICL demonstrates improvements with a much smaller model (770M).
MetaICL uses a multi-task learning scheme over a large collection of meta-training tasks to learn how to condition on a small set of training examples, recover task semantics, and predict output.
MetaICL training is drastically more efficient than recent prior work (e.g., Sanh et al., 2022).

findings.claim: LLaVA-OneVision is the first single model that can simultaneously push the performance boundaries of open LMMs in single-image, multi-image, and video scenarios.
The design of LLaVA-OneVision allows strong transfer learning across different modalities/scenarios, yielding new emerging capabilities.
LLaVA-OneVision improves the performance boundaries of open LMMs in single-image, multi-image, and video scenarios
LLaVA-OneVision demonstrates strong video understanding through task transfer from images
LLaVA-OneVision-72B yields superior performance between GPT-4V and GPT-4o on most benchmarks
A relatively larger gap remains in complex tasks such as visual chat scenarios for LLaVA-OneVision
LLaVA-OneVision surpasses GPT-4V and approaches the performance level of GPT-4o on Chart, Diagram, and Document Understanding benchmarks.
LLaVA-OneVision significantly outperforms GPT-4V on various perception and reasoning benchmarks and is comparable to GPT-4o on MathVista.

LLaVA-OneVision achieves competitive performance with open-source models of similar parameter size on real-world understanding and visual chat benchmarks, though it has room for improvement compared to GPT-4V and GPT-4o.
LLaVA-OneVision performs well on MM-LiveBench, demonstrating broad world knowledge and strong generalization abilities.
After additional tuning on multi-image and video data, LLaVA-OneVision shows a marked improvement over GPT-4V in specific areas, with significant margins.
LLaVA-OneVision demonstrates strong performance in complex tasks such as multi-image reasoning, identifying differences, and understanding 3D environments.
LLaVA-OneVision is capable of understanding and reasoning over the joint of diagram and chart, a task not appearing in multi-image training data.
LLaVA-OneVision recognizes GUI screenshots of an iPhone and provides operational instructions to search for and open the TikTok app.
LLaVA-OneVision demonstrates excellent set-of-marks (SoM) reasoning, which is hypothesized to be composed by visual referring and OCR.
LLaVA-OneVision is the first open LMM to report good emerged SoM ability.
LLaVA-OneVision can generate detailed video creation prompts based on a static image, generalizing from the composition of single-image editing instruction and video detailed description tasks.
LLaVA-OneVision extends the capability of understanding differences in images to videos, analyzing differences between two video sequences.
LLaVA-OneVision can analyze and interpret multi-camera video footage from self-driving cars, describing each view and planning the ego car's next move.
LLaVA-OneVision generalizes to vertical videos with two sub-scenes, understanding and describing the content and layout of a composed sub-video.
LLaVA-OneVision displays the capability of understanding visual prompts in videos without training on video data with visual prompts.
LLaVA-OneVision is a new, open LMM that shines when transferred to a broad range of tasks in the scenarios of single-image, multi-image and videos.
LLaVA-OneVision is trained by scaling the recipe with a larger dataset and stronger LLMs.
LMMs trained with the open recipe and resources of LLaVA-OneVision achieve state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks.
LLaVA-OneVision exhibits excellent set-of-mark prompting capabilities, ie, referring to marks when answering questions.
LLaVA-OneVision learns to generate detailed video creation prompts based on a static image.
LLaVA-OneVision learns to analyze differences between videos with the same starting frame but different endings.
LLaVA-OneVision learns to analyze differences between videos with similar backgrounds but different foreground objects.
LLaVA-OneVision consolidates insights from previous explorations and implements the new model with available compute without extensively de-risking individual components.
LLaVA-OneVision (SI) consistently outperforms existing multi-image LMMs in all benchmarks.
Strong video understanding and cross-scenario capabilities are demonstrated through task transfer from images to videos.
Stronger LLM typically supercharge stronger multimodal capabilities in the wild
The scaling of resolution is more effective than that of token numbers for visual input representation.
Representing an image with a long sequence that mimics video representation facilitates a smoother capability transfer from image to video understanding.
For video representation, bilinear interpolation to reduce tokens per frame provides a better trade-off between performance and computational cost.
Given a limited compute budget, focusing on high-quality knowledge learning is recommended over scaling low-quality web-scale data to maximize compute efficiency.
99.8% of the high-quality knowledge data used is synthetic due to the high cost and copyright constraints of collecting large-scale high-quality data in the wild.
A stronger image model can better transfer to multi-image and video tasks.
